title: xTech|Kinetic Reach Competition
summary: The U.S. Army is seeking innovative force sustainment solutions from eligible small businesses across the U.S. through the xTech Kinetic Reach competition. This platform offers participants the opportunity to engage with the Department of War (DoW), earn prize money and submit a Direct to Phase II Army Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) proposal.
description:
Objective:
The U.S. Army is seeking innovative force sustainment solutions from eligible small businesses across the U.S. through the xTech Kinetic Reach competition. This platform offers participants the opportunity to engage with the Department of War (DoW), earn prize money and submit a Direct to Phase II Army Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) proposal.

The U.S. Army FUZE xTech Program, in partnership with the U.S. Army Europe and Africa (USAREUR-AF) and Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate (G-TEAD) is executing the xTech|Kinetic Reach competition as part of the G-TEAD Accelerated Capability Event (ACE) series. xTech|Kinetic Reach addresses the growing uncrewed aerial system (UAS) threat by identifying high-potential solutions and accelerating transition through funding and integration into live USAREUR-AF-led exercises. Integrating into a USAREUR-AF-led exercise is critical to: (1) validate capabilities under operationally realistic conditions, (2) inform acquisition and integration decisions, and (3) address near-term gaps in autonomous ground operations and effects delivery in contested environments.

The Army recognizes that the DoW must enhance engagements with U.S. small businesses by (1) understanding the spectrum of world-class technologies being developed commercially that may benefit the DoW; (2) integrating the sector of non-traditional innovators into the DoW Science and Technology (S&T) ecosystem; and (3) providing expertise and feedback to accelerate, mature, and transition technologies of interest to the DoW.

Description:
xTech|Kinetic Reach is a focused open-topic competition designed to identify cutting-edge technology solutions that will drive significant advancements in military capabilities while addressing complex challenges and enhancing national security. In largescale combat operations, U.S. Army forces must sustain dispersed, continuously moving formations while operating inside highly contested environments characterized by persistent observation, long range fires, electromagnetic interference, degraded mobility corridors, and severely constrained logistics. Current sustainment and recovery methods rely heavily on manned systems that are increasingly vulnerable, slow to adapt, and unable to meet the demands of operations conducted near or within the Autonomous Zone. The Army requires a suite of interoperable, autonomous or minimally manned capabilities - spanning ground and air distribution, power generation, forward arming and refueling, and vehicle recovery - that can operate with minimal oversight, low signatures, reduced logistical burden, and seamless command and control (C2) integration. These capabilities must sustain tempo, reduce soldier exposure, and ensure survivability and mission continuity across the entire sustainment and recovery enterprise in high-threat, GPS and communications degraded environments where traditional methods are no longer feasible or survivable.

The Army is seeking to evaluate capabilities that demonstrate performance in one of six (6) capability areas, and meet the following criteria for its capability area:

Topic 1: Uncrewed Ground Payload Transportation

Topic 2: Autonomous container Handling/Movement System

Topic 3: Future Power Generation

Topic 4: Autonomous UAV/UGV Forward Arming and Refueling Point (FARP) System

Topic 5: Uncrewed Aerial Payload Transportation

Topic 6: Uncrewed, Automated, Ground Recovery System

Full competition details including details on these 6 topic areas of interest can be found in Appendix A section of the xTech|Kinetic Reach competition RFI here: https://www.xtech.army.mil/competitions/.

The U.S. Army intends to award up to $1,500,000 in cash prizes throughout the competition. Up to 15 finalists will be selected at the conclusion of the Part 1 evaluation period and will be provided the opportunity to participate in the Part 2 live Soldier exercise, anticipated to occur in November 2026. Finalists who attend the Soldier exercise will receive a cash prize of $25,000, following the event. Finalists who also participate and have their technology integrated in the exercise will receive an additional $25,000, following the event. Following completion of the exercise, up to five (5) final winners will be selected to receive an additional cash prize of $150,000 each. Final winners may be considered for potential follow-on agreements and contracting opportunities. Part 2 winners that qualify as U.S. Small Businesses will have the opportunity to submit a Direct to Phase II Army SBIR proposal worth up to $2,000,000.

Phase I:
This topic is accepting Direct-to-Phase II submissions with a cost limit of $2,000,000 and a period of performance of 12-18 months. Only winners of the xTech|Kinetic Reach competition are permitted to submit a proposal for this topic. In order for proposers to submit a DP2 proposal, they must provide the justification documentation to substantiate that the scientific and technical merit and feasibility described above has been met and describes the potential military and/or commercial applications. Documentation should include all relevant information including, but not limited to: technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results.

Phase II:
Produce prototype solutions that will be easy to operate by a Soldier. These products will be provided to select Army units for testing and experimentation with end Users in a realistic field environment. Feedback from testing and experimentation will be provided directly to Small Businesses to iterate rapidly on recommended modifications or improvements for Army operational use. In addition, companies will work with Army partners to develop a draft technology transition and commercialization plan for DoW and commercial markets.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Complete the maturation of the company’s technology developed in Phase II to TRL 8/9 and produce prototypes to support scaling and fielding of the technology with the Army and pursue commercialization pathways.

title: Ground-Based Affordable Mass (G-BAM)
summary: The United States currently faces an "unprecedented" military buildup by China and increasing air and missile threats that demand a robust deterrent. However, the current inventory of long-range strike weapons is dominated by high-cost, low-volume systems or aging strategic assets like the Minuteman III, which dates back to the 1960s.
description:
Objective:
The United States currently faces an "unprecedented" military buildup by China and increasing air and missile threats that demand a robust deterrent. However, the current inventory of long-range strike weapons is dominated by high-cost, low-volume systems or aging strategic assets like the Minuteman III, which dates back to the 1960s. The lack of a cost-effective, ground-launched payload delivery system prevents the Joint Force from achieving producibility at scale, leaving the U.S. vulnerable in high-intensity, multi-domain environments where high-end munitions would be rapidly depleted. The objective of this topic is to facilitate innovative research on low-cost, rapidly manufacturable, payload delivery systems.

Description:
The Department of War (DoW) is pivotally shifting toward "affordable mass" to counter peer adversaries who are rapidly expanding their military capabilities. While hypersonic systems offer high speeds, their exorbitant costs—exceeding $50 million per round—limit the military's ability to achieve the "magazine depth" necessary for prolonged conflict. This project proposes a ground-based, non-hypersonic, long-range precision payload delivery system that leverages low-cost production methods and commercial technologies to provide a scalable, high-volume alternative that is a tenth of the price of current high-end munitions. NOTE: The following topic number, ARM26BX04-DV011 – Ground-Based Affordable Mass (G-BAM), in this release is tied to a Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) Challenge Commercial Solutions Openings. The DIU G-BAM Challenge will be used to identify small business concerns that meet the criteria for a potential SBIR Direct-to-Phase II (DP2) award under this topic. Winners selected from the DIU G-BAM Challenge will be the only firms eligible to submit an SBIR DP2 proposal under this topic. Proposals submitted to this topic by non-winners of the DIU G-BAM Challenge will not be evaluated.

How to Apply: Visit the DIU Open Solicitations page to read the full Challenge Announcement, topic details, and application instructions here:

https://www.diu.mil/work-with-us/open-solicitations

Phase I:
This topic is accepting Direct to Phase II submissions for a cost limit up to $2,000,000 and an 18-24-month period of performance.

Phase II:
This topic is a DP2 topic. In order for proposers to submit a DP2 proposal, they must provide justification documentation to substantiate that the scientific and technical merit and feasibility described above has been met and describes the potential military and/or commercial applications. Documentation should include all relevant information including, but not limited to: technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results. This justification must be provided during the DIU G-BAM Challenge in order to be selected as a winner and eligible to submit a DP2 proposal under this topic The results from the DIU G-BAM Challenge demonstration event, will be used to determine eligibility for DP2.

The objectives during Phase II are to produce prototype solutions that will be easy to operate by a Soldier. These products will be provided to select Army or other Department of War (DoW) units for testing and experimentation with end Users in a realistic field environment. Feedback from testing and experimentation will be provided directly to Small Businesses to iterate rapidly on recommended modifications or improvements for Army operational use. In addition, companies will work with Army partners to develop a draft technology transition and commercialization plan for DoW and commercial markets. Prototype capabilities sought include:

• Cost Efficiency: Cost-per-effect below $500K based on system reliability and mission success rate, with a sub-$250K all-up flyaway cost at scale.
• Producibility: Demonstrate a company manufacturing process capable of producing 100+ units monthly (1,200+ annually), or a credible path to that rate.
• Operational Range: Validate a ground-launched range with an objective of 600+ nm, consistent with DIU’s Area of Interest (AoI) Statement stated preference for extended-range effects.
• Employment: Should not require the Army to develop or modify other systems for employment. Should be a “plug and play” system that easily integrates with existing transport, targeting, and situational awareness systems.
• Payload: Deliver a payload capacity of at least 35 pounds, with a strong preference for greater than 100 pounds.
• Survivability: Demonstrate mission-capability in Denied, Disrupted, Intermittent, and Limited (DDIL) and electronic-warfare (EW)-contested environments.

Reliability: Demonstrate reliability and mission success under representative operational conditions.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The sub-system technologies developed for low-cost, long-range payload delivery have significant applications in the civilian/commercial aerospace and logistics sectors. The artificial intelligence (AI) and autonomous navigation systems required for these munitions can be adapted for commercial cargo delivery drones and autonomous maritime vessels. Additionally, the push for additive manufacturing and rapid prototyping in the Indo-Pacific region to support these systems can revitalize domestic high-tech manufacturing, providing private companies with advanced production techniques that reduce costs for civilian infrastructure projects. Additionally, this space lends itself to the potential for development of low-cost alternate fuel technologies. Companies participating in the shoot-off are encouraged to propose tech development for manufacturing methods materials/guidance/seekers/alt propulsion, etc. to enhance their products. These are the primary opportunities for commercialization.

title: xTech|Search 10 Competition
summary: xTechSearch is an open-topic competition designed to identify groundbreaking technologies with strong commercial traction that may also provide game-changing capabilities for the Army. This competition will be used to competitively down-select up to 16 finalists who can submit a Phase I Army SBIR proposal for a potential follow-on award of up to $300,000.
description:
Objective:
xTechSearch is an open-topic competition designed to identify groundbreaking technologies with strong commercial traction that may also provide game-changing capabilities for the Army. This competition will be used to competitively down-select up to 16 finalists who can submit a Phase I Army SBIR proposal for a potential follow-on award of up to $300,000.

Description:
The SBIR|STTR Program has aligned technologies that are experiencing rapid commercial traction with critical Army priorities into four portfolios of priority interest for this competition, each with core technology components identified. While xTech|Search encourages submissions aligned to the following SBIR|STTR portfolios and the associated core technology components, the program also welcomes proposals in any other technology domain with the potential to provide a disruptive advantage to the Army:

• Sensors: Electronic devices used to measure physical parameters, often enabling enhanced automation through the Internet of Things.
• Immersive and Wearables: Integration or extension of the real world through digital or simulated reality, such as augmented, virtual, and mixed reality. Wearables focus on smart electronic devices that can be worn by or attached to the user to gather data or provide insight during mission operations.
• AI/ML: Technology that incorporates human intelligence into machines (AI) and allows machines to learn from data without explicit programming (ML).
• Contested Logistics and Sustainment: Strategic and operational technologies that involve planning and executing the movement and maintenance of forces and materials under adversarial conditions.

Note: The topic listed below is part of the xTech|Search 10 Prize Competition. See the full xTech|Search 10 competition RFI here: https://www.xtech.army.mil/competitions/.

xTech|Search 10 will be used to identify small business concerns that meet the criteria for award. Finalists selected from the xTech|Search 10 prize competition will be the only firms eligible to submit a SBIR proposal under the topic listed above. Proposals submitted to the topic listed above by non-finalists or non-participants of the xTech|Search 10 competition will not be evaluated.

Phase I:
This topic is accepting Phase I submissions for a cost limit of $300,000 and a 6-month period of performance. Only finalists of the xTech|Search 10 competition are permitted to submit a phase I proposal for this topic.

Companies will complete a feasibility study that demonstrates the firm’s competitive technical advantage relative to other commercial products (if other products exist) and develop concept plans for how the company’s technology can be applied to Army modernization priority areas. Studies should clearly detail and identify a firm’s technology at both the individual component and system levels, provide supporting literature for technical feasibility, highlight existing performance data, showcase the technology’s application opportunities to a broad base of customers outside the defense space, a market strategy for the commercial space, how the technology directly addresses the Army’s modernization area as well as include a technology development roadmap to demonstrate scientific and engineering viability.

At the end of Phase I, the company will be required to provide a concept demonstration of their technology to demonstrate a high probability that continued design and development will result in a Phase II mature product.

Phase II:
Produce prototype solutions that will be easy to operate by a Soldier. These products will be provided to select Army units for further evaluation by the soldiers. In addition, companies will provide a technology transition and commercialization plan for DOD and commercial markets.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Complete the maturation of the company’s technology developed in Phase II to TRL 6/7 and produce prototypes to support further development and commercialization. The Army will evaluate each product in a realistic field environment and provide small solutions to stakeholders for further evaluation. Based on soldier evaluations in the field, companies will be requested to update the previously delivered prototypes to meet final design configuration.

References:
• https://www.xtech.army.mil/competitions/

title: Command Electromagnetic Management & Command-node Awareness, Management, and Obscuration (CEMA CAMO)
summary: Develop and demonstrate Command Electromagnetic Management & Command-node Awareness, Management, and Obscuration (CEMA CAMO), a low-cost, distributed, and attritable electromagnetic spectrum capability that enhances Command Post Survivability and RF Signature Management during Large-Scale Combat Operations (LSCO).
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate Command Electromagnetic Management & Command-node Awareness, Management, and Obscuration (CEMA CAMO), a low-cost, distributed, and attritable electromagnetic spectrum capability that enhances Command Post Survivability and RF Signature Management during Large-Scale Combat Operations (LSCO). The desired capability will employ distributed, software-configurable nodes to sense and shape the electromagnetic environment, creating controlled electromagnetic ambiguity that complicates adversary intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), reduces targeting confidence, and degrades adversary decision-making and targeting cycles while preserving friendly freedom of maneuver. The capability will be demonstrated in partnership with Joint Innovation Out Post (JIOP) through XVIII Airborne Corps (XVIII ABC) experimentation to assess operational effectiveness, inform capability refinement, and demonstrate integration with Army formations and command-and-control architectures.

Description:
Army formations, including XVIII Airborne Corps (XVIII ABC) and its subordinate formations, operating in Large-Scale Combat Operations (LSCO) face increasingly capable adversary intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) systems that can exploit electromagnetic emissions to detect, characterize, locate, and target command posts, platforms, and other mission-critical nodes. The proliferation of networked sensors and increasingly rapid sensor-to-shooter processes creates a need for affordable and scalable capabilities that reduce the effectiveness of adversary electromagnetic sensing and targeting.

XVIII ABC requires capabilities that can be rapidly employed and distributed across formations to improve electromagnetic signature management and enhance survivability and freedom of maneuver in contested environments. This topic seeks innovative approaches for Command Electromagnetic Management & Command-node Awareness, Management, and Obscuration (CEMA CAMO), a low-cost, modular, distributed, and attritable capability for electromagnetic signature management. The desired solution should enable multiple software-configurable nodes to operate cooperatively across an operational area to sense the local electromagnetic environment and generate controlled electromagnetic activity that increases ambiguity and uncertainty for adversary ISR and targeting processes. Potential approaches may include distributed electromagnetic signature shaping, configurable RF effects representations, coordinated emissions, and adaptive management of distributed nodes. Proposed solutions should address the ability to sense and characterize the local electromagnetic environment, coordinate activity across distributed nodes, generate Government-authorized RF effects representations, and dynamically adapt system behavior as the electromagnetic environment changes.

The solution should emphasize low cost, low size, weight, and power (SWaP), modularity, scalability, software configurability, distributed operation, and interoperability with Army command-and-control architectures at Corp and Division. Innovative approaches to autonomous coordination, AI-enabled processing, electromagnetic environment awareness, and dynamic signature management are encouraged. The capability should be scalable from individual nodes to distributed networks and adaptable to different platforms and operational environments. Offerors should characterize key trades including frequency coverage, bandwidth, processing requirements, network latency and synchronization, RF-generation capability, SWaP, node density, and unit cost. Solutions should demonstrate a credible pathway toward a fielded node cost below $50,000, with $30,000 desired where technically feasible.

The desired outcome is a prototype capability that demonstrates how XVIII ABC and Army formations can employ distributed, attritable electromagnetic spectrum technologies to improve survivability and freedom of maneuver by complicating adversary ISR, reducing confidence in electromagnetic-derived targeting information, and degrading adversary decision-making and targeting cycles during LSCO.

Throughout the SBIR|STTR Phase I and Phase II, CEMA CAMO prototype capabilities will be demonstrated in partnership with Joint Innovation Out Post (JIOP) through XVIII Airborne Corps (XVIII ABC) experimentation to assess operational effectiveness, inform capability refinement, and demonstrate integration with Army formations and command-and-control architectures.

Phase I:
This topic is accepting Phase I submissions with a cost limit of $300,000 and a period of performance of 6 months. Phase I will establish the technical approach and develop an initial CEMA CAMO prototype leveraging mature technologies, including software-defined radios, modular RF front ends, low-SWaP computing, distributed networking, and AI-enabled signal processing. The effort should demonstrate automated electromagnetic sensing and characterization, software-configurable generation or regeneration of Government-authorized RF effects representations, coordinated operation of multiple distributed nodes, and automated or AI-enabled adaptation of node behavior. The effort should also characterize key performance, SWaP, networking, and cost trades, including a preliminary hardware architecture and bill of materials. Proposed solutions should also address resilient operation under degraded communications or loss of individual nodes and approaches for protecting or sanitizing sensitive mission data, software, and configuration information in the event of physical capture or compromise. Experimentation should align, where prototype maturity and contracting timelines permit, with anticipated Scarlet Dragon opportunities tentatively planned for April and August 2027 at Ft. Bragg, NC, and other XVIII ABC-supported experimentation opportunities. Specific dates, locations, and objectives for experimentation may shift based on operational priorities, exercise schedules, prototype maturity, and Government direction.

Phase II:
Phase II will design, integrate, test, and mature a CEMA CAMO prototype for Warfighter integration and continued experimentation through Joint Innovation Out Post (JIOP)and XVIII Airborne Corps (XVIII ABC). The prototype will demonstrate distributed electromagnetic sensing and RF signature-management capabilities in representative LSCO scenarios focused on Command Post Survivability and complicating adversary ISR and targeting. Experimentation will build on Phase I activities and leverage Scarlet Dragon and other XVIII ABC experimentation opportunities, as available, to assess performance, refine capabilities, and inform operational integration. The effort will culminate in prototype delivery to the Warfighter, performance assessment, documented results, and continued maturation and transition to MEMSS.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
CEMA CAMO technologies may have commercial applications where distributed, low-cost electromagnetic sensing and spectrum awareness are required. Potential uses include wireless network monitoring, spectrum management, interference detection and localization, critical infrastructure spectrum awareness, communications testing, and distributed RF monitoring. The modular hardware, software-defined architecture, edge processing, and distributed sensing capabilities may also support commercial telecommunications, utilities, transportation, and industrial wireless networks.

title: Battle Damage Indications / Battle Damage Assessment Collection, Aggregation, and Analytics Improvement
summary: To accelerate decision-making and enhance space domain awareness across the joint force, the United States Space Force (USSF) requires an advanced data fusion and automated analytics platform.
description:
Objective:
To accelerate decision-making and enhance space domain awareness across the joint force, the United States Space Force (USSF) requires an advanced data fusion and automated analytics platform. This effort will deliver integrated collection, aggregation, and analytics software capabilities that automate multiple heterogeneous sensor and telemetry sources and telemetry sources into a unified Battle Damage Indication and Assessment (BDI/A) data store Ontology to optimize the Tasking, Collection, Processing, Exploitation, and Dissemination (TCPED) lifecycle. Targeted solution will execute automated cross-domain event correlation, implement a dynamic confidence scoring framework with user-adjustable thresholds, provide explainable Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML) diagnostics reaching >80% agreement with Government analysts, and supply a role-based user interface supporting tactical, operational, strategic, and Intelligence Community (IC) workflows.

Description:
To preserve decision advantage during contested-space operations, the United States Space Force (USSF) must rapidly correlate multi-source operational data to streamline Phase 5 (Mission Planning & Force Execution) and Phase 6 (Assessment) of the Space Tasking Cycle (STC) and Joint Targeting Cycle (JTC). The Space Systems Command (SSC) System Delta 85 (SYD 85) Program Management Office (PMO) and the Kronos Program of Record (PoR), in support of the Battle Management, Command, Control, Communications, and Space Intelligence Portfolio Acquisition Executive (BMC3I PAE), is seeking software-based solutions for the BMC3I TAP Lab (Tools, Applications, & Processing) to automate, aggregate, and score multi-phenomenology collection activities in a standardized, Unclassified environment designed for the eventual seamless scaling to classified operational networks. Within this request, there are 5 associated subtasks:

• Automated ingestion and schema mapping of multiple heterogeneous sensor and telemetry sources telemetry and sensor sources into a common BDI/A data store Ontology definition model while preserving metadata and timestamp traceability;
• Cross-domain synchronization and analytics of Electro-Optical/Infra-Red (EO/IR), Radio Frequency (RF), and Radar data products (such as resolved/unresolved observations, Doppler Residuals, and Area-to-Mass Ratio datasets) to detect pre-defined anomalous behaviors using configurable threat signatures;
• Execution of a dynamic, multi-phenomenology confidence scoring framework that evaluates collection source reliability and sensor quality metrics;
• Development of user-friendly, explainable AI/ML-assisted correlation diagnostics that expose the underlying analytical rationale to human operators to assist in target adjudication; and
• Delivery of a segmented user interface enabling Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) to isolate and execute workflows across the four distinct echelons of the BDI/A lifecycle (Tactical BDI, BDA Phase 1, BDA Phase 2, and BDA Phase 3).

Sample inputs include;

- Real-time or historical feeds;

- Ground- and space-based multi-phenomenology sensor data (commercial and government);

- Historical event repositories for change detection; and

- Simulated operational event logs.

Possible techniques may include but are not limited to;

- Automated schema mapping and metadata parsing;

- Change detection algorithms against historical patterns of life;

- Multi-hypothesis data association and Kalman filtering; and

- Explainable AI (XAI) natural language explanation generation.

The software product must be designed to integrate with existing and legacy Mission Unique Software (MUS) toolchains, publishing assessments back to source repositories via standardized application programming interfaces (APIs) and meeting all development requirements for future transition to secure operational networks.

Phase I:
: Phase I will focus on establishing the scientific, technical, and operational feasibility of the proposed automated, multi-phenomenology BDI/A collection, aggregation, and analytics capability. The primary objective is to validate the product-mission fit and construct a high-fidelity conceptual architecture for the unified BDI/A data store Ontology and cross-domain correlation engine. During the Phase I feasibility study, the small business concern (SBC) must:

• Identify and collaborate with specific United States Space Force (USSF) and U.S. Air Force stakeholders, operational end-users, and technical transition partners (aligning with Space Forces-Space (S4S), National Space Defense Center (NSDC), Combined Space Operations Center (CSpOC), Space Force Deltas, and the Intelligence Community) to map existing BDI/A workflows, data formats, and classification boundaries.
• Develop a comprehensive technical architecture and data schema for the proposed BDI/A Ontology, outlining how the system will ingest and normalize multiple heterogeneous sensor and telemetry sources and sensor sources (such as TT&C, RF, optical, and radar datasets) without losing source metadata or timestamp traceability.
• Define the algorithmic approach for multi-phenomenology sensor fusion, change detection, dynamic confidence scoring, and explainable AI/ML correlation models, detailing how the software will communicate its analytical reasoning to human operators to achieve >80% agreement with Government analysts.
• Create an integration and cybersecurity plan detailing how the proposed capability will interface with legacy and novel Mission Unique Software (MUS), comply with Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) frameworks, and transition from an Unclassified proof-of-concept environment to TS//SCI Classified networks.
• Formulate a commercialization strategy demonstrating how these decentralized analytics, multi-source fusion algorithms, and diagnostic user interfaces can be commercialized for private space operators, commercial satellite fleet managers, and space logistics providers.

The Phase I effort must culminate in a detailed feasibility study report and a low-fidelity mock-up or architectural software proof-of-concept validating user experience flows for the four distinct echelons of the BDI/A warfighting lifecycle.

Phase II:
Phase II will focus on developing, refining, and validating the software capabilities outlined in the Phase I feasibility study within the BMC3I TAP Lab testing environment. Specifically, Phase II aims to deliver the fully functional BDI/A data store Ontology, multi-phenomenology collection and aggregation engine, and dynamic confidence scoring framework, maturing the overall solution to a target technology readiness level (TRL) 7/8. The development process will require multiple heterogeneous sensor and telemetry sources, establishing automated schema mapping, and implementing real-time event correlation algorithms. The software must prove capable of detecting pre-defined anomalous signatures using configurable threat parameters, displaying event sequencing dependencies, and enabling deep-dive drill-down traceability to the originating raw data records. Evaluators will test the system's performance using realistic historical and simulated operational scenario runs, verifying that the AI/ML correlation recommendations and dynamic scoring outputs achieve >80% agreement with validated Government analyst assessments. The final operational assessment will require demonstrating thirty (30) days of continuous, high-availability operations on representative networks to ensure seamless integration with the Kronos PoR. The platform will undergo sustained operational assessments on representative networks, establishing a verified baseline of operational reliability and mission-essential resilience.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Potential Phase III efforts will focus on scaling and transitioning the matured BDI/A collection, aggregation, and scoring capabilities directly to operational joint targeting and space tasking systems under designated Programs of Record. Successful solutions will transition to TS//SCI Classified environments to automate target adjudication and operations assessment reporting for S4S, CSpOC, NSDC, USSC, and their IC partners. This ensures a rapid, automated flow from tactical BDI events to strategic and national-level BDA Phase 1, 2, and 3 intelligence outputs, significantly accelerating the targeting cycle loop.

Additionally, the technologies developed under this topic have dual-use potential within the commercial space sector. Commercial satellite fleet operators, mega-constellation managers, and space situational awareness (SSA) service providers require robust, automated systems to conduct vehicle health diagnostics and anomaly resolution. When commercial satellites experience sudden subsystem dropouts or structural degradation (due to orbital debris collisions, space weather events, or local RF interference), operators must quickly assess the damage, isolate the cause, and adjust operational risk postures. Applying this multi-source data fusion, change detection, and explainable AI-assisted scoring algorithms allows commercial operators to automate damage assessment pipelines, lower telemetry analysis overhead, and streamline insurance claim validations, directly increasing the safety and survivability of commercial orbital assets.

References:
• bmc3itaplab.space

title: Reusable Illumination System
summary: The technology within this topic is restricted under the International Traffic in Arms Regulation (ITAR), 22 CFR Parts 120-130, which controls the export and import of defense-related material and services, including export of sensitive technical data, or the Export Administration Regulation (EAR), 15 CFR Parts 730-774, which controls dual use items.
description:
Objective:
The technology within this topic is restricted under the International Traffic in Arms Regulation (ITAR), 22 CFR Parts 120-130, which controls the export and import of defense-related material and services, including export of sensitive technical data, or the Export Administration Regulation (EAR), 15 CFR Parts 730-774, which controls dual use items. Develop a reusable illumination system for high-speed photo-optic data collection used at the Holloman High Speed Test Track (HHSTT) and other sled test tracks.

Description:
The PF300 flash bulbs, that provide high-intensity illumination for high-speed video acquisition, are no longer in production. The objective is to award a contract to a small business to engineer, design, and manufacture a modern, robust, reusable replacement for the legacy PF300 flash bulb. This new system must meet or surpass the existing illumination and performance requirements of the original flash bulbs to ensure seamless integration with current high-speed video systems. The ideal solution would leverage Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) or near-COTS technologies to qualify this project as a direct-to-Phase-II effort. A successful reusable replacement would immediately solve the impending obsolescence issue, securing a reliable illumination source for future missions. Furthermore, transitioning to a reusable system would dramatically reduce consumable cost. This technological update could also pave the way for enhanced capabilities, such as adjustable light intensity and longer duration illumination, offering greater flexibility and improved data quality for high-speed video analysis across various applications

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made as a result of this topic. Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work. Prior “Phase I-type” work by other companies has produced similar illumination methods, but not to the requirements needed to operate in the Test Track Environment. The technology exists, but the operating environment of the Test Track is unique enough there is not a readily available product. The Test Track is ready to define requirements up to, but not limited to illumination levels, illumination duration, connectivity and ruggedness.

Phase II:
The Phase II effort should develop a detailed design and operational procedures for a prototype reusable illumination system that meets requirements established by 846 TS Customers. Component level prototypes will be developed and tested to validate performance and mitigate risks prior to the development of the complete system prototype. The Phase II effort will culminate with the demonstration of an operational reusable illumination sled on the test track. The demonstration shall showcase the performance and reusability of the system.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The Phase III effort should further refine the illumination system design following lessons learned from the Phase II demonstration. The matured system should be ready for operational use at the HHSTT as well as other DoW test tracks. Phase III may involve follow-on non-SBIR/STTR funded R&D or production contracts for products, processes or services intended for use by the U.S. Government.

title: Technical Data Package Modernization for Information Assurance and Secure Data Exchange
summary: The technology within this topic is restricted under the International Traffic in Arms Regulation (ITAR), 22 CFR Parts 120-130, which controls the export and import of defense-related material and services, including export of sensitive technical data, or the Export Administration Regulation (EAR), 15 CFR Parts 730-774, which controls dual use items.
description:
Objective:
The technology within this topic is restricted under the International Traffic in Arms Regulation (ITAR), 22 CFR Parts 120-130, which controls the export and import of defense-related material and services, including export of sensitive technical data, or the Export Administration Regulation (EAR), 15 CFR Parts 730-774, which controls dual use items. Offerors must disclose any proposed use of foreign nationals (FNs), their country(ies) of origin, the type of visa or work permit possessed, and the statement of work (SOW) tasks intended for accomplishment by the FN(s) in accordance with section 3.5 of the Announcement. Offerors are advised foreign nationals proposed to perform on this topic may be restricted due to the technical data under US Export Control Laws.

The objective of this Directed to Phase II (D2P2) SBIR effort is to develop an innovative, secure, and scalable solution for modernizing Technical Data Packages (TDPs) associated with complex Air and Space Force platforms. This initiative seeks to address challenges in managing large, diverse datasets by enhancing configuration control, ensuring data integrity, and strengthening Information Assurance (IA) in support of mission-critical operations. Specifically, the focus of this phase is to demonstrate the feasibility of advanced technologies that enable secure data lifecycle management and seamless data exchange within operational environments. Proposed solutions should align with Trusted AI and Autonomy modernization priorities by incorporating robust cybersecurity measures and leveraging cutting-edge advancements in autonomy, data management, and secure manufacturing capabilities. Outcomes of this phase are expected to validate technical concepts and establish a functional prototype that meets the operational imperative of readiness to deploy and fight, contributing to future scalability and transition opportunities in operational use cases.

Description:
Background and Problem Statement:

The modernization of Technical Data Packages (TDPs) is imperative to address the Air and Space Force’s operational challenges in securely managing large-scale, complex datasets associated with advanced platforms and their sustainment life cycles. Current TDP systems often lack robust Information Assurance (IA) capabilities, seamless integration with Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) environments, and effective mechanisms for secure data exchange across operational networks. This limitation not only hinders data integrity and configuration control but also increases vulnerabilities to cyber threats, jeopardizing mission-critical operations. The rapid pace of platform evolution and the increasing reliance on Model-Based Definition (MBD) and digital twin technologies further exacerbate the need for a comprehensive solution that ensures TDP security, scalability, and operational readiness.

Opportunity and Desired Outcome:

This Directed to Phase II (D2P2) SBIR effort aims to develop an innovative, scalable, and secure solution to modernize TDPs to support the lifecycle of highly complex Air and Space Force platforms. The envisioned solution will integrate advanced IA protocols, cryptographic protections, and tools for encrypted data exchange to facilitate the secure management of the "as-sustained" configuration state of critical assets. The outcome will be a functional prototype capable of enabling secure TDP lifecycle management while aligning with the Trusted AI and Autonomy modernization priorities and Zero Trust Architecture principles. The proposed solution will enhance operational efficiency, minimize cyber risks, and establish a foundation for scalable implementation across DoD platforms.

The project’s Technology Readiness Level (TRL) at the start is anticipated to be TRL 4, with the target of reaching a minimum TRL 6 by the conclusion of Phase II, including validation of core capabilities in a relevant operational environment.

Required Efforts and Phase Activities:

To achieve the stated objectives, the following efforts and activities are required for each phase of the project:

Phase II:

Develop a secure visualization tool for displaying large-scale MBD geometry and associated data through encrypted web-based interfaces.

Implement an encrypted configuration management system to maintain and update the "as-sustained" asset state while ensuring strict data integrity.

Create advanced tools for automated data quality checks, incorporating rules-based IA compliance validation to ensure all TDPs meet security and contractual requirements.

Design an end-to-end encrypted exchange framework for TDPs, incorporating user authentication, authorization, and audit trails while conforming to DoD Zero Trust Architecture guidelines.

Integrate AI/ML methodologies to enable secure damage detection, sustainment planning, and actionable insights into asset health.

Demonstrate the prototype in an operationally relevant environment, proving feasibility, security compliance, and system performance in handling large and diverse data streams.

Minimum Deliverables:

A secure web-based MBD visualization prototype capable of rendering large-scale geometry and TDP datasets with sub-second response times and role-based access controls.

Tools for encrypted configuration management and secure "as-sustained" state maintenance, integrated with PLM systems.

An automated framework for data quality checks and IA compliance validation of TDPs using defined security protocols and rules-based engines.

A cryptographic data transfer and exchange framework, with test results demonstrating alignment with DoD security policies and successful inter-organizational data exchange.

Technical documentation detailing methodologies, system architecture, and IA protocols implemented during the project, including recommendations for further scaling and operationalization.

A transition plan for integrating the developed TDP modernization technology into operational environments within the Air and Space Force platforms, supported by a detailed commercialization strategy aligned with mission needs.

Significance and Contribution to DoD Objectives:

The proposed solution directly addresses the Operational Imperative 7—Readiness to Deploy and Fight—by delivering secure and reliable tools for managing critical asset data. The project also supports the DoD’s Trusted AI and Autonomy priorities by incorporating advanced data protection mechanisms, secure autonomous processes, and scalable solutions for data management across platforms. Successful execution of this effort will enhance the DoD’s ability to maintain readiness, ensure data security, and streamline collaboration with stakeholders while safeguarding sensitive information in a rapidly evolving threat landscape.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work, demonstrating clear technical merit, alignment with Trusted AI/Autonomy priorities, and DoD Zero Trust standards, such as validated data, performance metrics, technical reports, prototype success, or demonstrated capabilities in relevant operational environments.

Phase II:
The Phase II effort will deliver a secure, scalable prototype for modernizing Technical Data Packages (TDPs). Focus areas include encrypted configuration management, MBD visualization tools, automated IA compliance frameworks, and secure data exchange via Zero Trust Architecture. The solution will achieve TRL 6 with validated performance in operational environments, aiding readiness and alignment with Trusted AI and Autonomy priorities.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The Phase III effort will advance the secure TDP modernization prototype to TRL 8, employing non-SBIR funds to integrate with Air and Space Force systems. Military applications include secure lifecycle management of technical data for advanced platforms, enhancing readiness and cybersecurity. Commercial use spans aerospace, manufacturing, and defense industries for data security and configuration management. Transition efforts target expanded adoption within DoD and allied partners.

References:

• DoDI 8500.01 Cybersecurity, 2020, highlighting policies and strategies for enhancing Information Assurance (IA) within DoD systems and operational environments.
• DoD Modernization Strategy Report, 2023, emphasizing priorities in Trusted AI, autonomy, and secure data management as critical focus areas for advancing mission readiness and operational deployment capabilities.
• Technical Guide: "Model-Based Definition (MBD) for Digital Engineering Transformation," Air Force Institute of Technology, 2022, exploring the application of MBD in enhancing data handling and lifecycle integration processes.
• SBIR Policy Directive, May 2023, detailing requirements for transitioning innovative solutions from development to deployment in alignment with operational imperatives and DoD’s modernization priorities.
• Technical Report: "Leveraging AI/ML for Predictive Maintenance in Aerospace Systems," AFRL, 2021, discussing secure data analytics approaches in maintaining integrity and enhancing sustainment of DoD platforms.
• DoD CIO Cybersecurity Discipline Implementation Plan, March 2023, focusing on cryptography, identity management, and secure data exchange practices ensuring resilience against cyber threats.

title: US Production of Ultra-High Temperature Ceramic-Yielding Preceramic Polymers
summary: The Department of the Air Force seeks to establish the domestic production of ultra-high temperature ceramic (UHTC)-yielding preceramic polymers. UHTCs are used for demanding aerospace applications, including propulsion and aeroshell components.
description:
Objective:
The Department of the Air Force seeks to establish the domestic production of ultra-high temperature ceramic (UHTC)-yielding preceramic polymers. UHTCs are used for demanding aerospace applications, including propulsion and aeroshell components.

Description:
The scaled production of C/C-UHTCs composites (UHTCMCs) for defense applications requires the manufacturing of UHTC precursors in quantities sufficient to support acquisition programs. This SBIR will establish production of an AFRL-patented UHTC preceramic polymers so that the materials are available, at scale and affordable price point, to the high-temperature composite production community.

Phase I:
This topic is intended for technologies ready to move directly into a Phase II program. As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work. Offerors must provide detailed documentation in their Direct to Phase II (D2P2) proposal that demonstrates the successful completion of a "Phase I-like" effort. This includes a feasibility study showing expertise in synthesizing and handling air/water-sensitive chemical compounds. Demonstrated experience in scaling chemical synthesis processes from the lab to pilot scale (e.g., 5-50 kg batches) is required. The feasibility study should clearly illustrate past successes in producing high-purity materials and a foundational understanding of the safety protocols necessary for handling the relevant precursors and reagents.

Phase II:
During the Phase II program, the awardee shall: 1) Establish and document a safe, robust, and scalable chemical process for the manufacturing of the AFRL-patented UHTC-bearing preceramic polymers that meets specified purity and production volume targets. 2) Conduct a thorough safety and handling analysis for all reagents, intermediates, and waste products. Production facilities must ensure safety and environmental compliance are permissible. 3) Deliver a 5x 1 kg samples of the UHTC preceramic polymer to AFRL for internal analysis, characterization, and quality verification. The offeror shall show i) for the produced polymer: NMR, elemental analysis, rheology, and ICP/MS of the produced polymer and ii) for the polymer-derived ceramic XRD, TEM/EDS, and SEM analysis, for each lot of material made. The offeror can assume a cost of $6300/kg in raw material cost if reagents, were to be purchased from commercial chemical suppliers, to produce UHTC preceramic polymers. 4) Establish and demonstrate a dedicated production capability yielding at least 50 kg per month (>600 kg per year). 5) Deliver a total of 75 kg of the qualified UHTC preceramic polymer, appropriately packaged, to the Government by the end of the Phase II effort. 6) Provide a comprehensive cost analysis and business plan for UHTC-bearing preceramic polymer production at the target scale of >1000 kg/year a target retail price of <$5000/kg, preferably <$4000/kg, identifying key supply-chain or processing factors to drive down per-kilogram costs.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The awardee will be expected to transition the preceramic polymer production established during Phase II into a viable commercial business unit. This will involve supplying certified preceramic polymers to prime contractors and Tier 1/2 composite manufacturers supporting defense and commercial programs of record. Phase III efforts may include further scaling of chemical operations, qualifying the material across a broader vendor base (for high-speed aeroshells), and establishing long-term supply agreements to support critical national security missions.

Zhu, et al., “Progress in preparation and ablation resistance of ultra-high-temperature ceramics modified C/C composites for extreme environment”, Reviews on Advanced Materials Science, 62, 20220276, 2023

title: Low SWaP, 2-micron Fiber Amplifiers
summary: Develop and demonstrate a rugged, kilowatt class 2-micron fiber amplifier module that matches size, weight, and power metrics of state-of-the-art 1-micron systems to accelerate the transition of laboratory technology to operational Department of the Air Force capabilities.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate a rugged, kilowatt class 2-micron fiber amplifier module that matches size, weight, and power metrics of state-of-the-art 1-micron systems to accelerate the transition of laboratory technology to operational Department of the Air Force capabilities.

Description:
High-power fiber lasers operating in the 2-micron regime offer critical advantages for defense, medical, and industrial applications, including eye-safer directed energy, advanced sensing, and precision materials processing. While kilowatt-class, narrow-linewidth thulium-doped fiber amplifiers have been demonstrated, the Department of the Air Force aims to reduce the size and weight of existing kilowatt-class 2-micron fiber amplifiers into a highly compact system with similar size, weight, and power metrics of existing 1-micron fiber amplifiers. This topic seeks to leverage existing Air Force laboratory architectures to prime industry for production of robust 2-micron fiber amplifiers, paving the way for transition into active directed energy programs.

Phase I:
This topic is intended for technologies ready to move directly into a Phase II program. As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work. Applicant(s) should provide documentation demonstrating a clear understanding of high power, 2-micron fiber amplifier design, thermal management in constrained operating spaces, and package ruggedization for high-stress environments. Qualifying 'Phase I-type' efforts would include but not limited to the prior design, development, and demonstration of low SWaP, kilowatt-class, 1-micron fiber amplifier modules.

Phase II:
In Phase II, the USAF requires the execution, physical build, and delivery of a fully functional, low SWaP, 2-micron fiber amplifier prototype. This system must deliver kilowatt-class output while complying with the mandatory low-SWaP requirements of state-of-the-art 1-micron fiber amplifiers. The delivered hardware must undergo laboratory verification to validate output power (> 1 kW), beam quality (M2 < 1.2), spectral stability, narrow linewidth (< 5 GHz), and electro-optical efficiency (E-O > 25%). Final deliverables for this effort must include the physical prototype, complete electrical and optical schematics, and a comprehensive test and characterization report.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III success will be driven by transitioning the 2-micron fiber amplifier design into full-rate production and securing commercial market pathways.Additionally, work on the system-level integration of the proven 2-micron fiber amplifier into a deployable, multi-kW laser defense system for real-world environmental validation.

References:
• B. M. Anderson, J. Solomon, and A. Flores, “1.1 kW beam-combinable thulium doped all-fiber amplifier,” Proc. SPIE 11665 (2021).
