title: High-Efficiency Expeditionary Group 2 and Group 3 VTOL UAS for Long-Range Distributed ISR/SOF Operations
summary: Develop, mature, integrate, and flight-demonstrate technologies enabling an autonomous, runway-independent Group 2/3 VTOL UAS capable of persistent ISR/SOF operations, extended-duration flight, modular payload employment, resilient beyond-line-of-sight communications, and integration into distributed mission architectures.
description:
Objective:
Develop, mature, integrate, and flight-demonstrate technologies enabling an autonomous, runway-independent Group 2/3 VTOL UAS capable of persistent ISR/SOF operations, extended-duration flight, modular payload employment, resilient beyond-line-of-sight communications, and integration into distributed mission architectures.

Description:
Runway independence provides substantial operational flexibility for ISR/SOF missions but creates significant technical penalties in aircraft weight, propulsion complexity, energy consumption, endurance, payload, reliability, and cost. The research challenge is to minimize these penalties while enabling a persistent, expeditionary autonomous aircraft capable of operating from austere and distributed locations. The Government seeks emerging VTOL technologies combining reliable vertical operations with efficient forward flight, extended endurance, useful payload capacity, resilient communications, and autonomous mission execution. Solutions may employ tilt-wing, tilt-rotor, lift-plus-cruise, tailsitter, distributed propulsion, hybrid propulsion, or other technically viable architectures. Companies should specifically highlight demonstrated capabilities, current maturity, projected performance, and remaining technical risks in the following areas:

VTOL Endurance: Capability to achieve 12-15 hours of flight time is critical. Offerors should identify payload, speed, altitude, loiter profile, environmental assumptions, and propulsion configuration associated with demonstrated or projected endurance. Propulsion: Gas-powered propulsion is of particular interest for meeting extended sortie-duration requirements. Fully electric, hybrid-electric, or alternative propulsion solutions are acceptable if they can meet the required sortie duration and mission-performance objectives. In-Flight Recharge: Technologies enabling in-flight energy replenishment or recharge are of interest, including architectures supporting a six B.A. battery configuration, where applicable. Payload: Adjustable and modular payload capacity with a minimum desired capability greater than 60 pounds while maintaining an 12-15-hour loiter/endurance profile. Offerors should additionally characterize performance and design tradeoffs associated with payload growth toward 75 pounds.

Network Node / Layered Effects / Force Packaging: Ability to operate as an airborne network node and participate in distributed, layered effects and multi-platform force packages. BLOS: Resilient beyond-line-of-sight communications and autonomous mission execution without reliance upon continuous line-of-sight C2. Vigilant Spirit: Existing integration, interoperability, or a clearly defined integration pathway with Vigilant Spirit. Dynamic Targeting: Ability to receive mission updates and dynamically retask, revisit/retest areas or objects of interest, reassess previous observations or effects, and conduct authorized subsequent mission actions. NKE / ESM: Ability to host, support, and employ modular non-kinetic effects and Electronic Support Measures payloads. Extended Autonomy: Architecture capable of supporting autonomous missions approaching 15 hours, including reliable operation for representative periods of at least 5 minutes without human intervention. Companies should characterize autonomy reliability, intervention rate, failure modes, contingency behavior, recovery, and lost-link performance. VTOL Efficiency Demonstrate autonomous vertical takeoff and recovery. Quantify hover and VTOL fuel/energy consumption. Demonstrate efficient transition between vertical and forward flight. Quantify VTOL energy penalty relative to total mission energy. Range and Endurance Demonstrate or substantiate a credible path to8 hours of flight endurance with representative payload. Characterize mission radius, maximum range, endurance, and loiter time. Quantify payload/range/endurance trade space. Characterize forward-flight propulsion efficiency. Identify fuel or energy requirements associated with representative ISR/SOF mission profiles. For fully electric systems, demonstrate the ability to achieve required sortie duration. Where proposed, characterize in-flight recharge or energy replenishment. Payload and Mission Systems Support an adjustable/modular payload of at least 25 pounds at the desired 8-hour profile. Characterize growth potential toward60 pounds. Characterize payload mass, volume, power, data, thermal, RF, and mechanical interfaces. Support Government or third-party payload integration. Support NKE and ESM payloads. Support airborne network-node functionality. Provide documented interfaces supporting integration with Vigilant Spirit and other Government mission systems. Expeditionary Operations

Minimize launch/recovery footprint. Minimize personnel and ground-support equipment. Minimize arrival-to-launch and recovery-to-relaunch timelines. Minimize assembly, disassembly, maintenance, and site-preparation requirements. Support distributed ISR/SOF employment from austere locations. Autonomy and Dynamic Mission Execution Autonomous takeoff and landing. Autonomous transition. Autonomous navigation, loiter, mission execution, return, and precision recovery. Dynamic inflight mission retasking. Support dynamic targeting and authorized retest/revisit and reattack/re-engagement sequences. Deterministic contingency and lost-link behavior. Architecture capable of missions approaching12 hours of autonomous operation. Demonstrate representative mission periods of at least5 minutes without human intervention. Characterize autonomy reliability, intervention frequency, mission-completion rate, fault tolerance, failure modes, and recovery behavior. Resilient Communications and Operations

Maintain useful navigation and mission capability during GNSS degradation or loss. Support BLOS communications and mission operations. Maintain autonomous mission capability during intermittent, degraded, or lost C2. Demonstrate deterministic lost-link behavior. Support network-node functionality within distributed force packages. Exchange mission, sensor, platform-status, and targeting information with Government systems. Affordability and Producibility Quantify projected recurring unit cost. Identify major cost drivers. Demonstrate production-relevant manufacturing. Quantify manufacturing labor, lead time, supply-chain constraints, and scalable production rate. The Government seeks existing aircraft and enabling technologies requiring engineering maturation and integration. Clean-sheet aircraft without demonstrated underlying flight technology are not the target of this effort.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. To qualify, applicant(s) must provide Feasibility Documentation demonstrating prior completion of Phase I-equivalent efforts outside SBIR funding. Offerors shall demonstrate prior technical work establishing feasibility of the proposed aircraft and critical enabling technologies. Relevant evidence may include: VTOL flight demonstrations. Autonomous takeoff/recovery. Transition-flight demonstrations. Forward-flight performance data. Propulsion testing. Range and endurance testing. Payload flight testing. Autonomous mission demonstrations. Degraded-PNT demonstrations. BLOS communications testing. Structural/environ mental testing. Prototype manufacturing. Hardware-in-the-loop or system-level testing. Network-node or collaborative mission demonstrations. Dynamic inflight retasking. NKE or ESM payload integration. Vigilant Spirit or comparable Government mission-system integration. In-flight energy recharge/replenishment where proposed. Offerors should specifically provide available data characterizing: Maximum demonstrated VTOL endurance and associated payload. Ability or technical path to achieve 8 hours of flight time. Propulsion architecture and fuel/energy consumption. Payload/endurance trade space, including performance with 60-pound and larger payloads. BLOS communications performance. Autonomous mission duration and reliability. Frequency and nature of required human intervention. Network-node or distributed force-package functionality. Dynamic targeting/retest/reattack functionality. NKE/ESM integration capability. Vigilant Spirit integration status or pathway. Offerors shall identify remaining technical risks associated with VTOL efficiency, endurance, payload, propulsion, autonomy, communications, mission-system integration, affordability, and production.

Preferred entry maturity is TRL 4–5, with demonstrated TRL 5 hardware considered where a credible maturation pathway exists toward TRL 6-8. This remains consistent with the original WIS topic.

Phase II:
The technical effort shall use progressive ground and flight testing and culminate in the integrated expeditionary performance flight demonstration within the period of performance. Task 1 – Engineering Maturation and System Integration Resolve identified technical risks and integrate a flightworthy system incorporating propulsion, autonomy, navigation, communications, modular payload interfaces, networking, and production-relevant hardware. Task 2 – Vertical Launch/Recovery Efficiency and Transition Demonstration. Demonstrate autonomous vertical takeoff and precision vertical recovery from an unprepared or space-constrained operating location, followed by efficient transition to and from wing-borne forward flight. Sustained hover or hover-based mission execution is not required. Measure fuel or energy consumed during launch, transition, and recovery and quantify the vertical-lift penalty relative to the complete representative mission profile. Task 3 – Endurance, Range and Payload Demonstration Flight-demonstrate endurance, mission radius, range, payload capacity, loiter performance, cruise efficiency, and relevant trade spaces. The critical Government area of interest is 12-15 hours of flight endurance. Demonstrate or provide measured evidence supporting performance with a representative mission payload and characterize performance with a minimum desired 60-pound payload, including trade space associated with growth toward 75 pounds.

Task 4 – Propulsion and Energy Management Characterize propulsion performance across the representative mission profile. Gas-powered, hybrid, electric, or alternative architectures may be demonstrated provided they satisfy operational endurance requirements. Where proposed, demonstrate in-flight energy recharge or replenishment, including the applicable six-battery architecture. Task 5 – Autonomous Mission and Dynamic Retasking Demonstration Demonstrate autonomous vertical takeoff, transition, navigation, loiter in efficient forward flight, mission execution, inflight retasking, return, and precision vertical recovery; sustained hover is not required. Demonstrate representative autonomous mission periods of at least 5 minutes without human intervention, characterize reliability and intervention requirements, and demonstrate the architecture's ability to support missions approaching 12 hours of autonomous operation. Task 6 – BLOS and Resilient C2 Demonstration Demonstrate useful autonomous mission performance during BLOS operations and representative GNSS/C2 degradation, including intermittent connectivity and lost-link conditions. Task 7 – Networked and Layered Effects Demonstration Demonstrate operation as an airborne network node within a representative distributed force package. Characterize the ability to exchange mission, sensor, status, and targeting data with other platforms and Government mission systems. Task 8 – Mission-System and Payload Integration Integrate and fly at least one representative Government-relevant payload or approved surrogate. Demonstrate documented interfaces supporting NKE/ESM payloads and provide a Government-acceptable Vigilant Spirit integration demonstration or transition pathway. Task 9 – Dynamic Targeting Demonstration Demonstrate receipt and execution of authorized inflight mission updates, including representative dynamic retasking, revisit/retest, reassessment, and subsequent mission action.

Task 10 – Expeditionary Operations Demonstration Demonstrate: Transport → Setup → Launch → Mission → Recover → Turnaround → Relaunch/Relocate Measure personnel, equipment, footprint, setup time, turnaround time, maintenance actions, and fuel/energy requirements. Task 11 – Manufacturing and Cost Maturation Use prototype fabrication to validate manufacturing processes, labor requirements, production lead time, supply-chain risks, projected recurring cost, and production scalability.

Task 12 – Delivery of final systems to designated units for government owned, goverment operated specific feedback. Desired Phase II End State The demonstrated concept shall provide runway-independent vertical launch and recovery and required to sustain hover during mission execution. A flight-demonstrated autonomous VTOL UAS at approximately TRL 4-5 or greater, supported by measured data characterizing:

12-15 hour endurance performance. Mission radius and maximum range. Payload at representative endurance. 60-pound payload performance and growth potential toward 75 pounds. Propulsion efficiency. In-flight recharge performance, where applicable. BLOS performance. Network-node functionality. Vigilant Spirit integration. NKE/ESM payload integration. Dynamic retasking/retest/reattack capability. Autonomous mission duration. Human intervention requirements. Autonomy reliability.PNT resilience. Expeditionary footprint. Personnel requirements. Setup and turnaround time. Projected recurring unit cost. Production rate. Manufacturing labor. Primary technical measure of merit: useful ISR/SOF mission capability and payload delivered over extended mission duration relative to total system cost and expeditionary footprint.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Successful technology is intended to provide AFSOC, ACC, and operational organizations a rapidly fieldable VTOL aircraft capability with NKE or alternative payload integration with employment and a reusable modular integration pathway for future electronic-warfare, communications, sensing, processing, and self-protection payloads. The transition owner is PAE ISR SOF / Asymmetrical Warfare Division – WISS. The VTOL system is intended to support future adaptation to additional platforms through further NKE integration, loiter requirements, and minimized cost burden. Follow-on funding is exploratory from AFSOC based on D2P2 results.

title: Collaborative Autonomous UAS for Distributed Non-Kinetic Effects
summary: Develop, integrate, and demonstrate modular technologies enabling Group 2/3 UAS or similarly expendable autonomous aircraft to collaboratively generate distributed non-kinetic mission effects in contested environments.
description:
Objective:
Develop, integrate, and demonstrate modular technologies enabling Group 2/3 UAS or similarly expendable autonomous aircraft to collaboratively generate distributed non-kinetic mission effects in contested environments.

The objective is to enable multiple low-cost autonomous platforms to coordinate sensing, positioning, task allocation, timing, communications, and payload employment to produce useful mission-level effects without requiring continuous human control or persistent high-bandwidth communications.

The desired architecture should employ a human-on-the-loop approach, allowing autonomous systems to conduct distributed mission execution while retaining oversight, positive control, and the ability for human operators to intervene when required.

The Government is particularly interested in technologies that distribute mission capability across multiple affordable aircraft rather than concentrating sensing, processing, communications, or effects on a single exquisite platform.

Description:
Traditional non-kinetic capabilities can be constrained by platform availability, cost, survivability, operator workload, communications requirements, and centralized mission architectures.

Distributed autonomous UAS create the opportunity to separate the mission effect from a single exquisite platform and distribute sensing, decision-making, communications, and payload employment across multiple lower-cost aircraft.

The Government seeks modular technologies enabling Group 2/3 UAS and similarly expendable autonomous aircraft to collaboratively carry and employ Government-approved non-kinetic payloads while operating under a human-on-the-loop command architecture.

Potential mission functions may include lawful and authorized:

Electronic support. Communications relay. Spectrum sensing. Deception and decoy functions. Distributed RF effects. Cooperative sensing. Network extension. Authorized cyber-physical mission effects. Signature generation. Mission-support effects. Other non-destructive effects.

This topic is focused on enabling technologies, payload integration, distributed autonomy, mission coordination, and command-and-control architecture, not development of offensive cyber capabilities.

Fundamental engineering considerations include:

Modular Mission Systems

Modular payload integration. Open mechanical, electrical, power, data, RF, and software interfaces. Integration of Government or third-party payloads without fundamental aircraft redesign. Support for multiple payload types and aircraft architectures. Low-SWaP-C implementation suitable for expendable UAS.

Collaborative Autonomy

Autonomous task allocation. Collaborative mission planning and execution. Distributed decision-making. Dynamic reassignment of tasks following aircraft or payload loss. Cooperative sensing and information sharing. Graceful degradation as individual aircraft become unavailable. Quantifiable collaborative mission performance.

Human-on-the-Loop Control

Human-on-the-loop mission command and authorization. Positive control over initiation and termination of mission effects. Operator ability to modify objectives, constraints, or mission priorities. Deterministic responses to loss of communications. Abort and safe-state functionality. Appropriate human authorization for mission functions requiring Government approval.

Communications and Distributed Operations

Operation with intermittent, degraded, or unavailable communications. Distributed decision-making without persistent centralized control. Low-bandwidth coordination methods. Time and spatial synchronization. Network extension and relay capability. Resilient interfaces with Government mission and C2 systems.

Mission Assurance

Geographical, temporal, frequency, target-set, or mission-based constraints as applicable. Prevention of unintended or unauthorized effects. Defined operating boundaries. Fault detection and graceful degradation. Quantifiable reliability and mission-effect performance.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. To qualify, applicant(s) must provide Feasibility Documentation demonstrating prior completion of Phase I-equivalent efforts outside SBIR funding. Offerors should possess existing technology applicable to autonomous UAS, collaborative autonomy, spectrum operations, modular payloads, resilient communications, electronic support, distributed mission systems, human-machine teaming, or related capabilities.

Phase I-equivalent evidence may include:

Hardware demonstrations. Flight demonstrations. Collaborative autonomy testing. Multi-aircraft demonstrations. Modular payload integration. Electronic support or spectrum-sensing demonstrations. Communications relay or network-extension demonstrations. Distributed task-allocation demonstrations. Human-on-the-loop mission-control demonstrations. Degraded-communications testing. Hardware-in-the-loop or system-level testing. Relevant modeling supported by physical test data. Operational experimentation.

Offerors should identify:

Number and type of aircraft previously demonstrated collaboratively. Level and duration of autonomous operation. Human intervention requirements. Communications architecture and bandwidth requirements. Behavior during communications degradation or loss. Payload interfaces. Supported non-kinetic mission functions. Current aircraft and payload SWaP-C. Collaborative autonomy reliability. Current TRL and remaining technical risks.

Preferred entry maturity is TRL 5-6, with TRL 4 considered where the core technology has been demonstrated and can credibly mature within approximately three years.

Phase II:
The technical effort shall culminate in the multi-aircraft collaborative flight demonstration described in Task 6 within the period of performance.

Task 1 – Open Mission Architecture Define and implement modular interfaces among aircraft, autonomy software, operators, mission-planning systems, communications networks, and Government-approved payloads.

Document mechanical, electrical, power, RF, data, software, and command interfaces necessary to support additional aircraft and payloads.

Task 2 – Collaborative Autonomy Develop and integrate distributed task allocation, aircraft coordination, synchronization, cooperative behaviors, and degraded-communications mission execution.

Demonstrate the ability for the collaborative system to dynamically adapt to changes in aircraft availability, communications, sensor information, mission priorities, and payload availability.

Task 3 – Non-Kinetic Payload Integration Integrate one or more representative Government-approved non-kinetic payloads or suitable surrogates.

Characterize payload SWaP-C, aircraft interfaces, operator controls, and the ability to integrate additional payloads without fundamental redesign.

Task 4 – Human-on-the-Loop Mission Command and Effect Control Demonstrate a human-on-the-loop command architecture supporting autonomous execution while maintaining appropriate Government authorization and oversight.

Demonstrate:

Positive control. Authorization logic. Effect boundaries. Mission constraints. Abort functionality. Operator intervention. Deterministic lost-link behavior. Prevention of unintended or unauthorized mission effects.

Task 5 – Degraded Communications and Distributed Operations Demonstrate useful collaborative mission performance under representative communications degradation, intermittent connectivity, bandwidth constraints, and temporary loss of centralized C2.

Quantify communications requirements and the degree to which mission execution can continue without persistent connectivity.

Task 6 – Multi-Aircraft Collaborative Demonstration Conduct an operationally relevant demonstration involving multiple autonomous aircraft collaboratively generating a measurable Government-approved non-kinetic mission effect.

The demonstration should characterize:

Mission completion rate. Task-allocation performance. Coordination latency. Communications requirements. Human intervention rate. Effectiveness following loss of individual aircraft. Autonomy reliability. Mission-effect performance.

Task 7 – Raider Platform Integration and Transition Architecture

Integrate the collaborative-autonomy capability with the Government-designated Raider platform using Government-furnished or Government-authorized interfaces, data, facilities, and security guidance. Demonstrate end-to-end exchange of the mission-planning, command, status, timing, and payload-control data required for the representative mission. If physical flight aboard the Raider platform is not authorized within the period of performance, complete Government-witnessed hardware-in-the-loop or system-integration-laboratory verification using the authoritative Raider interfaces.

Document integration pathways for additional aircraft, payloads, mission-planning systems, C2 systems, and Government networks, including platform-specific modifications, cybersecurity, airworthiness, data/interface requirements, and remaining transition risks.

Desired Phase II End State

A TRL 7+ collaborative autonomous UAS architecture integrated with the Government-designated Raider platform and demonstrated using multiple Group 2/3 or similarly expendable aircraft and at least one representative Government-approved non-kinetic payload in an operationally relevant environment.

The system should demonstrate distributed autonomous mission execution, human-on-the-loop oversight, degraded-communications operation, modular payload integration, graceful degradation following individual-aircraft loss, and measurable mission-level performance.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Successful technology is intended to provide AFSOC, ACC, and operational organizations a rapidly fieldable NKE capability with payload integration ability and employment. This shall include a reusable modular integration pathway for future electronic-warfare, communications, sensing, processing, and self-protection payloads. The transition owner is PAE ISR SOF / Asymmetrical Warfare Division – WISS. The NKE capability is intended to support future adaptation to additional platforms through further integration and minimized cost burden. Follow-on funding is exploratory from AFSOC based on D2P2 results.

title: Long-Range, Expendable Autonomous Air Vehicle for Distributed Effects in Contested Environments
summary: Develop, integrate, flight-test, and demonstrate an affordable, expendable autonomous air “One-Way Attack” (OWA) vehicle capable of delivering a mission-relevant payload over operational ranges of 400 nautical miles threshold to 1,200 nautical miles at varying ranges in between while operating in communications-degraded and GNSS-degraded or denied environments.
description:
Objective:
Develop, integrate, flight-test, and demonstrate an affordable, expendable autonomous air “One-Way Attack” (OWA) vehicle capable of delivering a mission-relevant payload over operational ranges of 400 nautical miles threshold to 1,200 nautical miles at varying ranges in between while operating in communications-degraded and GNSS-degraded or denied environments.

Description:
Future contested operations may require the ability to generate large numbers of distributed airborne effects at ranges beyond those achievable by many existing Group 2/3 UAS.

The desired system should combine sufficient aerodynamic efficiency, propulsion performance, autonomous mission execution, modular payload integration, resilient navigation, and low-cost manufacturing to enable operations at ranges between approximately 400 and 1,200 NM.

Solutions should emphasize a modular vehicle architecture allowing Government or third-party payloads, autonomy, navigation, and communications components to be integrated without redesigning the entire aircraft.

Range and Mission Performance

≥400 NM threshold to 1,200 NM with demonstrable varying ranges under a clearly defined mission profile. Document payload/range/endurance trade space. Characterize representative payload, launch conditions, altitude, speed, propulsion configuration, and mission profile. Demonstrate sufficient aerodynamic and propulsion efficiency to achieve long-range operation at acceptable recurring cost.

Autonomous Mission Execution

Autonomous launch and transition to mission flight. Autonomous navigation and mission execution. Autonomous terminal mission functions appropriate to the proposed concept. Continued mission execution during intermittent or extended loss of command-and-control connectivity. Deterministic and configurable lost-link behavior. Mission-planning interfaces that minimize operator workload. Architecture capable of incorporating Government-provided autonomy.

Resilient Navigation

Maintain useful navigation during representative GNSS degradation, denial, interference, or loss. Characterize navigation performance, accumulated error, availability, and recovery. Support integration of complementary navigation sources. Collaborative navigation approaches are of interest where sufficiently mature for Phase II integration and flight demonstration. Navigation technologies should be mature enough to support the overall D2P2 schedule; maturation of 5-6 TRL fundamental navigation concepts is not the primary intent of this effort.

Modular Mission Architecture

Modular mechanical, electrical, power, data, and software interfaces. Integration of Government or third-party payloads without fundamental air-vehicle redesign. Architecture capable of accepting Government-provided autonomy, navigation, communications, and payload components. Document Government-accessible interfaces necessary for transition.

Propulsion

Characterize propulsion performance. Quantify fuel/energy consumption across representative mission profiles. Identify propulsion reliability and remaining maturation risks. Characterize range, payload, and propulsion trade space.

Environmental and Structural Performance

Demonstrate environmental and structural suitability for representative operational employment. Characterize launch loads, flight loads, environmental limitations, and relevant storage/transport constraints.

Affordability and Scalable Manufacturing

Treat recurring unit cost as a primary system-level design consideration. Identify major unit-cost drivers. Demonstrate production-relevant manufacturing approaches. Reduce dependence on scarce materials, specialized tooling, and labor-intensive production where technically feasible. Quantify production scalability, lead time, labor content, and supply-chain risks. Consider rapid, distributed, or high-rate manufacturing approaches.

The Government is interested in existing technologies requiring integration and maturation, not clean-sheet conceptual aircraft requiring extended basic research.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. To qualify, applicant(s) must provide Feasibility Documentation demonstrating prior completion of Phase I-equivalent efforts outside SBIR funding. Offerors should demonstrate Phase I-equivalent prior work establishing that the underlying air vehicle and critical subsystems are technically viable. Relevant evidence may include:

Existing aircraft or representative flight testing.

Long-range flight performance.

Propulsion testing.

Aerodynamic analysis supported by test data.

Autonomous flight demonstrations.

Resilient-navigation testing.

Collaborative-navigation demonstrations, where proposed.

Payload integration.

Structural and environmental testing.

Manufacturing demonstrations.

Hardware-in-the-loop or system-level testing.

Offerors should provide available measured data characterizing:

Current maximum demonstrated range.

Payload associated with demonstrated range.

Propulsion efficiency and fuel/energy consumption.

Aircraft aerodynamic performance.

Autonomous mission capability.

Performance under degraded or unavailable GNSS.

Lost-link and degraded-C2 behavior.

Payload interfaces.

Current recurring-cost estimate and principal cost drivers.

Manufacturing maturity and achievable production rate.

Phase II:
The technical effort shall use progressive ground and flight testing and culminate in the integrated mission-relevant flight demonstration described in Task 5 within the period of performance.

Task 1 – Vehicle and Mission Architecture

Baseline the aircraft, propulsion, payload, autonomy, communications, navigation, manufacturing, and mission-system architecture.

Document modular interfaces and identify remaining technical risks associated with meeting the desired range, payload, autonomy, resilient-navigation, cost, and production objectives.

Task 2 – Range and Propulsion Validation

Characterize aircraft aerodynamic and propulsion performance through progressively representative ground and flight testing.

Demonstrate the ability to satisfy the 400 NM threshold, with measurable progress toward the 1,200 NM objective.

Characterize:

Range. Payload. Endurance. Fuel/energy consumption. Propulsion reliability. Cruise efficiency. Relevant environmental factors. Payload/range/endurance trade space.

Task 3 – Autonomous and Degraded-Environment Operations

Demonstrate autonomous mission execution, resilient navigation, degraded-C2 operation, and deterministic lost-link behavior.

Testing should include representative:

GNSS degradation. GNSS denial/loss. Communications degradation. Extended loss of C2. Mission continuation. Recovery or terminal behavior.

Where sufficiently mature collaborative-navigation technology is proposed, integrate and characterize its contribution to navigation performance and mission resilience.

Task 4 – Modular Payload Integration

Integrate and demonstrate at least one representative Government-relevant payload or approved surrogate.

Validate modular:

Mechanical interfaces. Power. Data. Software. Communication Mission-system interfaces.

Demonstrate that additional payloads can be accommodated without fundamental redesign of the aircraft.

Task 5 – Integrated Flight Demonstration

Conduct progressively representative flight testing culminating in a mission-relevant demonstration of the integrated autonomous air vehicle.

The demonstration should characterize:

Operational range. Payload. Autonomous mission completion. Degraded-GNSS performance. Degraded-C2 performance. Propulsion performance. Reliability. Navigation error. Operator involvement.

Task 6 – Manufacturability, Cybersecurity and Transition

Demonstrate the production approach and quantify:

Projected recurring unit cost. Cost drivers. Manufacturing labor. Production lead time. Supply-chain risks. Production-rate scalability. Tooling requirements.

Develop cybersecurity and system-security artifacts required to support integration and an appropriate authorization pathway.

Document the proposed transition pathway and remaining platform-, mission-, airworthiness-, cybersecurity-, and production-related activities.

Desired Phase II End State

A flight-demonstrated autonomous air vehicle at approximately TRL 7 or greater, with measured performance sufficient to support follow-on operational evaluation and transition.

The prototype should have documented:

≥400 NM demonstrated range or Government-accepted evidence of threshold performance. Progress toward 1,200 NM objective. Representative payload performance. Autonomous mission performance. Resilient-navigation performance. Degraded-C2/lost-link behavior. Propulsion performance. Recurring-cost estimate. Production scalability. Modular mission-system interfaces.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Successful technology is intended to provide AFSOC, ACC, and operational organizations a rapidly fieldable OWA aircraft capability with payload integration. The transition owner is PAE ISR SOF / Asymmetrical Warfare Division – WISS. The OWA system is intended to support future adaptation to additional platforms through further payload integration, distance requirements, and minimized cost burden. Follow-on funding is exploratory from AFSOC based on D2P2 results.

title: Rapidly Reconfigurable Pod-Based System Survivability Suite for Air Operations in Contested Environments
summary: Investigate, design, prototype, and experimentally evaluate advanced open-architecture methodologies and reconfigurable subsystem integration concepts within an external modular pod construct (threshold baseline: Air Force Research Laboratory [AFRL] Agile Pod).
description:
Objective:
Investigate, design, prototype, and experimentally evaluate advanced open-architecture methodologies and reconfigurable subsystem integration concepts within an external modular pod construct (threshold baseline: Air Force Research Laboratory [AFRL] Agile Pod). The primary R&D objective is to explore novel approaches for abstracting platform-to-payload interdependencies, solving multi-physics obscuration and thermal/electromagnetic boundary problems, and demonstrating dynamic, autonomous self-protection threat-warning, correlation, and countermeasure techniques via distributed edge compute without requiring host-platform system recertification.

Description:
Modern multi-domain operational environments present increasingly agile, multi-spectral threat emitters spanning radio frequency (RF), infrared (IR), and electro-optical (EO) regimes. Conventional aircraft survivability equipment (ASE) suffers from hardwired, federated implementations, tightly coupled mechanical and electrical host dependencies, and high-latency upgrade cycles. Overcoming these barriers requires foundational research into containerized, hardware-agnostic modular payloads, high-efficiency edge processing architectures, and adaptive aperture configurations that can operate autonomously while remaining fully interoperable with joint command-and-control networks.

This topic solicits applied research and experimental development into an externally carried, modular open-system survivability architecture. While leveraging mature sensing and countermeasure components where appropriate, the primary technical investigation focuses on heterogeneous compute abstraction and advanced processing architectures. This entails researching novel architectural patterns that abstract diverse federated signal processing, countermeasure arbitration, threat correlation, and cross-platform networking into a unified, modular, software-defined compute environment. Key research activities include evaluating containerization paradigms, real-time deterministic virtualization, and Open Mission Systems / Universal Command and Control Interface (OMS/UCI) standard execution under strict size, weight, power, and thermal (SWaP-C) limitations.

Simultaneously, the effort must resolve multi-physics boundary constraints and sensor obscuration challenges. This requires developing high-fidelity analytical, computational fluid dynamic (CFD), and electro-optical/electromagnetic models to characterize and mitigate aircraft-induced obscuration and aero-optical distortion across diverse carriage regimes. Research will further focus on distributed aperture hand-off algorithms and multi-pod sensor correlation to synthesize complete, gapless spherical coverage (steradian field-of-regard) across heterogeneous, dynamic flight profiles.

Finally, the investigation addresses dynamic interoperability and low-latency autonomous response mechanisms. Investigation is needed into machine-to-machine autonomy algorithms capable of conducting real-time threat detection, localized track clustering, and immediate self-protection countermeasure dispense and pointing without operator-in-the-loop dependencies, while concurrently synthesizing threat telemetry for dissemination across communications links. Underpinning this entire capability is the design of open, non-proprietary physical and logical interface syntax aligned with Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA) guidelines to enable zero-rework substitution of future experimental payloads.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. To qualify, applicant(s) must provide Feasibility Documentation demonstrating prior completion of Phase I-equivalent efforts outside SBIR funding. Evidence must include: Architectural Trade Studies & Modeling (comparative performance models evaluating physical, thermal, and electrical integration of multi-spectral survivability components inside modular pod form factors), Algorithm & Interface Simulation (preliminary software simulations validating hardware abstraction layers, synthetic threat correlation pipelines, and OMS/UCI-compliant data schemas), Aero-Optical and Sensor Obscuration Analysis (ray-tracing, installed field-of-regard modeling, and host aircraft interaction analyses proving the conceptual viability of 360-degree coverage via single or distributed pod arrangements), and Bench-Scale Experimental Data (measured bench-test, hardware-in-the-loop (HWIL), or prototype range test results verifying core detection, processing latency, and countermeasure control feasibility).

Phase II:
During Phase II, the contractor shall advance the theoretical architecture and preliminary models into an experimental flight-research prototype using the AFRL Agile Pod framework, executing rigorous laboratory, environmental, captive-carry, and flight-test investigations. Initial efforts will focus on fabricating and bench-testing the experimental pod prototype, incorporating an integrated suite of advanced EO/IR threat sensors, directed infrared countermeasure (DIRCM) and countermeasure dispensing interfaces, and dedicated edge compute. This effort entails implementing and empirically evaluating non-proprietary, machine-readable data bus architectures and containerized processing blocks, specifically measuring execution latency, processor overhead, and bus contention during simulated high-density threat saturation events.

Concurrently, the contractor shall execute an extensive obscuration and field-of-regard experimentation program using ground rigs and environmental test chambers to validate sensor line-of-sight and optical sensitivity across diverse aircraft station mountings. This research must quantify blind sectors created by wing, engine, and airframe geometry, while experimentally validating predictive sensor-fusion and track-handoff algorithms designed to share situational awareness dynamically across multi-pod or off-board networks to compensate for airframe shadowing.

To resolve integration multi-physics boundaries, the prototype shall undergo environmental stress testing, thermal-vacuum profiling, structural vibration and shock characterization, and electromagnetic interference/compatibility (EMI/EMC) laboratory evaluations. These trials will establish the structural and vibrational limits of tightly coupled sensor payloads and evaluate innovative thermal dissipation strategies (including ram-air heat exchangers and conductive thermal management) for high-density compute cores operating in unconditioned external pod compartments.

Finally, the contractor shall conduct an instrumented captive-carry and flight-research campaign aboard a designated surrogate aircraft or research platform. Flight testing will collect empirical aerodynamic, structural, thermal, and sensor-tracking data under operational flight maneuvers, evaluating the autonomous threat detection, handoff latency, and countermeasure pointing accuracy of the integrated system against calibrated ground and airborne threat simulators. This campaign will also validate over-the-air modular communications links, demonstrating the capability to stream real-time sensor data, threat alerts, and system telemetry to ground control stations and networked mission nodes.

DELIVERABLES AND TECHNICAL DATA:

Deliverables under this effort encompass experimental flight-hardware prototypes, modular software pipelines, architectural standards documentation, and empirical research datasets. The contractor shall deliver one or more flight-representative experimental pod systems integrated with reconfigurable edge-compute chassis, power conditioning modules, and active threat-warning and countermeasure payloads. Accompanying software deliverables must include all underlying source code, container definitions, firmware configurations, and algorithmic models governing sensor fusion, threat arbitration, and interface abstractions.

To ensure non-proprietary extensibility, the contractor shall provide comprehensive, open Interface Control Documents (ICDs), machine-readable schemas, and interface syntax definitions that enable independent third parties and future researchers to integrate alternative sensors and payloads without architectural rework. Technical data deliverables must also include complete empirical test datasets and scientific reports spanning computational fluid dynamics and wind-tunnel evaluations, bench-scale and hardware-in-the-loop test logs, EMI/EMC compatibility reports, environmental thermal logs, and full flight-test telemetry. Finally, the contractor shall provide an R&D Transition and Maturation Roadmap detailing remaining technical risks, manufacturing readiness metrics, airworthiness qualification deltas, and scaling strategies for transition into operational defense acquisition programs.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Successful technology is intended to provide AFCENT, ACC, and operational organizations a rapidly fieldable aircraft-survivability capability for initial employment and a reusable modular integration pathway for future electronic-warfare, communications, sensing, processing, and self-protection payloads. The transition owner is PAE ISR SOF. The architecture is intended to support future adaptation to additional platforms through standard lug spacing, power requirements, and minimized host-aircraft integration burden.
