title: Multi-Function Processor, Rapid Architecture, Miniaturized (MFP-RAM)
summary: Develop and flight-demonstrate a standards-compliant, rapidly reconfigurable hybrid communications system using a SOSA Small Form Factor Line Replaceable Unit capable of supporting multiple waveforms, frequency bands, and Multi-Level Security.
description:
Objective:
Develop and flight-demonstrate a standards-compliant, rapidly reconfigurable hybrid communications system using a SOSA Small Form Factor Line Replaceable Unit capable of supporting multiple waveforms, frequency bands, and Multi-Level Security.

Description:
Tactical communications systems must operate in RF-dense and contested environments while adapting to changing mission requirements. Current tightly coupled, proprietary, single-purpose hardware limits rapid technology insertion and the coexistence of multiple security domains. The Government seeks a COTS-first, modular, reconfigurable hybrid communications Line Replaceable Unit that integrates multi-band Software Defined Radios, modular open-system interfaces, secure RED/BLACK separation, and a containerized software environment. The capability must support integration into representative air platforms while reducing host-aircraft modification burden and enabling future waveform or payload changes with minimal redesign. Proposals must address the remaining system-level research and development required to integrate, validate, qualify, and flight-demonstrate the hybrid communications capability. Proposals do not have to result in a production-ready capability, but must be sufficient to facilitate a minimum viable product (MVP) which can be used in a surrogate flight demonstration.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. Applicants must demonstrate readiness for Phase II through prior Phase I-type efforts. Required evidence shall include validated data, prototype performance metrics, subsystem-integration results, and evidence of compliance with applicable SOSA standards. Applicants must demonstrate successful multi-band waveform operation, modularity, and secure RED/BLACK separation. The submitted evidence must identify the remaining system-level architecture, integration, qualification, validation, and flight-demonstration work proposed for Phase II.

Phase II:
Offerors may propose the system architecture, implementation approach, and integration strategy needed to meet the Government’s required operational, interoperability, security, and platform-integration objectives. Offerors may propose equivalent technical approaches that satisfy the Government’s operational, interoperability, security, platform-integration, and verification objectives. The proposed approach shall advance an existing prototype or set of mature subsystem technologies into a surrogate flight-demonstrable MFP-RAM hybrid communications capability.

The effort shall advance the physical, mechanical, electrical, thermal, software, and logical architectures required to integrate a SOSA Small Form Factor Line Replaceable Unit within representative tactical-aircraft constraints. The system shall integrate and demonstrate multi-waveform Software Defined Radios, associated power amplification, secure switching, cryptographic modules, and supporting compute, power, and chassis-management elements. The architecture shall support modular waveform and payload changes with minimal redesign and reduced host-aircraft modification burden.

The effort shall implement a containerized software environment in the Government Reference Architecture Open Compute Environment and demonstrate mission-critical and network processes. The system shall incorporate applicable Cross Domain Solutions and cryptographic capabilities supporting Multi-Level Security, RED/BLACK separation, Zero Trust authentication, and over-the-network keying and rekeying.

The effort shall begin appropriate software-in-the-loop, hardware-in-the-loop, laboratory, electrical-interface, power, thermal-management, vibration, electromagnetic compatibility, cybersecurity, environmental, and system-level testing under representative surrogate aircraft conditions. The contractor shall generate engineering data, interface documentation, cybersecurity artifacts, flight-safety documentation, and test evidence needed to support applicable initial airworthiness and cybersecurity approval processes. A minimum viable product (MVP) MFP-RAM LRU shall be integrated on a Government-designated tactical or surrogate air platform for captive-carry and live-fly testing.

Deliverables shall include flight-representative MFP-RAM hybrid communications LRUs; a containerized baseline software suite; interface documentation; cybersecurity validation results; applicable compliance documentation; thermal and environmental test results; supporting engineering data; and a transition and scaling plan for adaptation to operational Air Force command systems and the Joint Fires Network. Performance thresholds, interface limits, and configuration-specific constraints will be Government-defined. Where these constraints are unavailable, offerors shall identify assumptions for subsequent Government validation and describe proposed verification methods.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Following successful laboratory demonstration, PAE Weapons, C3BM anticipates pursuing exploratory follow-on funding through PAEs to support flight demonstration on typical small air vehicles, including weapons and ACPs. Transition activities may include operational assessment and integration into Air Force command systems, joint command-and-control experimentation, crewed-uncrewed teaming platforms, and the Joint Fires Network. The intended operational outcome is a rapidly deployable, secure, reconfigurable tactical communications capability supporting Agile Combat Employment and electromagnetic spectrum operations.

References:
• Technical Standard for SOSA Reference Architecture, Edition 2.0.
• Air Force Doctrine Publication 3-85, Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations,2023.

title: A unified model for specification and simulation to design, acquire, and sustain a hybrid- or multi-cloud large scale data analytics system that balances cost, performance, modularity, and security.
summary: Develop and validate an innovative unified financial operations (FinOps) and Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) solution to solve lifecycle cost, resource predictability, and performance modeling challenges within modern defense Condition-Based Maintenance Plus (CBM+) hybrid-cloud systems.
description:
Objective:
Develop and validate an innovative unified financial operations (FinOps) and Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) solution to solve lifecycle cost, resource predictability, and performance modeling challenges within modern defense Condition-Based Maintenance Plus (CBM+) hybrid-cloud systems.

Description:
Modern software-centric data systems across the Department of War operate in highly dynamic, shared cloud and hybrid infrastructure environments. Within complex weapon system sustainment platforms, such as the RSO CBM+ enterprise, accurately predicting and managing lifecycle resource consumption, computing performance, and ongoing operational costs presents a substantial operational challenge. Cloud and hybrid hosting costs fluctuate due to stochastic workload behaviors, data egress, and dynamic compute allocation. Across commercial and defense sectors, approximately 49% of organizations lack dedicated FinOps capabilities, resulting in frequent budget variances exceeding 18% and inefficient allocation of critical resources.

Traditional MBSE methodologies and legacy toolchains (e.g., static Cameo models, detached MATLAB scripts, disconnected spreadsheets) lack the capability to execute high-fidelity, time-dependent simulations directly within the primary system specification model. This fragmentation creates significant lag between architectural planning, empirical software telemetry, and financial governance, severely limiting rapid system analysis and trade-space optimization.

To address this capability gap, this project seeks innovative solutions that bridge DevOps, FinOps, and MBSE into a unified, executable environment. The proposed solution must demonstrate how system design specifications and executable simulation software can coexist within a cohesive architecture, such as an extensible, layered Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) utilizing Systems Modeling Language (SysML) or equivalent open modeling frameworks. Offerors should propose methods to capture continuous empirical data from operational and developmental environments, allowing the model to dynamically update, calibrate, and predict both Capital Expenditures and Operational Expenditures. The solution must support hybrid operational constraints, verifying that on-premise components sustain secure, disconnected operations while remaining optimized alongside cloud assets.

The entry Technology Readiness Level (TRL) for this D2P2 effort is expected to be TRL 4, progressing to TRL 6 by the conclusion of Phase II, culminating in a fully integrated, operationally viable prototype model and software suite demonstrated under representative operational conditions.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards are anticipated. To qualify for this D2P2 topic, the Department of the Air Force expects applicants to demonstrate feasibility through prior "Phase I-type" research and commercialization efforts that do not constitute work undertaken as part of an active SBIR/STTR funding agreement for the identical scope.

The scientific and technical merits of foundational systems modeling, commercial FinOps telemetry, and cloud monitoring tools is established in the commercial marketplace. Therefore, traditional Phase I feasibility studies exploring basic MBSE modeling syntax or standard cloud billing dashboards are considered redundant. Applicants must provide verifiable documentation substantiating that the underlying technology is mature (TRL 4) and that the offeror possesses deep technical capability in unified modeling, simulation execution, and resource forecasting.

Sufficient Feasibility Documentation should include, but is not limited to:

• Commercial or Operational Deployment Records: Verifiable case studies, white papers, or performance data demonstrating prior implementation of predictive cost analytics, FinOps platforms, or advanced MBSE tools within complex enterprise IT or defense-adjacent environments.
• Executable Simulation Metrics: Technical reports, architecture diagrams, or code demonstrations validating the ability to couple visual system models (e.g., SysML or comparable schemas) with computational or discrete-event simulation engines to model stochastic system behavior.
• Telemetry & Feedback Integration Data: Documented capability to ingest continuous empirical log data, infrastructure metrics, or telemetry streams to dynamically calibrate system models or baseline behavioral algorithms.
• AI/ML or Advanced Algorithmic Validation: Preliminary data or benchmark analyses demonstrating algorithmic feasibility (e.g., machine learning regression, multi-objective optimization, Pareto-frontier analysis) to accurately predict resource utilization or detect anomalous cost drivers.

Submission of this documentation confirms that the technology has progressed beyond conceptual formulation and laboratory proof-of-concept into relevant environment validation, establishing the baseline needed to proceed directly to advanced Phase II operational maturation and defense integration.

Phase II:
The Phase II effort requires performers to conduct targeted research, development, and operational validation that elevates the proposed technology from TRL 4 to TRL 6. Performers should propose innovative methods to develop, tailor, and demonstrate an executable modeling and simulation platform aligned to the operational challenges of the RSO CBM+ architecture.

To establish feasibility, evaluate effectiveness, and execute the required R&D, Phase II capability demonstrations should address the following operational and technical parameters:

-Unified Executable Architecture: Develop and demonstrate an integrated modeling framework wherein system specifications and simulation software interact seamlessly. Offerors should demonstrate methods to execute multi-objective optimization simulations (exploring thousands of iterations) to map Pareto-optimal balances across lifecycle costs, compute performance, latency, and data security constraints.

·Empirical FinOps Telemetry Loop: Implement mechanisms to ingest live or simulated empirical telemetry from hybrid-cloud environments, demonstrating that model parameters dynamically update to forecast CapEx and OpEx under fluctuating operational tempos and disconnected on-premise operational states.

·Behavioral Modeling: Explore, evaluate, and integrate techniques to capture complex, non-linear system behaviors and enhance predictive accuracy for workload and cost spikes.

·Defense System Integration & Transition Readiness: Demonstrate the capability within an operationally representative RSO CBM+ hybrid-cloud scenario, verifying model fidelity, ease of schema integration, and cyber resilience.

·Knowledge Transfer & Sustainment Enablement: Produce comprehensive technical documentation, data packages, training curricula, and provide collaborative engineering support to enable government engineers and Advisory & Assistance Services (A&AS) personnel to operate, extend, and sustain the tool chain independently.

Phase II Minimum Acceptable Deliverables:

• A comprehensive, unified modeling environment (SysML or equivalent open standard) and integrated simulation software capable of predicting resource consumption, lifecycle costs, and operational performance across both cloud and disconnected on-premise architectures.
• A functional demonstration showcasing the utilization of AI/ML or advanced heuristic techniques to capture, predict, and optimize complex system behaviors within the simulation environment.
• A complete technical data package (TDP), system documentation, interface control descriptions, and an operator/administrator training package with an executable training plan for organic government and A&AS sustainment.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Potential Military Applications: Beyond the primary target of optimizing the Rapid Sustainment Office's (RSO) Condition Based Maintenance Plus (CBM+) hybrid-cloud system, this technology has incredibly broad military applications. The unified modeling solution can be directly applied to optimize cost, performance, and security for other large-scale data analytics systems, IT architectures, and complex software-centric systems such as aircraft avionics and sensor suites. Furthermore, the executable Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) artifacts produced by this model provide immense value for securing mandatory Department of Defense (DoD) compliance approvals, including Authority To Operate (ATO) packages, safety, airworthiness, and nuclear certifications, depending on the system it is applied to.

Potential Commercial Applications: The commercial sector faces the exact same cloud resource management and budget challenges as the DoD. Currently, 49% of organizations lack a dedicated Financial Operations (FinOps) team for cloud management. Consequently, many of these organizations waste roughly 28% of their cloud budget and are frequently 18% over their annual cloud spend. The commercial application of this unified modeling approach allows enterprise organizations to integrate predictive FinOps and DevOps capabilities directly into their software development and Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) data pipelines. By adopting this technology, commercial entities operating large multi-cloud or hybrid-cloud analytical systems can accurately predict stochastic software behaviors and save tens of millions of dollars annually.

References:
• Booth, T., Ghosh, S., Yet Another MBSE Methodology (YAMM): A DevOps and Empirically-Based Unified-Modeling, Design, Analysis, and Optimization Methodology for Software-Centric Data Systems. PhD Dissertation
• Colorado State University, 2025 Booth, T., Ghosh, S., A Modular Simulation-based MBSE Approach Applied to a Cloud-Based System. 34th INCOSE International Symposium, 2024

title: Mobile Expeditionary 3D Concrete Printer (MX3DCP)
summary: Mature and validate expeditionary 3D concrete printing technologies, materials, and geometries so military personnel can rapidly construct combat-relevant, blast-resistant force-protection structures at contested airbases.
description:
Objective:
Mature and validate expeditionary 3D concrete printing technologies, materials, and geometries so military personnel can rapidly construct combat-relevant, blast-resistant force-protection structures at contested airbases.

Description:
Problem: The U.S. Air Force faces an urgent and growing gap in its ability to rapidly harden, repair, and reconstitute expeditionary airbase infrastructure during combat operations. Recent attacks against airbase infrastructure in the Middle East have reinforced a reality already evident in planning for the Indo-Pacific and other contested theaters: U.S. forces must be able to operate from bases that are vulnerable to missiles, rockets, artillery, one-way unmanned aircraft, and fragmentation-producing weapons. Current expeditionary infrastructure is often too slow to construct, too logistics-intensive to transport, or too lightly protected to provide meaningful survivability under modern attack conditions. Put bluntly, the Air Force has spent decades building exquisite kill chains while too often housing the Airmen who sustain them in tents, trailers, and flat-walled structures that were never designed for the threat environment now arriving overhead.

Opportunity: 3D concrete printing offers a potential step-change in expeditionary construction by enabling military engineers to rapidly print protective structures using automated or semi-automated construction workflows, reduced skilled labor, and locally available cementitious materials where feasible. Prior work has demonstrated that cementitious materials can be printed, that full-scale structures can be produced with mobile 3DCP systems, and that limited blast testing can be performed on printed wall assemblies. However, the existing state of the art has not yet fully addressed the combined problem that matters most for combat survivability: printable expeditionary materials, field-executable operator workflows, and structure geometry deliberately optimized to mitigate blast-wave behavior and fragmentation effects.

This Direct-to-Phase II effort will improve the current DoD technological state by integrating three related areas of technical development: advanced cementitious materials suitable for expeditionary printing; mobile, field-operable 3D concrete printing systems and workflows; and printable protective geometries designed to mitigate blast and fragmentation effects. First, the project will evaluate advanced cementitious materials, including Air Force Civil Engineer Center-developed materials and other candidate mixes, for printability, strength gain, curing behavior, environmental tolerance, pumpability, layer adhesion, and compatibility with native or in situ material sourcing. Second, the effort will develop and evaluate novel printable geometries that improve survivability beyond conventional flat-wall construction, including shapes intended to reduce blast reflection, limit pressure amplification, interrupt fragmentation paths, and improve internal occupant protection. Third, the project will validate these material and geometry combinations through representative printing, structural evaluation, and controlled blast/fragmentation testing.

The initial technology readiness level is estimated at TRL 5, with discrete material, printer, and structure demonstrations approaching TRL 6. The current manufacturing readiness level is estimated at MRL 4 to 5, because the underlying processes exist but require maturation for repeatable production in austere conditions by lightly trained military personnel. The target at the end of Phase II is TRL 6 to 7 and MRL 5 to 6, supported by relevant-environment demonstrations, printed test articles, validated print parameters, documented material performance, and blast-response data suitable for transition planning.

The required Phase II effort will include material screening and characterization; evaluation of locally sourced or partially substituted cementitious feedstocks; printability testing under relevant environmental conditions; development of candidate protective geometries; computational modeling of blast interaction and fragmentation exposure; printing of representative components and structure sections; controlled structural, blast, and fragmentation testing; operator workflow development; logistics and deployment analysis; and documentation of design rules, print parameters, safety considerations, and transition recommendations.

Minimum deliverables will include a material characterization report; a printability and expeditionary logistics assessment; a geometry design and modeling report; representative printed test articles; blast and fragmentation test results; validated print parameters for selected material/geometry combinations; operator-ready draft technical procedures; and a final transition package identifying recommended use cases, limitations, equipment requirements, training requirements, and follow-on test needs.

The desired outcome is a validated technical foundation for rapidly printed protective infrastructure that can be employed by Air Force civil engineers in expeditionary and combat environments. A successful effort will not replace all conventional construction, but it may give commanders a faster and more survivable option when the choice is currently between slow construction, vulnerable temporary shelters, or telling Airmen to make do with whatever was shipped before the shooting started.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made as a result of this topic. To qualify for this D2P2 topic, the Air Force expects applicant(s) to demonstrate feasibility by means of a prior “Phase I-type” effort that does not constitute work undertaken as part of a prior or ongoing SBIR/STTR funding agreement. Applicant(s) shall provide documentation demonstrating that the proposed technology has already achieved sufficient scientific and technical merit to proceed directly into applied Phase II development, integration, testing, and validation.

At a minimum, applicant(s) should provide evidence that they understand and have previously demonstrated the core technical elements required for expeditionary 3D concrete printing of protective infrastructure. This includes documented experience with large-scale additive construction; cementitious material formulation, mixing, pumping, and extrusion; layer-by-layer structural behavior; print path generation; printer set up, calibration, and operation; quality control; curing behavior; and construction of representative vertical or protective structures.

Feasibility documentation may include prior test reports, technical papers, government or commercial demonstration records, prototype performance data, photographs or video of printed structures, material characterization data, print logs, mix designs, structural calculations, equipment specifications, operator workflow documentation, environmental test data, and customer or government evaluation reports. Documentation should show that the applicant’s technology is not merely conceptual or architectural slideware in a hard hat, but has been demonstrated through physical printing, measured performance, and repeatable technical processes.

Applicant(s) should provide sufficient prior technical evidence, as applicable to the proposed approach, to substantiate feasibility in the following areas. These elements are not tasks to be completed as part of a new Phase I effort; rather, they identify the types of prior Phase I-equivalent work and evidence that may demonstrate that the proposed technology has advanced beyond basic feasibility and is ready to proceed directly into Phase II maturation, integration, testing, and validation:

• Printing System Feasibility. Evidence that the proposed system, subsystem, or technology has successfully printed cementitious materials at a scale relevant to infrastructure construction. Documentation should describe printer architecture, build volume or repositioning approach, positioning accuracy, extrusion method, pump and hose configuration, power requirements, transportability, setup time, crew size, and environmental limitations.
• Material Feasibility. Evidence that candidate cementitious materials can be mixed, pumped, extruded, layered, and cured with predictable performance. Documentation should include, as applicable, compressive strength, flexural strength, tensile or bond strength, interlayer adhesion, open time, set time, pumpability, extrudability, buildability, shrinkage, durability, and curing sensitivity. Applicant(s) should also describe prior experience with alternative aggregates, locally sourced materials, supplementary cementitious materials, admixtures, or other approaches that reduce logistics burden.
• Structural Feasibility. Evidence that printed components or structures can achieve relevant structural performance. Documentation may include calculations, finite element analysis, load testing, wall stability data, reinforcement strategies, printed geometry performance, or comparison to applicable construction or force-protection criteria. Applicant(s) should identify known limitations of printed concrete construction and proposed methods to mitigate them.
• Expeditionary Use Feasibility. Evidence that the technology can be adapted for use in austere or expeditionary environments. Documentation should address crew training, operator skill level, field setup, equipment transport, material sourcing, quality assurance, maintenance burden, environmental operating range, dust/heat/wind effects, power generation, water demand, and repairability. The Air Force is specifically interested in approaches that can be executed by uniformed civil engineer personnel without requiring a boutique team of PhDs, factory technicians, and a spiritually fragile printer that only works in perfect weather.
• Blast and Force Protection Relevance. Evidence that the applicant understands blast loading, fragmentation hazards, structural response, and protective design considerations. Because comprehensive blast validation of 3D-printed geometries remains a major technical gap, prior full-scale blast testing is not required for D2P2 eligibility. However, applicant(s) should provide documentation of any related blast, impact, structural, or protective design work; relevant modeling capability; prior testing of protective systems; or experience designing structures for overpressure, fragment control, progressive collapse resistance, or occupant survivability.
• Geometry and Design-to-Print Feasibility. Evidence that the applicant can generate printable designs beyond simple flat walls or demonstration objects. Documentation should show capability to translate protective geometry concepts into printable toolpaths, control layer geometry, manage openings and transitions, and evaluate constructability. Preferred documentation includes prior printed curved, cellular, ribbed, sacrificial, energy-dissipating, or non-rectilinear geometries.7. Measurement and Quality Control Feasibility. Evidence that the applicant can measure and control key process variables during printing. Documentation may include print speed, extrusion rate, bead dimensions, layer height, layer timing, material temperature, ambient conditions, slump/flow measurements, dimensional accuracy, destructive or nondestructive test data, and acceptance criteria used during prior demonstrations.

For purposes of D2P2 eligibility, the Air Force expects the proposed technology to be at approximately TRL 5 or higher at the start of the Phase II effort, with selected subsystems or prior demonstrations at TRL 6 where applicable. The applicant should demonstrate that the core concept has been validated in laboratory or relevant environments and that the proposed Phase II work is focused on maturing, integrating, and validating the capability rather than establishing basic feasibility.

The notional Phase I-type feasibility threshold is satisfied when an applicant can show that: cementitious material has been successfully printed in representative form; printed components have achieved measurable structural or material performance; the printing process has been repeated with documented parameters; the applicant understands how to adapt the process for expeditionary constraints; and the applicant has a technically credible approach for evaluating blast-mitigating geometry during Phase II.

Successful D2P2 applicant(s) should enter Phase II prepared to produce representative printed test articles, evaluate advanced materials, develop and print novel protective geometries, support structural and blast/fragmentation testing, and deliver validated technical data suitable for Air Force transition planning.

Phase II:
Phase II will mature, integrate, and validate an expeditionary 3D concrete printing capability for force-protection infrastructure at contested airbases. The effort shall culminate in a well-defined deliverable prototype consisting of validated material formulations, printable protective geometries, representative printed test articles, blast and fragmentation performance data, and operator-ready technical procedures suitable for transition into Air Force civil engineering, Agile Combat Employment, airbase survivability, and base recovery use cases.

The desired outcome is not simply a printed concrete wall or a visually impressive demonstration structure. The desired outcome is a technically defensible, repeatable, and field-relevant construction capability that enables uniformed military engineers to rapidly print protective shelters, walls, revetments, equipment enclosures, personnel fighting positions, and other mission-support structures using expeditionary equipment and locally available or minimally transported cementitious materials where feasible.

The Government is interested in innovative technical approaches that advance the following Phase II objectives. These objectives describe areas of interest and desired outcomes rather than a prescribed statement of work. Offerors should propose the technical approach, methods, sequencing, materials, system architecture, analytical tools, testing strategy, and other activities they determine most appropriate to achieve the topic objective.

• Advanced Material Evaluation. The Government is interested in approaches that identify and evaluate candidate cementitious materials suitable for expeditionary 3D concrete printing. Candidate approaches may consider AFCEC-developed or government-furnished materials where available, commercially available printable mixes, formulations incorporating native or in situ materials, or other technically credible material solutions proposed by the offeror. Relevant considerations may include pumpability, extrudability, open time, set time, layer stability, interlayer bond, curing sensitivity, compressive strength, flexural behavior, durability, environmental performance, logistics burden, and field usability.
• Expeditionary Printability Demonstration. The desired outcome is evidence that the proposed printing approach can operate repeatably under conditions relevant to expeditionary use. Offerors should identify the field variables most significant to their proposed solution, which may include heat, dust, wind, water quality, aggregate variability, batch consistency, equipment setup time, crew size, power demand, maintenance burden, and operator skill level. The Government is particularly interested in approaches suitable for operation by uniformed personnel without persistent reliance on specialized vendor technicians.
• Blast-Mitigating Geometry Development. The Government is interested in printable structural geometries or other design approaches intended to improve survivability compared with conventional flat-wall or rectangular expeditionary construction. Candidate concepts may include curved, angled, ribbed, cellular, buttressed, sacrificial, double-wall, voided, berm-integrated, energy-dissipating, or other configurations proposed by the offeror. Desired outcomes include measurable reduction of blast-wave reflection, pressure amplification, fragmentation exposure, structural failure risk, hazardous debris effects, or other relevant hazards to occupants or protected assets.
• Modeling and Design-to-Print Workflow. The Government is interested in approaches that effectively connect structural design, blast-informed geometry selection, toolpath generation, constructability assessment, and field printing parameters. Offerors may propose computational modeling, simulation, physical experimentation, or other analytical methods appropriate to their solution. The desired outcome is a technically defensible design-to-print process that identifies relevant design rules, limitations, and acceptance criteria for printable force-protection structures.
• Representative Prototype Construction. The Government is interested in physical demonstration of the proposed material, geometry, system, or integrated approach at a scale sufficient to substantiate its technical and operational potential. Representative test articles or prototype structures may demonstrate material and geometry combinations, openings or penetrations where applicable, constructable transitions, dimensional accuracy, repeatable print quality, or other characteristics relevant to the proposed solution. Potential use cases include personnel shelters, protective walls, equipment enclosures, entry-control protective features, aircraft support-area protection, or rapid base-recovery structures.
• Structural, Blast, and Fragmentation Testing. The Government is interested in approaches that generate objective data sufficient to characterize the structural and protective performance of proposed printed materials, geometries, or integrated solutions. Offerors should propose testing and validation methods appropriate to their technical approach, which may include structural evaluation, blast or fragmentation-relevant testing against representative threats or scaled surrogates, modeling correlated with physical testing, or other technically defensible methods. Comparison against an appropriate baseline configuration is encouraged where it provides meaningful evidence of performance improvement. Relevant measures may include damage mechanisms, failure modes, displacement, cracking, spalling, fragmentation behavior, overpressure effects, and post-event usability.
• Operator Workflow and Transition. The Government is interested in solutions capable of transitioning from specialized development or vendor-led demonstrations toward practical employment by Air Force civil engineer personnel in expeditionary environments. Relevant considerations may include operator procedures, quality control, training requirements, safety, material handling, field setup, troubleshooting, sustainment, maintenance, and other factors necessary to support repeatable field use. Offerors should propose the documentation, training, or transition products appropriate to their technical approach.

Offerors should propose Phase II deliverables appropriate to their unique technical approach and sufficient to substantiate the results of the effort. Depending upon the solution proposed, anticipated technical outputs may include:

Phase II success will be evaluated by the extent to which the proposed effort demonstrates repeatable printing performance; measurable structural and/or blast-relevant performance of the proposed protective solution; execution under relevant expeditionary constraints; and sufficient technical maturity and supporting data to provide the Air Force with a credible pathway to further operational testing, military utility assessment, and transition.

The target maturity at the completion of Phase II is TRL 6 to 7 and MRL 5 to 6. A successful Phase II will provide the Air Force with validated data, prototype structures, and operator-ready documentation needed to determine whether expeditionary 3D concrete printing can become a practical tool for protecting Airmen, aircraft support functions, critical equipment, and mission operations in contested environments.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Following successful Phase II completion, Phase III will focus on transitioning validated expeditionary 3D concrete printing materials, blast-mitigating geometries, and operator-ready construction workflows into military and commercial applications using non-SBIR/STTR funding. The expected Phase III entry maturity is TRL 6 to 7, with selected materials, printed geometries, and construction workflows validated through relevant-environment printing, structural testing, and blast/fragmentation evaluation. Phase III will mature the capability toward TRL 8 to 9 through operational demonstrations, military utility assessments, field exercises, design standardization, training development, procurement planning, and integration into Service construction and force-protection programs.

A successful Phase III military effort would transition the capability from “we can print something interesting” to “a civil engineer unit can deploy, set up, print, inspect, and use protective infrastructure fast enough to matter.” That distinction is critical. The wartime value of this technology is not novelty; it is the ability to harden or reconstitute infrastructure within operational timelines when conventional construction, imported barriers, or temporary shelters are too slow, too heavy, or too vulnerable.

Potential government funding pathways may include operations and maintenance funding for demonstrations and exercises; procurement funding for deployable printer systems and support equipment; military construction or unspecified minor construction funding where appropriate; installation resilience funding; rapid capability or combatant command-sponsored transition funding; and Service or joint force protection modernization lines. Phase III may also support transition into pre-positioned equipment sets, theater engineering packages, base recovery kits, and contingency construction planning.

The dual-use commercial potential is substantial. The same material, geometry, and printability research needed to protect expeditionary airbases can be adapted to protect critical civilian infrastructure. A printable, locally adaptable construction method could provide faster and more affordable hardening options for infrastructure that is currently too expensive or too slow to protect using conventional construction.

Commercial transition partners may include critical infrastructure utilities, electric cooperatives, water and wastewater authorities, telecommunications providers, rail and port operators, airport authorities, emergency management agencies, state National Guard civil support organizations, industrial facility owners, insurance-driven resilience programs, and construction firms specializing in hardened or resilient infrastructure. The technology may also support humanitarian assistance and disaster response by enabling rapid construction of durable shelters, sanitation structures, retaining walls, and protective barriers in locations where supply chains are disrupted.

Phase III commercialization will likely require additional engineering approvals and code alignment, including development of structural design guidance, material quality-control standards, inspection criteria, environmental compliance processes, occupational safety procedures, and acceptance pathways under applicable building codes and infrastructure owner requirements. For military use, additional approvals may include explosive safety review, force-protection engineering validation, cybersecurity review for digitally controlled equipment where applicable, airworthiness or airfield operational compatibility review where structures are used near flightline operations, and environmental or host-nation review for deployed construction. Ultimately, the objective is a deployable and commercially scalable construction capability that helps protect Airmen at contested bases and civilians whose infrastructure is increasingly exposed to physical attack, extreme weather, and system-level disruption.

References:
• U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center (ERDC), Automated Construction of Expeditionary Structures (https://www.erdcinnovation.org/technology/automated-construction-of-expeditionary-structures-aces/)

title: Wide Pass Bandwidth, High Selectivity, Continuously Tunable Notch Filters
summary: Wideband receivers used in electronic warfare (EW), signals intelligence (SigInt), and electronic support measures (ESM) need to instantaneously capture broad swaths of spectrum to avoid missing frequency agile radio frequency (RF) signals. Wideband receivers, however, lack the dynamic range to capture wide bandwidths of spectrum containing both large interferers and weak signals of interest.
description:
Objective:
Wideband receivers used in electronic warfare (EW), signals intelligence (SigInt), and electronic support measures (ESM) need to instantaneously capture broad swaths of spectrum to avoid missing frequency agile radio frequency (RF) signals. Wideband receivers, however, lack the dynamic range to capture wide bandwidths of spectrum containing both large interferers and weak signals of interest. Thus, multiple receivers are needed in these applications which results in large size and power consumption.

Description:
The objective of this topic is to develop miniature, low power, and high selectivity tunable notch filters capable of protecting wideband receivers from large interferers. The effort will target the largest interferers which are in L, S, C, and X bands with tunable notch filters, while allowing pass bandwidths spanning L through Ku bands. Each notch filter must be continuously tunable across a minimum of 3 of the 4 targeted bands (L, S, C, and X) while having a notch depth > 20 dB and a notch bandwidth < 1 % across all tuned frequencies. With a narrow notch bandwidth, each notch filter must be programmable and maintained with an accuracy of 50% of the notch bandwidth and should maintain this accuracy over temperature. The notch filters must be able to reject large interfering signals and therefore should be able to notch receive interference levels greater than 5 dBm. In the bandpass each filter must cover L-Ku band (1-18 GHz) while maintaining a low insertion loss and noise figure of less than 1.5 dB and low passband distortion with an IIP3 > +50 dBm. Each notch filter must be small, less than 3 cc, and should be connectable in series without interfering with one another to notch multiple frequencies in the same receive chain. Finally, the power consumption, including any tuning electronics, of each notch filter should be less than 100 mW. The required metrics are:

Passband frequency range (GHz)1 – 18

Maximum passband insertion loss or noise figure (dB) ≤ 1.5

Passband IIP3 (dBm)≥ 50

Notch band tunable frequency range (GHz)1 – 12

Number of bands covered by a single, continuously tunable notch≥ 3

Minimum notch depth across all tuned notch states (dB)≥ 20

Maximum notch fractional bandwidth (%)≤ 1Size (cc)≤ 3

Power consumption (mW)≤ 100

Phase I:
This topic is intended for a technology proven ready to move directly into a Phase II program. A Phase I SBIR award will not be made. The offeror is required to provide details and documentation in the Direct to Phase II (D2P2) proposal which demonstrates accomplishments of a "Phase I-like" effort, including demonstrating the expertise needed to design and fabricate miniature, high selectivity tunable notch filters. The offeror should have demonstrated, in a laboratory environment (TRL3), a notch filter achieving a 20dB deep notch with a bandwidth less than 5% of the tuned frequency, a continuous tuning range of at least 3:1, and a passband insertion loss below 3 dB across a wide frequency range. Demonstration of zero static power tuning and a filter volume of approximately 1 cc is desired. The offeror should have demonstrated the capability of maintaining low passband distortion and high notch depth across all tuned states. The proposal should illustrate past success at the aforementioned performance levels with tunable notch filter technologies fitting the above descriptions

Phase II:
The desired outcome of this topic is to demonstrate miniature, low power, and high selectivity tunable notch filters capable of protecting wideband receivers from large interferers. The effort will deliver prototype notch filters continuously tunable across a minimum of 3 of the 4 targeted bands (L, S, C, and X) while having a notch depth > 20 dB and a notch bandwidth < 1 % across all tuned frequencies.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III is accomplished when the DoW and/or commercial applications of this SBIR-funded R&D are developed using non-SBIR/STTR funds. The most direct military application is the integration of these miniature, continuously tunable notch filters into the RF front ends of wideband receivers used for electronic warfare (EW), signals intelligence (SigInt), and electronic support measures (ESM). By selectively rejecting large interferers and jammers in L, S, C, and X bands while preserving reception across the full L–Ku passband, the filters enable a single high-dynamic-range wideband receiver to replace multiple narrowband receivers, directly reducing platform size, weight, and power. Additional DAF and DoW transition opportunities include receiver protection in airborne and ground-based radar systems, jam-hardened wideband communications and SATCOM-on-the-move terminals, and reconfigurable RF front ends for software-defined radios, where the same look-through capability allows the system to respond to threat pulses without missing frequency-hopped waveforms. Potential commercial applications include interference mitigation for 5G systems operating adjacent to incumbent services (such as C-band interference into radio altimeters and co-channel interference in cellular receivers), test and measurement instrumentation, and spectrum-monitoring equipment, all markets where compact, low-power, high-selectivity tunable filtering is increasingly required as the spectrum becomes more congested. The expected Phase III effort would advance the technology from its Phase II exit point of TRL5 toward TRL7 and beyond through integration into a host receiver subsystem, environmental qualification to applicable military standards, and demonstration in a relevant operational environment. This effort would also include maturation of the manufacturing process to support production quantities, screening and reliability testing, and the establishment of a qualified supply chain. Transition planning anticipates partnership with a DoW prime contractor or system integrator as the host platform sponsor, with the small business supplying the notch filter as a component or subassembly. Known government activities required prior to fielding include security classification review, ITAR/export-control determination, and any platform-specific airworthiness or system certification associated with the selected transition host. Early engagement with DAF program offices, EW and SigInt system developers, and additional DoW customers during Phase II is recommended to identify a committed transition partner and to align the filter's form factor and interface with the targeted receiver architecture.

title: Domestic Liquid Phase Epitaxy of Yttrium Iron Garnet Films for Resilient Microwave Filter Supply Chains
summary: The United States Air Force relies on yttrium iron garnet (YIG)-based microwave filters for critical radar, electronic warfare, and communications systems. These components require high-quality YIG epitaxial films in the 10–150 µm thickness range grown by liquid phase epitaxy (LPE).
description:
Objective:
The United States Air Force relies on yttrium iron garnet (YIG)-based microwave filters for critical radar, electronic warfare, and communications systems. These components require high-quality YIG epitaxial films in the 10–150 µm thickness range grown by liquid phase epitaxy (LPE). Domestic production capability for LPE-grown YIG films does not currently exist, and the entirety of this supply chain depends on foreign sources — representing a significant vulnerability to Air Force readiness, modernization programs, and long-term system sustainment.

Description:
This topics seeks proposals to design, procure, and commission a fully domestic LPE growth facility capable of producing device-grade YIG films on gadolinium gallium garnet (GGG) substrates across the 10–150 µm thickness range. Efforts shall demonstrate system integration, process optimization, and material qualification sufficient for insertion into operational microwave filter architectures. Required technical performance thresholds include film thickness uniformity of ±5% across 1-inch wafers, surface roughness below 5 nm RMS, and saturation magnetization (4πMs) values within ±50 Gauss of specification. Offerors shall employ a systematic process characterization approach — such as design-of-experiments (DOE) methodology — to establish repeatable, production-ready growth processes governing flux composition, growth temperature, rotation rate, and cooling profile.Proposed solutions shall include a structured material qualification program incorporating X-ray diffraction (XRD), profilometry, vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM), and FMR spectroscopy. Qualified films shall be suitable for delivery to government-designated filter manufacturers and laboratories for device-level insertion and performance verification.Successful Phase II performance shall result in a domestic LPE production capability with documented process controls, material qualification data packages, and a clear transition roadmap to Phase III commercialization and direct supply to DoW prime contractors. This topic directly supports the AFRL strategic priority of eliminating foreign single-source dependencies for critical electronic materials and establishing a sovereign U.S. industrial base for high-performance garnet magnetic films.

Phase I:
This topic is intended for a technology proven ready to move directly into a Phase II program. A Phase I SBIR award will not be made. The offeror is required to provide details and documentation in the Direct to Phase II (D2P2) proposal which demonstrates accomplishments of a 'Phase I-like' effort, including demonstrating the expertise needed to grow, characterize, and qualify device-grade magnetic garnet epitaxial films. The offeror should have demonstrated experience with liquid phase epitaxy (LPE) or a comparable epitaxial growth method for yttrium iron garnet (YIG) or related magnetic garnet films on gadolinium gallium garnet (GGG) substrates, and should be able to show prior films characterized for crystalline quality, thickness, surface roughness, saturation magnetization, and ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) linewidth. Demonstration of prior films approaching device-grade quality - low FMR linewidth, good thickness uniformity, and low surface roughness - is desired, as is evidence of a systematic process characterization approach (such as design-of-experiments methodology) governing flux composition, growth temperature, rotation rate, and cooling profile. The offeror should also demonstrate an understanding of the material qualification tools required for device insertion, including X-ray diffraction (XRD), profilometry, vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM), and FMR spectroscopy. The proposal should illustrate past success at the aforementioned activities with magnetic garnet or comparable single-crystal oxide film technologies fitting the above descriptions, sufficient to substantiate that the small business is positioned to design, commission, and operate a domestic LPE production capability without a preceding Phase I effort.

Phase II:
The desired outcome of this topic is a domestic liquid phase epitaxy (LPE) production capability for device-grade yttrium iron garnet (YIG) films grown on gadolinium gallium garnet (GGG) substrates across the 10-150 um thickness range. During Phase II, the offeror shall design, procure, and commission the LPE growth system and supporting infrastructure, and shall demonstrate system integration, process optimization, and material qualification sufficient for insertion into operational microwave filter architectures. The effort shall establish repeatable, production-ready growth processes using a systematic process characterization approach, such as design-of-experiments (DOE) methodology, governing flux composition, growth temperature, rotation rate, and cooling profile. Required technical performance thresholds for qualified films include film thickness uniformity of +/-5% across 1-inch wafers, surface roughness below 5 nm RMS, and saturation magnetization (4-pi-Ms) values within +/-50 Gauss of specification. The offeror shall implement a structured material qualification program incorporating X-ray diffraction (XRD), profilometry, vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM), and FMR spectroscopy, and shall produce documented process controls and material qualification data packages. Qualified films shall be suitable for delivery to government-designated filter manufacturers and laboratories for device-level insertion and performance verification. Successful Phase II performance shall result in a domestic LPE production capability with documented process controls, material qualification data packages, demonstrated repeatability across multiple growth runs, and a clear transition roadmap to Phase III commercialization and direct supply to DoW prime contractors. The minimum acceptable deliverables are: a commissioned and operational LPE growth capability; a documented, repeatable growth process; a material qualification data package demonstrating films meeting the threshold metrics above; and delivery of qualified sample films to government-designated recipients. This effort is expected to advance the domestic-production capability from approximately TRL 3-4 at project start to TRL 5/6 at the end of Phase II.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III is accomplished when the DoD/DoW and/or commercial applications of this SBIR-funded R&D are developed using non-SBIR/STTR funds. The most direct military application is the supply of domestically produced, device-grade LPE-grown YIG films to manufacturers of YIG-based microwave filters, oscillators, resonators, and related ferrite components used in Air Force and DoW radar, electronic warfare (EW), signals intelligence (SigInt), and communications systems. These films are an enabling material for tunable and fixed microwave filter architectures - including the wide pass bandwidth, high selectivity, continuously tunable notch filters needed to protect wideband receivers from large interferers - and a sovereign supply directly reduces a critical single-source foreign dependency. Additional DAF and DoW transition opportunities include YIG-tuned oscillators for spectrum analyzers and frequency-agile sources, magnetically tunable preselectors and delay lines for wideband receivers, and non-reciprocal devices such as circulators and isolators used across airborne, ground, and space-based RF systems. Potential commercial applications include test and measurement instrumentation (spectrum analyzers and signal generators), commercial communications and SATCOM hardware, spectrum-monitoring equipment, and emerging magnonic and spintronic device research, all of which depend on low-loss single-crystal garnet films. The expected Phase III effort would advance the domestic production capability from its Phase II exit point of TRL 5/6 toward TRL 7 and beyond by scaling the LPE process to sustained production quantities, qualifying the films and process to applicable industry and military quality standards, establishing screening and lot-acceptance procedures, and integrating qualified films into fielded microwave component product lines. Transition planning anticipates direct supply agreements with DoW prime contractors and established YIG component manufacturers, with the small business operating as a qualified domestic material source. Known government activities that may be required prior to broad adoption include security and export-control (ITAR) determination, material and process qualification by government-designated filter manufacturers and laboratories, and any platform- or program-specific component qualification associated with the receiving systems. Early engagement with AFRL, DAF program offices, and DoW prime contractors during Phase II is recommended to identify committed transition partners and to align film specifications with the requirements of targeted filter and component architectures.

title: Quantum Sensing Analyzer
summary: Investigate and validate the feasibility of developing a novel quantum-based sensing technology utilizing Rydberg atomic sensors as an ultra-wideband universal measurement standard for electromagnetic systems. Demonstrate the potential of these sensors in a calibrated and highly sensitive universal measurement standard to enhance radar, electronic warfare, and antenna characterization.
description:
Objective:
Investigate and validate the feasibility of developing a novel quantum-based sensing technology utilizing Rydberg atomic sensors as an ultra-wideband universal measurement standard for electromagnetic systems. Demonstrate the potential of these sensors in a calibrated and highly sensitive universal measurement standard to enhance radar, electronic warfare, and antenna characterization.

Description:
The “Quantum Sensing Analyzer” project aims to address critical limitations in existing electromagnetic measurement technologies by developing a novel quantum-based sensing capability utilizing Rydberg atomic sensors. These sensors, leveraging quantum properties, exhibit extraordinary sensitivity and accuracy over a widespread frequency spectrum ranging from DC to 1 THz, with potential scalability to even broader ranges. This initiative is designed to modernize and standardize test and evaluation processes within the Department of Defense (DoD), particularly benefiting the Benefield Anechoic Facility (BAF) and its mission to support advanced electromagnetic system testing.

Problem Statement and Opportunity:

Current electromagnetic measurement techniques rely on diverse and complex instruments, which introduce inefficiencies, inconsistencies, and increased costs for the acquisition, testing, and integration of modern radar systems, electronic warfare platforms, communication systems, and antennas. These existing systems also face challenges in maintaining accuracy and repeatability, particularly when evaluating performance across a wide range of radio frequencies or within controlled environments like anechoic chambers.

The introduction of Rydberg sensor technology represents a disruptive opportunity to establish a universal, high-precision, SI-traceable standard for electromagnetic measurements. By adopting a single, compact, and adaptable sensor for diverse measurement tasks—including spectrum analysis, field strength monitoring, and chamber characterization—this capability promises to significantly reduce infrastructure requirements, simplify operational workflows, and enhance confidence in test data accuracy.

Project Objectives:

● Develop and validate a proof-of-concept Rydberg-based quantum sensing system capable of performing highly accurate and repeatable electromagnetic measurements across 1.5 MHz to 40 GHz.

● Demonstrate the ability of the sensor to serve as a universal measurement standard for radar, electronic warfare, communication systems, and antenna evaluation.

● Establish enhanced chamber characterization capabilities, including electromagnetic leakage detection, direction finding, near-field measurement, reflection mitigation, and quiet zone mapping, to improve the testing environment quality.

● Progress the technology readiness level (TRL) from TRL 2 at project initiation to TRL 6 by the conclusion of Phase II.

Required Efforts and Phase Activities:

Phase I:

● Perform a comprehensive feasibility study to assess the applicability of Rydberg atomic sensors as a universal electromagnetic measurement standard.

● Evaluate the sensors’ technical attributes, including sensitivity (targeting sub-microvolt/meter thresholds), dynamic range, and bandwidth.

● Identify potential integration challenges with existing test facilities and systems, particularly those used in the BAF.

● Deliverables: Feasibility study report detailing technical analyses, identified challenges, and potential solutions; preliminary system design for a prototype quantum sensing analyzer.

Phase II:

● Develop, fabricate, and demonstrate a functional prototype of the Rydberg-based quantum sensing system, incorporating key findings from Phase I.

● Conduct extensive testing and validation of the prototype in operationally relevant environments, including the BAF, with emphasis on precision, SI-traceability, and repeatability of electromagnetic measurements.

● Integrate the system into existing DoD testing workflows, showcasing improvements in efficiency, reduced equipment requirements, and testing performance.

● Deliverables: Fully operational prototype, detailed test and evaluation report, system integration plan, and transition strategy for scaling and deployment within the DoD.

Desired Outcome:

The successful development of a Quantum Sensing Analyzer will revolutionize the DoD’s electromagnetic measurement and testing capabilities by delivering a single, universal, quantum-enabled sensing standard. This solution will eliminate the need for multiple specialized instruments, streamline developmental and operational testing, and significantly enhance test accuracy and repeatability. Furthermore, the technology will address critical modernization priorities, such as advancing quantum science and enabling operationally focused Advanced Battle Management Systems (ABMS). This effort aligns with the Air Force’s strategic goals to improve mission readiness, accelerate technology deployment to the warfighter, and invest in cutting-edge testing capabilities that sustain innovation and technical superiority in defense systems.

Phase I:
Phase I will assess the feasibility of Rydberg sensors for precise electromagnetic measurements (1.5 MHz–40 GHz). Goals include evaluating sensitivity, bandwidth, and range while addressing DoD test needs. Deliverables: technical feasibility analysis, preliminary design, and simulated performance data to validate the sensors’ potential as a scalable, SI-traceable measurement standard for advanced defense applications.

Phase II:
Phase II focuses on developing, integrating, and testing a Rydberg-based quantum sensing prototype for 1.5 MHz–40 GHz electromagnetic measurement. Deliverables include a tested SI-traceable system demonstrating dynamic range, ultra-wideband operation, noise-level performance, operational integration, and resilience to interference. Success is defined by achieving TRL 6, validating accuracy, scalability, and compatibility with DoD testing environments such as BAF, and enabling future operational deployment.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III will advance the TRL 6 prototype Quantum Sensing Analyzer to TRL 8+ with non-SBIR funding, integrating it for operational assessments at BAF and other DoD labs. The system will support electromagnetic testing (1.5 MHz–40 GHz) for radar, EW, and communication systems. Commercial uses include electromagnetic compliance testing and telecommunications. Transition involves DAF partners, certifications, training, and infrastructure development for deployment.

title: Solid Propellant Environmental Effects Digital Twin
summary: The objective of the proposed effort is twofold: 1) Model and simulate the combined effects of thermal, temporal, chemical, and geometric changes to solid propellants that occur over time for in rocket motor grains, and 2) integrate predictive behavior tools into solid rocket motor design tools for decision-quality models and simulations.
description:
Objective:
The objective of the proposed effort is twofold: 1) Model and simulate the combined effects of thermal, temporal, chemical, and geometric changes to solid propellants that occur over time for in rocket motor grains, and 2) integrate predictive behavior tools into solid rocket motor design tools for decision-quality models and simulations. The intended result is a solid propellant aging and environmental process digital twin.

Description:
Solid Rocket Motors (SRMs) provide propulsion for many critical defense applications including surface launched, air launched, ballistic, and space vehicles. The propellant that creates acceleration through these SRMs is a complex active material that can be sensitive to environmental effects from thermal loads, exposure to air or humidity, chemical changes, pressure, or vibration loads due to time or ingredient changes. Both mechanical response characteristics and ballistic properties can be affected. This topic requests projects that will combine computational modeling and design capability from several sources to simulate aging responses due to environmental effects. The framework must follow Modular Open Systems Approach standards mandated in 10 U.S.C. § 4401 for compatibility with several commercially available computational tools such as ANSYS, ABAQUS, Python, MatLab, SysML, and others.

Phase I:
Define a ballistic or structural degradation mechanism in solid propellent that can be implemented in a damage tolerant design process for solid rocket motors. Develop the technical argument for transitioning non-continuum mechanisms to a continuum-based analysis techniques. Develop a Digital Engineering plan to create the desired capability to model Solid Rocket Propellant and predict behavior over extended periods of time and environmental conditions.

Phase II:
Phase 2 will build out the combined moderate fidelity predictive models of at least two environmental effects and anchor predictions to historical propellant aging data implemented through Cameo, OMG, or other SysML 2.0 platform. Performance predictions including both ballistic degradation and structural reactions should be included. Analytical techniques must be compatible with a MBSE enabled design threads.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase 3 is intended to create a “digital twin” of the solid propellant aging process that can be integrated into solid rocket motor design tools and SySML – based predictive and systems engineering tools. Models and tools have three opportunities for transition and commercialization: 1) transition to Government Refence Architectures for SRM design and vehicle integration, 2) incorporation into commercial SRM design capabilities through the SRM industry, or 3) transition or reuse into other commercially viable polymer-dependent industries such as rubber tires, automotive components, in-vivo medical devices, hazardous response Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), and sporting goods.

title: Next-generation Green Monopropellant Gas Generation
summary: Develop a low-power, real-time precision liquid-to-gas phase-change feed system featuring active molecular feedback control to enable the seamless integration of liquid propellants (including next-generation green liquid propellants such as ASCENT and LMP-103S) with high-efficiency in-space plasma propulsion systems.
description:
Objective:
Develop a low-power, real-time precision liquid-to-gas phase-change feed system featuring active molecular feedback control to enable the seamless integration of liquid propellants (including next-generation green liquid propellants such as ASCENT and LMP-103S) with high-efficiency in-space plasma propulsion systems. While legacy propellants like hydrazine vaporize with relative ease, next-generation green propellants possess near-zero vapor pressures that streamline ground operations but make efficient vaporization and stable gas-phase molecular composition extremely difficult to control. Proposed solutions must actively monitor and modulate the vaporization process in real time to deliver precise molecular species fractions under tight power constraints, ultimately establishing a versatile, fuel-agnostic propellant conditioning capability to support dynamic space operations and emerging in-space refueling architectures.

Description:
The USSF has a desire to use liquid monopropellants for high thrust propulsion (natively in chemical thrusters) and for low-thrust, very energetic missions (in electric propulsion thrusters) - so called Multimode Propulsion (MMP) capabilities - to support Dynamic Space Operations. Such MMP capabilities have a number of very favorable characteristics including high propellant density, reduced need for high pressure storage systems, continued need for chemical propulsion on DoW assets for high thrust prompt maneuver, and compatibility with future on-orbit liquid propellant refueling capabilities.

One critical capability gap is an energy efficient, precision propellant feed system which efficiently converts next-generation liquid monopropellant into non-reactive vapor phase products which can be fed into the electric propulsion (EP) thruster. Key challenges arise from the fact that next-generation monopropellants have negligible vapor pressure and are extremely difficult to combust at low temperature and pressure.

The desired technology should present a solution for a feed system capable of supporting sub-kW to 100 kW class EP systems:

- Operation at minimum on ASCENT propellant (T) or on ASCENT and other monopropellant formulations (O)

- Realtime telemetry, including mass flow rate, species composition, and temperature as inputs to the EP device

- Maintain consistently characterized molecular composition (T) and extremely stable molecular composition (O) of the output vapor and support both steady-state and pulsed operation at frequencies greater than 5 Hz

- Minimal SWaP with particular focus on low power consumption

- Incorporate fluid/vapor facing materials that can reliably withstand long-term exposure to green monopropellants and their breakdown products over the required lifespan. Potential issues also include condensation or freezing for long-duration propellant storage in ullage and plenums if these or similar components are used

- Demonstrate rapid warmup/gas generation in less than 10 minutes (T) or on-demand (O)

- Ensure lifetime design consideration for future multiple refueling opportunities

This work directly supports the Contested Logistics Technologies (LOG) Critical Technology Area with respect to space mobility operations.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2)2) topic, no Phase I proposals will be accepted and no Phase I awards will be made under this topic. Offerors responding to this topic shall demonstrate “Phase I-type” technical feasibility through prior research, development, laboratory validation, commercial development, or operational demonstrations performed outside of the SBIR/STTR program. Phase I proposals will not be evaluated and will be rejected as nonresponsive.

For this D2P2 topic, the Government expects that the small business would have accomplished the following in a “Phase I-type” effort via some other means (e.g. IRAD, or other funded work). It must have developed a concept for a workable prototype or design to address at a minimum the basic capabilities of the stated objective above. Proposal must show, as appropriate to the proposed effort, a demonstrated technical feasibility or nascent capability to meet the capabilities of the stated objective. Proposal may provide example cases of this new capability on a specific application. The documentation provided must substantiate that the proposer has developed a preliminary understanding of the technology to be applied in their Phase II proposal to meet the objectives of this topic. Documentation should include all relevant information including, but not limited to, technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results.

Phase II:
The rapid advancement of plasma thruster operation on next-generation molecular propellants is currently bottlenecked by the lack of an energy-efficient, precise, real-time vaporization solution. While previous research has explored thermal and catalytic vaporization strategies, existing options suffer from high power consumption, ill-defined operational lifetimes, inconsistent vapor-phase molecular output, and a total lack of real-time compositional feedback to the thruster. To bridge this critical technology gap and enable commercial transition, Phase II efforts must focus on developing a robust, energy-efficient liquid-to-gas propellant conditioning system when operating on both legacy and next-generation green monopropellants.

Proposals must deliver a low Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) vaporization solution capable of providing a well-quantified, repeatable vapor stream to high-efficiency plasma thrusters, such as Hall Effect Thrusters (HETs) or Magnetoplasmadynamic (MPD) thrusters. Key technical requirements include the ability to deliver real-time feedback on the actual molecular composition being provided, and the capacity to actively modulate operation to target and maintain specific molecular species fractions. While the target operational envelope spans plasma propulsion systems from <1 kW to 100 kW, a single hardware unit is not expected to cover the entire spectrum; rather, performers must demonstrate actual performance across a subset of this range alongside a credible, physics-based pathway for modular scalability.

To maximize commercial transition and support the emerging in-space refueling architecture, Phase II projects must focus on developing flight-like engineering development units (EDUs) designed for integration into existing and future plasma propulsion systems. While formal spaceflight qualification (e.g., strict shock, vibration, and radiation acceptance testing) is not required during this phase, performers are highly encouraged to team with established thruster manufacturers. This collaboration will ensure that relevant aerospace engineering best practices, interfaces, and integration protocols are incorporated into the design, positioning the technology for rapid transition.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
This technology is directly applicable to both defense and civil spacecraft, delivering a hybrid propulsion capability that enables both prompt, high-thrust maneuvers (e.g., threat and debris avoidance) and high-efficiency, low-thrust orbital transfers. In the near term, the primary market is centered on Department of War (DoW) applications to meet critical requirements for Dynamic Space Operations (DSO), enhanced space warfighting maneuverability, and the rapid emergence of tactical in-space refueling architectures. The primary Phase II deliverable-an Engineering Development Unit (EDU) gas generator-is optimized for direct integration into various molecular plasma thrusters currently under development by commercial space partners. Although final flight qualification must be accomplished on the integrated, combined propulsion system (thruster and gas generator), the Phase II EDU serves as the critical hardware stepping stone. Depending on future government and commercial funding profiles, this technology is well-positioned for independent maturation as a standalone, platform-agnostic product through a follow-on Phase III contract or Tactical Funding Increases (TACFI) effort.

References:
