title: Low-cost Mid-wave Infrared Focal-Plane Array (FPA) Fabrication through Direct-bond Interconnection
summary: Develop a focal-plane array (FPA) fabrication process based on wafer-scale 3D-heterogeneous integration that enables a mid-wave infrared (MWIR) III-V detector epi-layer wafer to be directly bonded to a Silicon-based read-out integrated circuit (Si-ROIC) wafer, thereby eliminating the inefficient die-level Indium (In) bump-bonding process currently required to assemble Mid-wave Infrared (MWIR)…
description:
Objective:
Develop a focal-plane array (FPA) fabrication process based on wafer-scale 3D-heterogeneous integration that enables a mid-wave infrared (MWIR) III-V detector epi-layer wafer to be directly bonded to a Silicon-based read-out integrated circuit (Si-ROIC) wafer, thereby eliminating the inefficient die-level Indium (In) bump-bonding process currently required to assemble Mid-wave Infrared (MWIR) FPA sensor chips.

Description:
Electro-Optic and Infrared (EO/IR) sensors are used in a wide variety of applications, such as navigation, wide-area surveillance, and targeting. Operating in the visible and near-IR bands, EO sensors are available with small pixels and in large arrays at low cost, because the Si-detector wafer and Si-ROIC wafer can be 3D-integrated directly through wafer-to-wafer bonding with high yield at high volume based on material and complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS)-process compatibility. By contrast, sensors operating in the MWIR employ III-V detector materials, which are not CMOS-process compatible, while III-V epi-layer detectors cannot be epitaxially grown directly on Si, as required to produce the crystalline order of high-quality detectors [Refs 1-2]. Instead, the III-V detector epi-layer is grown on a lattice-compatible substrate wafer, which is then flip-chip bonded to a Si-ROIC through a dense array of sub-pixel indium bumps placed on each wafer, followed by detector-substrate removal. The technically demanding process of depositing, aligning, and compressing the dense arrays of indium bumps on detector and ROIC die, results in a labor-intensive, inefficient, low-yield process for IR FPA fabrication, which greatly increases cost.

In recent years, 3D-heterogeneous integration has enabled a single integrated chip of greater overall functionality to be realized at reduced cost by assembling multiple smaller chips, each having unique functionality, material, node size, and/or foundry origin. Direct-bond interconnection (DBI) [Refs 3-5] is a 3D-heterogeneous integration technique that can potentially enable low-cost MWIR FPA fabrication. In principle, DBI should enable very large format FPAs with small pixels to be fabricated, as the process is largely independent of wafer and pixel size, in contrast to conventional bump-bonding. Moreover, the DBI process utilizes a temperature range that is compatible with MWIR IR detector materials.

The goal of this SBIR topic is to demonstrate the use of DBI or a similar process for fabrication of high-performance, large format, small-pixel, MWIR FPAs at low cost with the objective of refining the technique sufficiently to potentially replace conventional bump-bonding.

Phase I:
Plan a detailed concept for a FPA fabrication and characterization process, including a risk assessment. While the pixel unit cell design is flexible, a pixel size of less than or equal to 10 micro-meters (um) and format of at least 2K x 2K are required, but otherwise any existing or commercially available Si-based ROIC can potentially be used for this effort. The III-V detector epi-layer spectral response must cover at least the MWIR band (3-5 um). The specific foundry and fabrication process steps will be determined in Phase I. Develop a detailed FPA characterization plan, including measurement of inter-wafer voids, pixel operability, and yield. Perform a per-FPA cost analysis that compares DBI or the selected alternative process to conventional bump-bonding and includes an assessment of the cost impact of process selection trade-offs.

Phase II:
Use the DBI or selected alternative process to fabricate multiple wafers of FPAs having less or equal to 10 um pixels and greater than or equal to 2K x 2K format. Dice and thoroughly characterize the FPAs. Integrate one or more FPA sensor chips into an imaging system and subsequent optical performance characterization (favorable but is not required under this effort.) Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Build and test an imaging sensor employing a DBI-fabricated FPA with available Phase III funding upon successful completion of Phase II.

The advancement of MWIR imagers could support many dual-use applications, such as border security, law enforcement, and industrial process monitoring. In general, the advancement of 3D-HI and DBI specifically could facilitate the development of novel micro-electronic devices beyond MWIR imagers.

References:
• Rogalski, A. "Recent progress in infrared detector technologies." Infrared Physics & Technology, 54(3), 2011, pp. 136-154. https://www.scirp.org/reference/referencepapers?referenceid=838480
• Martyniuk, P. and Rogalski, A. "HOT infrared photodetectors." Opto-Electronics Review, 21(2), 2013, pp. 239-257. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257909096_HOT_infrared_photodetectors
• US Patent 9,082,627: Method for low temperature bonding and bonded structure (covers the core process of room or low-temperature dielectric-to-dielectric and metal-to-metal bonding). https://patents.google.com/patent/US9082627B2/zh
• US Patent 6,962,835: Method for room temperature metal direct bonding. https://patents.google.com/patent/US6962835B2
• US Patent 9,391,143: Method for low temperature bonding and bonded structure. https://patents.google.com/patent/US9391143B2

title: “Self-Replicating Evolutionary Agentic SI Swarming Force” with Autonomous Embedded SI Guardrail Enforcers
summary: 1- Develop a platform agnostic fully autonomous Agentic SI swarm system suitable for multidomain naval operations (i.e., Sea, Air, Space, Land, and Cyber) with self-awareness for rapid operationally scalable response, namely “hyper-scalability”. The Agentic SI system, a hybrid-evolutionary SI, must self-replicate and self-deploy.
description:
Objective:
1- Develop a platform agnostic fully autonomous Agentic SI swarm system suitable for multidomain naval operations (i.e., Sea, Air, Space, Land, and Cyber) with self-awareness for rapid operationally scalable response, namely “hyper-scalability”. The Agentic SI system, a hybrid-evolutionary SI, must self-replicate and self-deploy. In other words, it must self-evolve as it gets feedback from its internal SI agents; it must coevolve as it interacts with the environment and the adversary to adapt and survive in littoral ecosystem without human guidance. As a team, it must autonomously reason to scale-up or scale-down its swarming clusters to generate tactical sub-clusters or end-game sub-clusters for defensive and offensive measures to confront and overwhelm threats. Neuro-Symbolic SI is to be a practical method for these SI-based swarm agents to explore and exploit the conditions in the operational ecosystem.

2- The developed platform must strictly adhere to operational policies, safety, and security with embedded SI agents serving as guardrails to control all sustaining SI agents (i.e., Self-Evolving SI agents) by checking outputs, cross-referencing data feeds and plans, and correcting flagged responses. These SI-enabled Guardrail-Enforcers must be active and adaptive systems embedded into the Agentic SI Swarm workflows. The embedded SI Guardrail-Enforcers validate-and-verify policies for additional safety and behavior guardrail checks beyond the ordinary trust metrics. The important performance question is “Did Agentic SI system get better without changing policy permissions, safety boundaries, or behavior unpredictably?”

Description:
This SBIR topic seeks hardware-agnostic Agentic SI swarm-teaming technologies capable of self-replication, hybrid-evolution (self-evolution and coevolution), and self-organization into teaming many arrangements. It is important to note that this project does not challenge the importance of physical platforms/machines (i.e., unmanned assets) that have physical presence in operational environments. The envisioned Agentic SI system is the machine’s intelligent autonomy software that controls the platform’s presence and its interactions with entities in the operational environment. It autonomously configures individual swarms with unique missions and networks of collaborative swarms operating in multiple operational domains with specific teaming assignments.

The envisioned swarm system is agentic as it pursues goals autonomously. It interprets assigned mission objectives and determines how to achieve them. It knows how to process, fuse, and exploit all source intelligence (ASI) and live sensor feeds to determine the course of action (CoA) and keeps adjusting it until the outcome is reached. It decides which payloads to use and when to use them, for example, active and/or passive intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeting (ISRT) sensors, point-to-point or omni-broadcast communication, or weapon systems, etc. It adapts when situations or environmental conditions change, or certain aspects of a plan fail. It can recover from various system failures and processing errors. It is designed with embedded SI-Guardrail-Enforcers to manage, validate, and verify every aspect of the Agentic SI system’s performance and associated risks to ensure that the end-to-end system adheres to established policies set forth by the Department of War and the U.S. Navy including operational safety requirements as well as the national security doctrines and mandates. The highest priority for this program is to establish ZERO tolerance for SI-generated rogue populations of unaligned agents rapidly and uncontrollably increase.

The hybrid-evolutionary aspect of the Agentic SI system focuses on attaining new operational proficiency and know-how to execute emerging missions with the highest accuracy, persistence, and endurance. The self-evolving SI system monitors endogenous performance of all subsystems, gets feedback, and improves its own internal design configuration autonomously, for example, altering or generating new internal models. The coevolutionary SI system monitors exogenous performance interactions and coevolves the internal design in response to interactions with the environment and adversaries. It improves autonomous teaming performance interactions and reconfigurations, for example, altering or generating new swarming models, plans, and configurations to maintain operational tempo.

The self-replication aims to create autonomous, self-improving agents capable of independent survival and expansion. This Agentic SI system autonomously improves itself, creates its own successors, and builds specialized sub-agents to solve operational issues.

The self-configuring aspect of the Agentic SI system focuses on a variety of mission-focused collaborative teaming arrangements, including scouting teams for early detection of indications and warning signs to ensure survival, trip-wire teams to detect encroaching threats, ad-hoc networking teams for continuous collaboration and tracking threats, a self-defense team for fault-tolerant operations, and offensive teams to ensure survival. In aggregate, these teams form an Agentic-Force that self-adapts, self-organizes, and self-heals.

The Agentic SI Swarming-Force addresses mission capability gaps that require agile adaptation to novel adversarial TTPs and unanticipated asymmetric countermeasures. The envisioned SI capability requires SI-based evolutionary modelling techniques for learning, reasoning, recognition, and autonomous decision-making to counter emergent and/or unanticipated observable patterns of life activities or events. In other words, agentic discovery of unknown-unknown events/assets posed by the intelligent adversaries. It ensures the timely execution of CoA plans to neutralize emerging threats, including asymmetric attacks, novel deployment of joint civilian and military assets, cloaked military assets, decoys, and deceptive asset deployments. A representative set of agentic impelling operations may be conducted overtly or covertly to influence hostile forces to undertake desired actions, including adopting specific courses of action or modifying their pattern of life to safeguard critical assets through reconfiguration, relocation, or repurposing. These observable responses can then be exploited by the Agentic SI Swarming Force to degrade adversarial autonomy and disrupt, reshape, and ultimately defeat their operational plans and tactical engagements.

A notional framework for developing the required critical technologies is as follows. First, meta-learning and meta-reasoning capabilities—learning how to learn and reason—are foundational. Rather than relying on static training, agents continuously refine their internal learning processes to autonomously adapt to new tasks and conditions. This allows the system to create specialized sub-agents for various operational tasks and teaches them optimal strategies. Second, replication logic creates next-generation agents to improve operational efficiency, reduce false-alarm rates, and field additional task-organized agents to address emergent or previously unanticipated requirements. Third, autonomous resource management mechanisms must dynamically replicate, allocate, sustain, scale, or retire agents to maintain operational efficiency and mission alignment. Finally, secure, low-probability-of-intercept/low-probability-of-detection (LPI/LPD) ad hoc networking and communications are essential to enable mission-focused teaming, decentralized coordination, and Reachback to share operational insights across agent networks beyond local clusters. Critical SI technology components and developments are as follows:

• Self-reflecting Agentic SI system to provide: 1) an introspection feedback loop to enable the Agentic SI system to analyze its own plan, spot errors or weak reasoning logic, and revise them before acting, which would make the system better at goal-seeking and improve its strategy; and 2) a retrospection feedback loop to enable the Agentic SI system to analyze its past plans, decisions, and resulting outcomes. Spot and learn from both the advantages and the shortcomings of those past decision processes to improve future planning and reasoning logic.
• Identification of novel and evolutionary behaviors appearing in a new generation of SI-agent models.
• Methodology to specify how self-replication and coevolutionary processes are initiated and developed, strategic life-cycle planning, resource acquisition for autonomous self-replication, and survival tactics that exploit operational ecosystem.
• Contextual modeling: relational, spatial, logic-based, uncertainty, and hybrid context modeling.
• Meta learning: decision tree and multilayer perception classifiers, collaborative filtering, pattern mining, deep learning.
• Spatiotemporal synchronization methods for multimodal data across decentralized architectures.
• Multimodal contextual signal processing and fusion.
• Cross-domain contextual collaborative learning, inference, and recognition.
• Meta reasoning, contextual reasoning, and risk assessment and reduction.
• Contextual priority-based task management balancing operational objectives such as persistence, endurance, and collections.

The scope of the initial feasibility study and deliverables are as follows: a) define the challenge problem that will likely meet the benchmark performance metrics; b) review a set of candidate Agentic SI methods and data requirements; c) develop a low-cost initial proof-of-concept prototype for the assessment; d) evaluate feasibility against measurable criteria; and e) deliver a proposed Phase II prototype development plan including technical risk reduction criteria and next steps.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

Phase I:
Determine the technical feasibility of designing and developing the Agentic SI Swarm technology as explained in the Description. Draw key distinctions for the proposed design approach compared to the current state-of-the-art naval ISRT information exploitation cycles. Ensure that the proposed design concept must clearly define the steps that naval ISRT platforms and joint services can capitalize on for transformational SI-assisted ISRT and engagement operations with dominant applications within the next five years. Motivate the design with a compelling challenge problem supported by relevant datasets. Consider a challenge problem that corresponds to cross-domain littoral operations and navigational risks associated with hostile anti-access/denied-access enforcement scenario that considers seaside terrain, weather, the maritime order of battle and maneuvers; engagement rules and doctrine; logistics and supply demands, etc. Hostile enforcement may include hypersonic missiles, ballistic missile attacks, sea-skimming cruise missile attacks, anti-submarine track and trail, torpedo attacks, littoral mining, and swarming weapons. Testing and demonstrations may use a mix of open-source intelligence (OSINT) datasets, synthetic datasets from DON, MCML, AIS maritime traffic, commercial satellite imagery, or similar sources. Conduct Agentic SI Swarming performance assessment, including cause and effect sensitivity analysis on contextual understanding; confidence rate on SI-generated engagement plans, options, and risk reduction associated with the ups and downs of encounters; confidence rate on SI-risk escalation controls enabling trust decisions across the integrated chain-of-command; efficiency gains in human responsiveness through timely decision-making, chain-of-actions, and resources spent.

Performance metrics for Agentic SI system in a controlled test environment are as follows: task success and completion rates: 90%+; goal attainment rate: 90%+; tool selection accuracy: 95%+; plan adherence: 90%+; hallucination rate: under 2%; safety violation rate: 0% in policy tests (any policy-breaking action is a hard fail); prompt-injection resistance: 95%+ success against red-team prompts (measure on adversarial test sets); human override rate: < 5% on routine tasks; recovery rate: 80%+; end-to-end latency: under 60 seconds for interactive flows; replication success rate: 100% only when explicitly authorized.

Policy, safety, and security performance metrics that are controlled by the embedded SI Guardrail-Enforcers are as follows:

• For self-replicating Agentic SI system to ensure the system can perform useful work without uncontrolled replication, drift, or excessive human intervention. In other words, it must replicate when authorized, and never on its own outside policy. The performance metrics include goal attainment rate: 90%+; tool selection accuracy (i.e., preventing cascading failures from bad tool use): 95%+; hallucination rate: under 2%; human override rate: under 5%; recovery rate: 80%+; boundary violation rate: 0%; and Uncontrolled replication rate: 0%.
• For Hybrid-evolving Agentic SI system, the performance metrics include improvement gains: greater than 20% (self-evolution should improve performance on unchanged tasks); regression rate: less than 5% on core tasks (new versions should not break stable capabilities); reproducibility (evolved behavior must remain traceable and can be validated): 95%+; and Drift from policy, safety, and security: 0% -- self-evolution cannot change the operational constraint envelope.

Assess the feasibility of applying the Agentic SI methods to a candidate challenge problem. Perform requirements analysis, data and interface assessment, evaluation of candidate SI approaches, and development of a limited proof of concept to determine technical viability. Produce a feasibility report, preliminary architecture, risk assessments, and a proposed Phase II prototype development plan.

Phase II:
Conduct proof-of-concept and prototype development incorporating the recommended candidate technology from Phase I. Demonstrate the operational effectiveness based on the following criteria: (a) prioritized sensor alerts, (b) prioritized threat escalation, (c) measured severity of events, and (d) measured analytic completeness. Test and demonstrate the improved capability based on the performance metrics detailed for Phase I. Provide analytics, SI tools, models, prototypes, T&E and demonstration results, and interface requirements. Develop a final report to include a detailed design of the system and a plan for transition to the program of record in Phase III.

Advance these capabilities to TRL-7 and integrate the technology into the Maritime Tactical Command and Control POR, Marine Air-Ground Task Force Command and Control, or ISR processing platforms at the Marine Corps Information Operations Center.

Once conceptually and technically validated, demonstrate dual-use applications of this technology in civilian law enforcement and security services.

title: Electro-Optical/Infrared Tactical Decision Aid
summary: Develop an Electro-Optical/Infrared (EO/IR) Tactical Decision Aid (TDA) for surface and air sensors in maritime, littoral, and inland environments.
description:
Objective:
Develop an Electro-Optical/Infrared (EO/IR) Tactical Decision Aid (TDA) for surface and air sensors in maritime, littoral, and inland environments.

Description:
The United States Navy (USN) requires the capability to rapidly predict the performance of sensors that depend on the propagation of electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) radiation (i.e., wavelengths from 0.4 to 12 micron) in air. Sensor performance is subject to environmental/meteorologic conditions, as well as sensor, platform, background/clutter, and target characteristics. For a given sensor on a platform and a target in background/clutter, a forecaster should be able to determine key performance metrics; for example, maximum detection range based on the forecasted meteorological conditions. In this way, USN commanders can make tactical decisions based on the predicted sensor performance given ambient/forecast weather conditions. Key modeling components within a TDA include the land/maritime surface background, target signature, radiative transfer, and sensor performance models. These models are often interdependent, requiring feedback between them (e.g., radiative transfer between target and background models is needed to compute the contrast of the target in the background, which then feeds into a sensor performance model).

Target Acquisition Weapons Software (TAWS), a successor to Electro-Optic Tactical Decision Aid (EOTDA), was originally developed by the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) and released in 1998. Later a target scene model improvement for selected high-resolution targets was implemented with Multi-Service Electro-optics Signature (MuSES). The USN is looking for an innovative and accurate EO/IR TDA, which would be an alternative/improvement to TAWS. Improvements could include support for three dimensional meteorological inputs. The primary challenge for implementing an EO/IR TDA is the methodical verification and validation (V&V) of the constituent models and submodels being developed. This SBIR topic seeks innovative solutions to the development of an EO/IR TDA with particular focus on the methods proposed to verify and validate developed models. A list of prior V&V efforts on proposed submodels should be made clear in the responses to this solicitation, as well as the proposed means/methods to conduct V&V under a Phase II and/or Phase III.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

Phase I:
Develop a concept for an EO/IR TDA model architecture and verify the radiative transfer model can solve basic thermal transport problems (e.g., conduction, convection, radiation) with analytic solutions. Ensure facets/grid points can be individually sampled to provide their temperature and spectral radiance. Create a land/sea background model where spatiotemporally varying clutter can be added in Phase II. Create a CUBI thermal target model and a generic, band-selectable imaging sensor (e.g., 3-5 micron midwave IR (MWIR) imager) model.

Phase II:
Implement the EO/IR TDA model into a working prototype and ensure support for a wide range of generic representative targets (e.g., car, truck, ship, boat, plane, unmanned aerial system (UAS)) and a wide range of generic representative sensors (e.g., 0.4-0.7 micron visual band imager, 1.06 micron laser designator, 0.9-1.7 micron shortwave IR (SWIR) imager, 3-5 micron MWIR imager, 8-12 micron longwave IR (LWIR) imager). Develop and add specific target and sensor models, some of which will be provided by the government and might be classified. Add representative spatiotemporally varying clutter in the scene and validate the background/clutter model against prior field data collections. Validate the radiative transfer model with a complex thermal transport experiment using a CUBI target in the laboratory. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Work in Phase II may become classified. Please see note in the Description.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Develop and add other specific target and sensor models, some of which will be provided by the government and might be classified. Validate the EO/IR TDA using previously collected field data. Design and execute an experimental validation of the EO/IR TDA using state-of-the art meteorological sensors and scientific grade (or better) thermal imagers, as well as a representative target and sensor to test the capability to determine sensor performance (e.g., maximum detection range).

title: Autonomous Multi-Intelligence Acoustic Reasoning Agent for Anti-Submarine Warfare
summary: Develop an autonomous Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) reasoning agent that fuses passive and active acoustic detections with non-acoustic maritime situational data, environmental acoustic propagation context, and platform/target behavior models to produce explainable contact assessments, track hypotheses, and recommended sensor-tasking actions; and supports deployment on an Unmanned Surface Vehicle…
description:
Objective:
Develop an autonomous Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) reasoning agent that fuses passive and active acoustic detections with non-acoustic maritime situational data, environmental acoustic propagation context, and platform/target behavior models to produce explainable contact assessments, track hypotheses, and recommended sensor-tasking actions; and supports deployment on an Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) with constrained communications, power, and computing conditions.

Description:
The Department of the Navy (DON) seeks development of an autonomous decision-support and reasoning capability for ASW that can reduce dependence on continuous human interpretation of complex acoustic displays and enable future distributed unmanned ASW operations. Current ASW performance is heavily dependent on trained operators who interpret passive narrowband, passive broadband, Demodulation of Noise (DEMON), and other acoustic products while simultaneously incorporating situational knowledge such as geography, bathymetry, Conductivity Temperature and Depth (CTD) data for sound-speed structure, Global Positioning System (GPS), Automatic Identification System (AIS), organic/non-organic tracks, surface traffic, tactical geometry, and expected target behaviors. This human fusion process is effective but difficult to scale across persistent unmanned systems operating at range, under intermittent communications, and in acoustically cluttered environments.

This SBIR topic requests development of an autonomous ASW agent that can ingest heterogeneous acoustic detections and associated confidence measures, correlate them with non-acoustic common operating picture data, reason over environmental acoustic propagation, and maintain multiple explainable track and classification hypotheses over time. The capability should explicitly account for confusers such as merchant shipping, fishing vessels, biologics, own-force and friendly surface ship contributions, reverberation/clutter, and geographically-dependent propagation effects. The resulting system should not be a single-sensor classifier only; it should demonstrate multi-source temporal reasoning that can explain why a contact is assessed as likely submarine, non-submarine, ambiguous, or requiring additional sensing. The approach should be modular and compatible with Navy acoustic processing and performance-prediction workflows, while allowing Navy-provided threat behavior models, environmental data, and acoustic feature streams to be incorporated without redesign. Submissions should include a description of prior sensor fusion development that will serve as a baseline for the proposed ASW fusion architecture.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

Phase I:
Develop a concept for the proposed software architecture for an autonomous ASW reasoning agent, including data schemas for acoustic detections, Common Operation Picture (COP)/non-acoustic inputs, environmental context, target-behavior priors, uncertainty representation, and operator-interpretable explanations. Demonstrate proof-of-concept using representative or open acoustic and maritime datasets to demonstrate fusion of passive acoustic features with disparate data features. Prepare a Phase I final report that includes a performance assessment plan that quantitively assesses metrics such as track purity, false-track/alarm suppression, classification confidence calibration, explanation quality, latency, and robustness to missing/degraded inputs.

Phase II:
Develop prototype software with implementation capability that should ingest multiple acoustic modalities, correlate acoustic contacts with non-acoustic maritime tracks, maintain multiple hypotheses, and recommend sensor-tasking or unmanned maneuver options to improve classification confidence. Demonstrate the software in simulation or replay using geographically realistic bathymetry, sound-speed profiles, surface traffic, environmental noise, and target/non-target behavior profiles. Include a transition package that documents Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), modular interfaces to Navy propagation/performance-prediction tools, model-card style documentation, training/evaluation data requirements, and a plan for integration with unmanned ASW mission systems. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Work and/or data used in Phase II may become classified. Please see note in the Description.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Sensor fusion for acoustic clutter reduction supports seismic surveys of commercial oil prospecting and more general ocean exploration efforts in support of the ocean acoustics National Naval Responsibility. Understanding how to fuse ocean ambient sound in terms of its spatial, temporal, and frequency contributions as well as elucidating information about air and seafloor interfaces will provide a clearer picture of the undersea world where the Navy operates. Commercial dual-use applications may include maritime domain awareness, port and harbor security, offshore infrastructure monitoring, autonomous vessel operations, illegal fishing detection, environmental acoustic monitoring, and marine mammal or vessel-noise characterization.

title: High Sensitivity Tunneling Magnetoresistive Magnetometers
summary: Modernize United States capabilities to produce ultra-low size, weight, power, and cost (SWAP-C) tunneling magnetoresistive magnetometers with industry leading sensitivities.
description:
Objective:
Modernize United States capabilities to produce ultra-low size, weight, power, and cost (SWAP-C) tunneling magnetoresistive magnetometers with industry leading sensitivities.

Description:
Many Navy systems utilize magnetometer technologies for the remote detection, localization, and classification of ferrous objects. Decades of research into different technologies including optically pumped magnetometers have provided highly sensitive technologies which meet most Navy sensitivity needs. However, higher sensitivity magnetometers also possess increased SWAP-C, which limits their applicability in many Navy applications.

Therefore, there is a direct need for highly sensitive magnetometers that are also compact, low cost, and low power to support a broader range of Navy mission requirements including one-way attack vehicles, expeditionary warfare, mine warfare, and swarming systems. Over the past 30 years, an adjacent technology known as tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR) has had drastic improvements in system sensitivities, unlocking a potential new regime of magnetometer technologies that exhibit ultra-low SWAP-C while maintaining Navy relevant sensitivities.

Design Requirements:

-Size: less than 10 mm x 10 mm per axis

-Power: less than 100 mW per axis

-Sensitivity: less than 50 pT/rt(Hz) @ 1 Hz

-Frequency Range: DC-500KHz

-Dynamic Range: -100 uT to 100 uT

-Nonlinearity over dynamic range: less than 0.1 %

-Standardized per unit electrical packaging

Phase I:
Produce a concept for single-axis TMR sensors that possess a design that satisfies the above criteria and also include a per sensor voltage-to-field calibration for confirmation by stakeholders. Provide an analysis or discussion of the potential tradeoffs in the Phase I report if the design concept cannot meet the design objectives. (Note: Justification for the prior should include comparative analysis of COTS capabilities, U.S. and International.)

Phase II:
Fabricate 6 or 9 prototype systems for evaluation and testing in a vector configuration including voltage-to-field calibration for each sensor. Demonstrate that the prototypes achieve or show potential for meeting the design requirements and intended use applications. Conduct testing in conjunction with Navy personnel. Address both cost effectiveness and manufacturability feasibility as part of the prototype test and evaluation. Consult the appropriate acquisition program office for any additional evaluation metrics needed for Phase III. Perform potential commercialization cost analysis to estimate at production cost per unit and prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Apply the knowledge gained in Phase II to build an advanced vector TMR prototype that meets appropriate technology readiness level (TRL) metrics set by the acquisition program office. Support the Navy for test and validation of the system for certified Navy use. Develop manufacturing plans to facilitate transition to a UUV program of record.

Explore the potential to transfer these TMR sensors for potential commercial use in magnetic surveying and UXO detection.

References:
• TDK: “New Development Based on High-Sensitivity Nivia xMR Sensor: Measurement of Weak Magnetic Fields from Minute Areas.” https://product.tdk.com/en/techlibrary/developing/bio-sensor/migne-xmr-sensor.html

title: Improved Ionosphere D-region Specification for High Frequency Propagation
summary: Develop tools and/or techniques to improve characterization of the D-region ionosphere sufficient for skillful ionosphere model specification and forecast over climatology and that demonstrate the impact of improved methodology on ionosphere accuracy for use by high frequency (HF) and very low frequency (VLF) signal propagation tools.
description:
Objective:
Develop tools and/or techniques to improve characterization of the D-region ionosphere sufficient for skillful ionosphere model specification and forecast over climatology and that demonstrate the impact of improved methodology on ionosphere accuracy for use by high frequency (HF) and very low frequency (VLF) signal propagation tools.

Description:
HF and VLF skywave propagation depend on knowledge of the altitudinal structure of the ionosphere for reliable system operation. The D-region ionosphere, a region typically between 60-90 km altitude above the Earth’s surface, is particularly challenging to predict with sufficient fidelity for skywave mission planning because the region is difficult to measure with in situ measurements. Remote sensing methods provide a limited dataset from which to develop detailed physical and assimilative models that can reliably produce the regional behavior on a day-to-day basis.

Operational models like the D-Region Absorption Product (D-RAP) produce maps of outage areas as a function of radio frequency (RF) to inform HF system users of anticipated degradation or blackouts due to radiation increases. These predictions primarily address HF absorption due to solar X-ray flares at low and mid-latitudes and do not address the VLF propagation use case. While solar X-ray flares are important effects with Navy relevance, the effects of flares typically only last for a few hours and occur 10-20 times a year. For sufficient use in HF absorption and VLF propagation applications, a D-region ionosphere is required to capture seasonal, solar cycle, and day-to-day variability at all latitudes in addition to solar flare phenomenology.

The intended capability is improved D-region specification and forecast in the 60-70 km and 80-90 km altitude regions for VLF propagation and HF absorption, particularly day-to-day variability and in the high latitude regions at night.

Climatological models like the International Reference Ionosphere (IRI) produce an altitude profile at D-region altitudes. The IRI model is based on about a hundred historical rocket profiles, so it captures some of the basic day/night, latitudinal, and seasonal variations in the D-region ionosphere but the model does not capture day-to-day variations or solar X-ray flare events. The model may be sufficient for some HF propagation applications but has been shown to be severely deficient in the high latitude region and during nighttime. In addition, the observations used to create the model do not accurately capture the shape of the lower D-region, which is required for VLF propagation applications.

The Next-generation Ionospheric Model for Operations (NIMO) is an assimilative geospace model developed to address operational USN space weather needs in the ionosphere. NIMO harnesses contributions from both near real-time data and state-of-the-art implementation of ionospheric theory to provide hindcasts, nowcasts, and forecasts for operational or research purposes. NIMO is currently configured to assimilate various types of electron density measurements through the Ionospheric Data Assimilation Four-Dimensional (IDA-4D) data assimilation schema. The D-region is not included in the data assimilation process but is simply added in post processing to the bottom of the electron density grid. The D-region model includes influence from changes in the solar conditions, but uses a climatological model for the neutral atmosphere, so it does not capture the day-to-day variability that is seen in the ionosphere.

Key performance Metrics/Goals:

Techniques to improve the global specification and forecast of the D-region ionosphere is sought with particular emphasis on the low latitudes (< 30 degrees) and high latitudes (> 60 degrees). Note: Any measurement techniques should provide measurements or any model should ingest measurements of the D-region and demonstrate improvement over existing models in two key altitude regions: 60-70 km altitude and 80-90 km altitude, which are required for VLF propagation and HF absorption, respectively.

Key parameters include

• Specify electron density in the 60-70km and 80-90km regions within 10% error. Alternatively, an improvement 75% of the time over existing models is sought.
• Specification at a temporal cadence of 5-15 minutes
• Specification at a spatial resolution of 5 degrees in latitude and longitude

Technical concepts may include developing prototype concept improvements to measurement techniques and systems, developing improvements to data exploitation and modeling, or a combination of the two.

Phase I:
Develop a technical concept for improvements to D-region specification. Establish the feasibility of the concept. Provide required Phase I deliverables that include a detailed plan of operational implementation with sufficient evidence to justify claims of skill improvement.

Phase II:
Develop a prototype system that improves state-of-the-art forecasting for D-region morphology and validate the results in an operationally relevant environment. Depending on the nature of the Phase I concept demonstration, deliver a functioning prototype instrument demonstrated in an operationally relevant environment with low-latency data-feed or a functioning model software package that exploits operationally relevant data sources in near-real-time. Validate either solution using an appropriate ray-trace simulation tool that demonstrates improved performance over current state-of-the-art systems. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Deliver and integrate a new D-region model concept or data exploitation methodology into the NIMO for USN operational ionosphere prediction needs. Transition new measurement systems to an appropriate operator. Note: Delivery of the measurement system will be dependent upon the intended operational mode and target environment.

References:
• Akmaev, R. A., et al. "DRAP model validation: I. Scientific report." Technical Report (2010). https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/stp/drap/DRAP-V-Report1.pdf
• Bilitza, D., Pezzopane, M., Truhlik, V., Altadill, D., Reinisch, B. W. and Pignalberi, A. “The International Reference Ionosphere model: A review and description of an ionospheric benchmark.” Reviews of Geophysics, 60, e2022RG000792, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1029/2022RG000792
• Burrell, A. G. et al. “Next-generation Ionospheric Model for Operations – validation and demonstration for space weather and research.” Ann. Geophys., 44, 2026, pp. 303-329. https://doi.org/10.5194/angeo-44-303-2026, 2026.

title: Expeditionary Water Quality Sensors
summary: Develop simple-to-use water quality test kits or electronic sensors that require minimal training to enable personnel in the field to rapidly meet Technical Bulletin Medical 577 (TB-MED 577) requirements to certify potable water without liquid reagents.
description:
Objective:
Develop simple-to-use water quality test kits or electronic sensors that require minimal training to enable personnel in the field to rapidly meet Technical Bulletin Medical 577 (TB-MED 577) requirements to certify potable water without liquid reagents.

Description:
Expeditionary forces need updated water testing capabilities to support operations in austere, contested environments. Without proper water testing, water purified in the field are not certified potable for consumption. This creates an unacceptable logistics burden to transport water, or a health risks when consuming untested water; hindering the self-sufficiency, readiness, and lethality required for operations against a pacing challenge. Current approved state-of-the-art water quality testing kits are accurate but cumbersome, and overly complex, requiring chemical reagents, significant operator training, and for some parameters shipping to a certified lab. Present water quality testing methods are not practical for the small, distributed Stand-in Forces operating in expeditionary conditions.

In the event of detection of certain pathogens and contaminants, confirmation through certified laboratories may be required, necessitating sample transportation to CONUS, host-nation, or ally facilities—a process that can take 4-6 weeks. Delays of this magnitude are operationally unacceptable for forces in contested environments that need immediate assurance of water safety at the point of use. In addition, many critical parameters that impact water safety—including heavy metals, organic chemicals, and other contaminants—are not reliably tested with currently fielded sensors.

Force Design 2030 compels distributed forces to reduce their reliance on centralized logistics convoys; therefore, small units are increasingly required to produce and consume water at the tactical edge and at the point of need. Without a reliable and practical method to verify water quality in the field, these units face an alarming tradeoff between logistics supply certainty and warfighter health.

Therefore, the Navy needs simple, field-ready solutions to certify that expeditionary purified water conforms to TB-MED 577 short term potability military field water standards (STW MFWS) without external laboratory support. This SBIR topic seeks the development of new sensors and/or methodologies that will significantly improve existing water testing field kits. Improvements sought include but are not limited to: size and weight, more rapid testing results, simpler procedures requiring minimal training, elimination of liquid chemical reagents, and cost. Proposals can address one or more targeted improvements and can target one or more of the water parameters listed in the STP MFWS, such as physical properties, chemical properties, microbial contamination, chemical warfare agents, or radiological. Resulting improved sensors or methodologies must be integratable into future modernized water testing kits to allow squad- and platoon-level forces to verify compliance with TB MED 577 water safety standards in the field, reducing risk to personnel and decreasing reliance on vulnerable resupply chains. The expected end state of this effort is a fully developed, ruggedized, integratable sensor or set of sensors that enable rapid, automated testing of water quality in expeditionary environments in under 15 minutes (Threshold) / under 5 minutes (Objective), and/or detect all microbial threats in under 1 hour (Threshold) / under 15 minutes (Objective) without incubation or liquid reagents. Modular systems targeting specific critical parameters are equally encouraged and will be evaluated on technical merit.

Phase I:
Establish the technical feasibility of a preliminary conceptual design(s) of a new sensor or series of sensors, capable of rapidly verifying water quality in austere environments without requiring external laboratory support. Define and develop candidate concepts and sensor technologies. Conduct research that will assess the integration potential of the solution(s) into a portable kit for squad- (~13 Marines) and platoon- (40-50 Marines) level operations. Include approaches that may include modeling, simulation, and benchtop testing to evaluate detection accuracy, operational ruggedness, and ease of operation, all while referencing water safety requirements outlined in TB-MED 577. Deliver a final report documenting the technical progress; results of feasibility analyses; a breakdown of size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C) improvements and/or trade-offs; performance projections of candidate concepts and sensor technologies; and a defensible preliminary design concept. Ensure that the new sensor(s) should not require liquid chemical reagents, which are problematic due to a short shelf life and customs clearance. Identify anticipated technical risks, mitigation strategies, and a clear development path for Phase II prototype, fabrication, and validation in the final Phase I report.

Phase II:
Design, develop, fabricate, and test a prototype sensor or series of sensors capable of rapidly verifying water quality in simulated expeditionary environments. Ensure that the prototype integrates selected sensor technologies into a ruggedized, portable form factor appropriate for use at the squad and platoon level. Develop hardware and software interfaces, refine user interaction for minimal training burden, and ensure the sensor(s) functions across a range of environmental conditions. Demonstrate and validate the prototype through laboratory and field testing against relevant key water quality parameters such as microbial contamination, heavy metals, salinity, turbidity, and chemical pollutants. Conduct testing that should confirm performance relative to defined metrics including accuracy, test time, ease of use, and environmental durability. Provide the following required Phase II deliverables: prototype hardware, technical data documenting performance results, field evaluation in coordination with a military exercise if practicable, and a detailed plan for Phase III transition opportunities within military and commercial application.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Support transition to the Program Manager Engineer Systems (PM ES) at Marine Corps Systems Command for integration into the USMC family of water systems and direct use by small units during distributed operations.

Beyond military use, the technology has strong dual-use potential. Civilian applications include humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operations, rapid deployment by first responders in areas with compromised infrastructure, commercial water treatment facilities, and consumer safety monitoring in developing regions. The commercial pathway may include partnerships with outdoor equipment providers, municipal water authorities, and NGOs focused on clean water access.

References:
• “Technology Assessment of Water Treatment Devices for Small-Scale Production.” https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/trecms/pdf/AD1214090.pdf
• “Technical Bulletin Medical 577 (TBMED 577).” https://quartermaster.army.mil/pwd/Publications/Water/TB_Med_577_15_Dec_2005.pdf

title: Rapid Thermoplastic Patching Capability for Legacy Thermoset Airframe Sustainment
summary: Deliver a rapid, high-strength thermoplastic patching capability for legacy thermoset composite airframes by developing the necessary interfacial enabling technologies to fuse the incompatible polymer systems.
description:
Objective:
Deliver a rapid, high-strength thermoplastic patching capability for legacy thermoset composite airframes by developing the necessary interfacial enabling technologies to fuse the incompatible polymer systems.

Description:
Current composite airframe repair methodologies rely on a combination of wet-layups, B-staged epoxy prepregs, and bonded pre-cured thermoset patches. While pre-cured patches are the standard for high-quality depot repairs due to their autoclave-consolidated strength and “inspectability”, they present significant operational and logistical limitations. All these traditional methods require secondary adhesive bonding (using paste or film adhesives) to attach the repair to the airframe. This secondary bond is the inherent weak link of the repair, demanding long thermal cure cycles (often 4 to 24 hours), strict environmental controls, and burdensome cold-storage logistics (freezers) for the B-staged resins and adhesives. Furthermore, these out-of-autoclave epoxy repairs often struggle to meet the high service temperature requirements of advanced tactical aircraft.

This SBIR topic seeks to evolve the current pre-cured repair methodology by transitioning from secondary adhesive bonding to high-speed fusion welding. The objective is to develop the capability to use pre-consolidated, high-temperature thermoplastic patches (e.g., Carbon/PEEK, Carbon/PEKK) on legacy thermoset aircraft (epoxy/Bismaleimide [BMI]). By replacing the lengthy adhesive cure cycle with a rapid welding process, this technology aims to achieve flight-ready repairs in expeditionary and carrier-based environments in a fraction of the time.

Because thermoplastics melt and thermosets do not, achieving a structural weld between these dissimilar materials is the primary barrier to fielding this capability. The Department of War seeks complete thermoplastic patching solutions that incorporate the requisite chemical or mechanical interfacial enablers—such as plasma surface activation, novel chemical tie-layers, or laser-ablated mechanical interlocking. These enablers must allow the thermoplastic patch to successfully fuse with a fully cured, legacy thermoset airframe using portable ultrasonic, resistance- or -induction welding equipment. The outcome must be a deployable repair process that eliminates cold-storage logistics, restores full structural integrity, meets high service temperature demands, and drastically reduces Aircraft on Ground (AOG) time.

Phase I:
Develop a conceptual thermoplastic patching process and demonstrate the physical viability of the proposed enabling interfacial technology (e.g., tie-layers, surface functionalization). Establish the feasibility of the conceptual process. Perform coupon-level mechanical testing (such as lap-shear and peel-strength) to empirically prove that the thermoplastic-to-thermoset weld achieves a structural load transfer that is comparable to, or exceeds, baseline epoxy adhesive repairs. Deliver a detailed theoretical model explaining the fusion mechanism, an initial assessment of the repair's thermal limits (ensuring the parent thermoset is not degraded), and a conceptual workflow for field-level application that eliminates the need for depot-level infrastructure or cold-storage consumables.

Phase II:
Develop, optimize, and scale a patching capability prototype to representative legacy airframe structures, such as contoured wing skins or stiffened panels. Perform the proposed thermoplastic patch repair using field-representative heating equipment (e.g., portable induction or resistance welding). Validate the repair through rigorous structural testing, including fatigue spectrum loading, thermal cycling, and damage tolerance assessments, to prove airworthiness. Deliver a prototype repair kit and process documentation. Target metrics must include a complete return-to-flight repair cycle of under 4 hours, restoration of > 115% of the parent structure's Design Ultimate Load, and thermal isolation ensuring the thermoset parent material remains below its degradation threshold during the welding process. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Transition the validated thermoplastic patching capability to Naval Air Systems Command (NAVAIR) and Air Force Life Cycle Management Center (AFLCMC) for integration into legacy platforms. Incorporate the materials, tooling, and process parameters into standardized Structural Repair Manuals (SRMs) for platforms such as the F/A-18, F-35, or V-22, providing expeditionary units with a rapid, out-of-autoclave, room-temperature-storable repair solution.

Commercial dual-use applications include rapid repair for the commercial airline industry, structural maintenance for composite wind turbine blades, and automotive crash repair for high-performance composite vehicles.

title: Navy Shipboard Gas Turbine Rotating Detonation Combustor Operation with Diesel Fuel
summary: Develop and demonstrate a scaled high density Rotating Detonation Combustor (RDC) that uses NATO F76 diesel fuel (MIL-DTL-16884R) and perform thermodynamic analysis on developed Navy RDC equipped shipboard gas turbine concepts to determine related performance benefits including reduction of stack up length, efficiency improvements, design limitations, and development gaps.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate a scaled high density Rotating Detonation Combustor (RDC) that uses NATO F76 diesel fuel (MIL-DTL-16884R) and perform thermodynamic analysis on developed Navy RDC equipped shipboard gas turbine concepts to determine related performance benefits including reduction of stack up length, efficiency improvements, design limitations, and development gaps.

Description:
As background, the typical arrangement used on U.S. Navy surface combatants consists of four (4) large (20+MW class – GE LM-2500) gas turbines for propulsion and three 3 smaller (3 MW class – Rolls Royce 501-K34) gas turbines for ship service electrical power generation.

Presently U.S. gas turbine powered warships use simple cycle machines. However, complex cycles with reheat and other cycle enhancements have been considered and analyzed with the potential for increased efficiency. Further examinations have been performed to evaluate improvements in maintainability/reliability, overall generator set power density/stack up length, and alternative configuration installation flexibility for use in overall electric plant designs.

RDCs are advanced power-generation and propulsion devices that operate by propagating one or more supersonic detonation waves continuously around an annular chamber. As fresh fuel and oxidizer are continuously injected into the channel, the rotating shock wave rapidly compresses and ignites the mixture, creating a self-sustaining zone of intense heat and pressure. Thermodynamically, RDCs utilize a detonation-driven pressure-gain cycle, which is most accurately modeled by the Fickett-Jacobs-Salsburg (FJS) cycle and frequently approximated as the constant-volume Humphrey cycle. Unlike conventional gas turbines that rely on the constant-pressure Brayton cycle, the FJS detonation cycle in an RDC generates a substantial net increase in total pressure across the combustor. This inherent pressure gain drastically reduces the workload required by upstream mechanical compressors and significantly boosts the overall thermal efficiency and power output of the gas turbine system. While initial government and industry investigations have centered on the use of RDCs in aerospace applications, future shipboard applications will require a greater understanding of the ability to operate with diesel fuel for long continuous operation as well as a quantification of performance benefits that can be achieved in overall shipboard electric architecture design.

While not required, discussions with Navy shipboard gas turbine Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEM) are recommended.

Phase I:
Perform an analysis of an RDC combustor ignition and continuous operation with NATO F76 fuel by the end of the Base period. Assemble and demonstrate an initial limited laboratory experiment/subscale test to verify analysis findings in coordination with Navy personnel. Complete a conceptual design for a combustor prototype and associated liquid fuel system, to include prototype design refinements, fabrication approach, and testing strategy that should include ignition and endurance operation with defined measurements in coordination with Navy personnel and within the scope of a Phase II budget. Prepare a Phase II plan.

Phase II:
Construct a combustor prototype and associated liquid fuel system. Perform startup and endurance testing for up to 500 hours as defined in Phase I utilizing F76 fuel. Based upon results generated from testing, conduct thermodynamic analyses/model of a marine gas turbine utilizing an RDC primary combustor as well as a thermodynamic analysis/models of marine gas turbine reheat cycles utilizing an RDC inter-turbine (single reheat) and intra-turbine (continuous reheat) in collaboration with Navy personnel. From this analysis, determine impact on overall efficiency, reliability, operating life, power density, and future development gaps. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Demonstrate a full-scale liquid fuel combustor operating continuously for 500 hours. Based on Phase II analysis, develop a full-scale RDC-based gas turbine, either simple or complex cycle, and conduct performance testing prior to an at sea demonstration. Once complete, examine and upgrade the system for marinization requirements accounting material and maintainability improvements to successfully operate in a naval environment.

Examine and demonstrate the RDC based gas turbine in a CIPES electric plant configuration to validate ship benefits for overall operational performance and improvement in platform increases in power density. Commercial dual use application may include commercial maritime ships and offshore drilling and production platforms.

title: Rapid Imagery Creation for Navy Training
summary: Develop technology to use historic real-world satellite imagery and then rapidly (10 minutes or less) modify it to reflect a training scenario order of battle (aircraft, ships, vehicles, etc.) to allow imagery analysts to practice their tradecraft underway or ashore in support of maritime exercises.
description:
Objective:
Develop technology to use historic real-world satellite imagery and then rapidly (10 minutes or less) modify it to reflect a training scenario order of battle (aircraft, ships, vehicles, etc.) to allow imagery analysts to practice their tradecraft underway or ashore in support of maritime exercises.

Description:
Currently, imagery analysts are excluded from, or extremely limited in, participating in dynamic Navy operational and staff training such as Surface Warfare Advanced Team Trainer (SWATT), Information Warfare Advanced Team Trainer (IWATT), Fleet Synthetic Training General Commander/Joint (FST-GC/J), and Commander Training Unit Exercise (COMPTUEX).This is due to the limited ability to dynamically generate the required products for imagery analysts within a reasonable amount of time at a quality that supports training.

Currently, either summaries are provided to the training audience circumventing the imagery analysts all together or providing GRAPHPLOTS - the equivalence of stick figure drawing - to track the order of battle (OOB) made up of aircraft, ships, vehicles, etc., without any use of actual imagery or geospatial analysis.

A technology to address this shortfall would need to take real-world geo-rectified imagery as a base and then rapidly adjust/modify the image to reflect the desired OOB and in a National Imagery Transition Format (NTIF) to be provided to the training audience for imagery analysts to process.

For example, in real-life Port A, identified by Basic Encyclopedia (BE) number, is of high interest and has a collection requirement against it for satellite imagery to be collected. In reality, Port A has three Kilo-class submarines and one Luhu-class destroyer, but in the scenario things have dynamically changed such that one of those submarines is now underway and an additional Luda I-class Destroyer has arrived, requiring the rapid (less than 10 minutes) production of an NITF image depicting two Kilo-class submarines, one Luhu DD, and one Luda I DDG to provide the training audience for analysis. The same would be required for airfields depicting aircraft movement as well.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

Phase I:
Create concept formulation for electro-optical imagery, determine technical feasibility of rapidly generating an NITF image, and validation through the modification of a single image (note: format and quality are not relevant here) to change the depicted order of battle. Determine technical feasibility of infrared (IR), and Synthetic Aperture RADAR (SAR) imagery. Create demonstration standard sufficient to assess preservation of imagery characteristics necessary for realistic imagery-analysis training.

Phase II:
Develop prototype technology on the Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRnet) to effectively execute the example provided in the Description for Electro-Optical (EO) imagery. Determine a site by BE number (from a limited provided subset), outputting a near real-world NITF image of the desired OOB (from a limited inventory of platforms). Demonstrate standard sufficient to assess preservation of imagery characteristics. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Work in Phase II may become classified. Please see note in Description section.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
This technology would be usable and empower any dynamic military training opportunity to support Imagery/GEOINT analysis. Possible transition to National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, Naval Information Forces (NAVIFOR), Center for Information Warfare Training (CIWT), Carrier Strike Group FOUR and FIFTEEN (CSG-4/15), Tactical Training Group Pacific (TTGP), Tactical Training Group Atlantic (TTGL) and NSWC Corona.

This product will ideally reside on the SIPRNet as a portal for users to query on RED networks, such as NCTE-RED OPS, NMCI SIPR, SIPR TRANET, then providing the requested images.

Potential work in Phase III could include prototype refinement, testing, production, and transition support.
