title: Field-Friendly Super Intelligence and Machine Learning Systems
summary: Develop an Super Intelligence/Machine Learning (SI/ML) method that achieves the high-performance accuracy of modern Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) while mitigating their limitations.
description:
Objective:
Develop an Super Intelligence/Machine Learning (SI/ML) method that achieves the high-performance accuracy of modern Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) while mitigating their limitations.

Description:
Current DNN architectures suffer from inherent "Black Box" vulnerabilities, demanding massive computational scaling and offering no clear link between parameter count and performance. The proposed model must address these shortfalls:

- Optimized Resource Utilization: Unlike DNNs that heuristically overparameterize to boost accuracy, the proposed model must quantitatively map parameter count to expected performance and enable users to identify the minimum configuration required for mission success, significantly reducing computational overhead, complexity, and deployment costs.

- Transparency: The model must replace opaque, distributed neural layers with novel methods for interpretability and trust that go beyond the current post-hoc techniques. By making input-output logic similar to standard programming code, the model should ensure decisions are easily explainable, verifiable, and compliant with auditing standards.

- Reliability: The model must recognize whether it can provide a reliable output for a given problem instance, which will address another well-known criticism of DNNs wherein performance is typically measured as an average, e.g., average accuracy, over many instances of a problem and will help build user trust and acceptability of the model vs DNNs, particularly in sensitive areas like person identification in a crowd video and identifying the source of a cyber-security violation.

The model must deliver DNN-level performance with superior speed and a reduced memory footprint, optimized for lean, secure processing on low-cost CPU and embedded edge hardware. By eliminating cloud-dependence, the model will maximize data privacy and operational security while substantially reducing power consumption compared to GPU-reliant models. It must operate flexibly across mixed CPU-GPU environments, allowing operators to dynamically balance throughput against computational cost. Beyond standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the model’s architecture must be extensible to transformer-based and multimodal models handling text, image, and video.

The metrics below establish outer-edge targets specifically for CNN-based image classification. While satisfying every metric is not mandatory, the model will be evaluated on the number of targets achieved and the viability of the engineering trade-offs.

• Comparison with Base Architecture of ResNet-18 and larger
• Comparison of the Number of Classes 10 and 100 using 3 datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, having different combinations of numbers of classes and total number of image pixels (number of channels*number of pixels per image)
• Mean Average Accuracy of Classification: Same as DNNs or higher
• Number of Parameters (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less
• Training MFLOPs/Image (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less 6. Training Memory Size (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less7. Inference MFLOPs/Image: 50% of DNNs or less8. Rate of Growth of Metrics (5), (6), and (7): Sublinear

In Phase II, similar metrics and their extensibility and relevance to transformers and multimodality scenarios (images and videos as well as their combinations with text to form LLMs and VLMs) will need to be provided and their implementation explained.

This STTR topic requires combinations of research and development, and proposers must demonstrate a strong partnership between the small business and a research institution.

The proposed solution should eliminate the dependency on complex computing infrastructure (e.g., GPUs) by delivering comparable performance on standard off-the-shelf hardware (CPUs, edge devices). It should optimize the cost-to-performance ratio, balancing accuracy with reductions in time, storage, and computational cost. Furthermore, the architecture should ensure robust explainability—like conventional software programs—and provide reliable confidence metrics to establish user trust. At a minimum, the method should result in the development of an alternative to existing CNN-based architectures for image classification.

The many problems with the modern SI/ML architectures and models mentioned earlier are well recognized and reported. Many researchers and companies are currently attempting to address these shortcomings, including a number of startups. Most of the better-known ones are doing so by modifying hardware and software of the industry-leading NVidia systems. None seems to be rethinking the basic formulation of the problem which underlies the direction taken in the approach of the Model. If successful, the Model may turn out to have a major impact on the Naval systems and SI/ML industry which is already very large and growing fast. The deeper impact that could result from the lean design of Model could significantly add to the societal reach of SI/ML methods.

Phase I:
Develop a minimal complexity design to assess the value of the concept of the model. (Note: The design does not have to be optimal but should serve as a feasibility to assess the art-of-the-possible, by conducting an adequate, convincing subset of experiments of those specified in the Description.) Conduct a feasibility study that should investigate all known options that meet or exceed the minimum performance parameters suggested in the Description and should also address the trade-offs and risks, in accordance with the level of innovation. Prioritize demonstrating feasibility on the core image classification challenge even though the long-term vision for the model is extensibility. Prepare a final Phase I report on the design and experimental results and a Phase II plan.

Phase II:
Develop a minimal complexity model prototype and test it with at least all the experiments listed in the Description, ensuring that the results should clearly assess the absolute and relative (to DNN) performances of the scaled operational optimal prototype, and its scalability with increasing data complexity via the specified metrics, to demonstrate the model’s capabilities from the Phase I study determined to be most feasible. Provide the optimal model prototype; a report containing designs and testing results and how they demonstrate the power and future potential of the prototype; and a Phase III plan for prototype evaluation and other potential efforts as necessary. Provide metrics and their extensibility and relevance to transformers and multimodality scenarios (images and videos as well as their combinations with text to form LLMs and VLMs) and their implementation explained. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Generalize the CNN-targeted prototype model so it also applies to Transformers. Convert the prototype to an industry-friendly replicable form, implementable in one or multiple more progressive versions, as advised by industrial experts. Evaluate it on industry-grade large datasets of large images from very large numbers of classes. Deliver the final model prototype and a report containing designs and testing data. (Note: Detailed mission descriptions and effectiveness requirements will be addressed at a higher level of classification.)

Light-weight visual classification systems have many applications, particularly for autonomous robots.

References:
• Hadjis, S.; Zhang, C.; Mitliagkas, I.; Iter, D. and Ré, C. “Omnivore: An Optimizer for Multi-device Deep Learning on CPUs and GPUs.” arXiv:1606.04487, 2016. https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04487
• Han, S.; Mao, H. and Dally, W.J. “Deep Compression: Compressing Deep Neural Networks with Pruning, Trained Quantization and Huffman Coding.” 4th International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2016. https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00149
• Chen, B.; Medini, T.; Farwell, J.; Gobriel, S.; Tai, C. and Shrivastava, A. “SLIDE: In Defense of Smart Algorithms over Hardware Acceleration for Large-Scale Deep Learning Systems.” arXiv:1903.03129, 2019. https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.03129
• Zhou, X.; Qu, X. and Pan, F. “A lightweight neural network model for security inspection targets.” 2022 IEEE 5th Advanced Information Management, Communicates, Electronic and Automation Control Conference (IMCEC), Chongqing, China, 2022, pp. 270-275. doi: 10.1109/IMCEC55388.2022.10019899
• Pinto, D.G. and Mane, S.B. “Energy Efficient Implementation of CNNs Using Pruning: Techniques and Insights.” 2025 International Conference on Information, Implementation, and Innovation in Technology (I2ITCON), Pune, India, 2025, pp. 1-5. doi: 10.1109/I2ITCON65200.2025.11210640 https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11210640

title: Growth and Production of As2S3 Waveguides
summary: Determine and demonstrate how thin film deposits of As2S3 can be grown on an appropriate cladding material and etched to form a low loss waveguide for photonic applications of the Stimulated Brillouin Scattering (SBS) non-linearity in Radio Frequency (RF) applications.
description:
Objective:
Determine and demonstrate how thin film deposits of As2S3 can be grown on an appropriate cladding material and etched to form a low loss waveguide for photonic applications of the Stimulated Brillouin Scattering (SBS) non-linearity in Radio Frequency (RF) applications.

Description:
Multiple academic papers have indicated that the reverse mode of the SBS interaction between acoustic phonons and coherent 1.55 µm photons can cause Stoke’s peak gain on RF sidebands. It is desirable to harvest that effect for application in the burgeoning field of RF photonics. However, for that to happen, it is desirable that methods be developed to optimize the growth and etching of quasi-epitaxial As2S3, the material with the largest known SBS coefficient. In order to achieve low optical loss, achieving extremely low surface roughness of as-deposited films (< 10 nm rms roughness) is required plus ways to preserve that in producing waveguides of around 100 nm thickness and with high confinement bottom and top cladding. While atomic layer deposition (ALD) growth has produced other chalcogenides with very flat, conformal surfaces, it has not been used for As2S3; moreover, that other material was amorphous as deposited and drastically changed optical properties when crystalized. It may be that highly directional growth onto pre-etched substrate mesas produce better performance waveguides in which to produce amplification. Lastly, it is essential to demonstrate a way to achieve extremely low loss signal transfer on and off the die if RF photonics is to outperform conventional electronics in the future.

Phase I proposals for this STTR topic shall name the deposition and etching techniques that will be developed under the base award and estimate the surface smoothness of both the as-deposited material and the finished waveguides. The work plan must allow the validation of these estimates during the Base award so that the preliminary Phase II plan can define with good certainty the properties achievable in Phase II if awarded.

Measurement of the optical properties of completed waveguides during the Base award is highly desirable. First demonstrations of a method of coupling to the waveguide with losses under 2 dB in the Phase I Option is also desirable. A work division where the non-profit develops the fabrication technology and the company develops the many GHz wide band amplifier and coupling technologies is one possible division of the work. A clear discussion of the dependencies and determinants of the ultimate performance as a photonic amplifier should be included in the initial proposal.

It is highly desirable that, by the effort’s end, how feasible it is that by varying the optical carrier power in and the waveguide length, RF signal gains from 5 to 20 dB can be achieved with total noise figures including all coupling losses of <6 (threshold, 3 objective) dB. Paths to wafer scale fabrication yield above 90% should also be defined.

Phase I:
Determine the technical feasibility of using the proposed deposition and lithography techniques to produce an in-line photonic amplifier based on the SBS effect in As2S3. Demonstrate the potential compatibility of this material with use of SiN structures including surface grating couplers (desirable). Establish high reliability estimates of the ultimate performance feasible from this combination of materials, fabrication processes, and simple photonic circuit and technology roadblocks.

Phase II:
Develop prototype amplifier circuits via multiple design/fab/ test cycles in the Phase II Base period. Define paths to wafer scale fabrication yield above 90%. The Phase II Option period, if exercised, would then be spent improving the fabrication technology in order to deliver a specific many GHz wideband amplifier to the photonic circuit selected in collaboration with the governmental cost share source. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
This STTR topic is designed to create an enabling technology, that is a generic way of producing analog amplification of RF sidebands on photonic carriers so as to advance RF photonics. If the SiN out-couplers mentioned can also be perfected, these component devices could replace other inhomogeneous material technologies that are capable of producing localized, small amplification. In particular, the large size and difficult to control bursts of energy produced by EDFA amplifiers when used in not-CW applications can be avoided in full PIC circuits. Co-design of the SiN layer and a grating coupler to it will enable use in data center processor interconnects applications. In Phase III, the materials technology of this topic would be refined and combine with device maturation efforts. Commercial applications most likely in the telecommunications and SI world. Military applications will be within electromagnetic warfare systems.

References:
• Eggleton, Benjamin J. et al. “Brillouin integrated photonics.” Nature Photonics 13 (10), pp. 664-677. https://opus.lib.uts.edu.au/handle/10453/136605
• Yang Liu, et al. “Circulator-Free Brillouin Photonic Planar Circuit.” Laser Photonics Rev. 2021, 15, 2000481. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/lpor.202000481

title: Validated Modular Autonomy for Undersea Multi-Vehicle Coordination
summary: Develop software modules for existing autonomous undersea vehicles that support and extend existing system autonomy with multi-vehicle coordination behaviors.
description:
Objective:
Develop software modules for existing autonomous undersea vehicles that support and extend existing system autonomy with multi-vehicle coordination behaviors.

Description:
Autonomous undersea vehicles performing expeditionary missions require state-of-the-art cooperative sensing and engagement capabilities. The Navy seeks to enhance those capabilities with modular software designed for reliability and operational effectiveness. The advancement sought is development of a modular coordination layer extending existing single vehicle with decentralized multi-vehicle behaviors to enable autonomous decision making under degraded communications, sensing, and PNT conditions.

The software prototype needs to take in mission requirements provided by existing Navy command and control (C2) systems and sensor data provided by multiple platforms and use those inputs to coordinate mission performance with other vehicles. It should be compatible with modular unmanned autonomy architectures already in use by the Navy, such as the Open Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (OpenAUV) architecture and the Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2). Within those architectures, the prototype must interface with existing autonomy designed for single-vehicle operations with minimal changes to already established systems. When the prototype is disabled or unnecessary, vehicle performance and behavior must conform to what would be expected of an unmodified single vehicle.

The multi-mission management functions of the software prototype need to use a decentralized C2 scheme that is robust in low-information environments and that degrades gracefully if communications or sensing are limited. The C2 scheme must demonstrate sufficient scalability to effectively manage many vehicles: tens to hundreds. Real-time C2 is a must.

The prototype should assume the primary sensing mode of each vehicle is acoustic. Realistic sensors include forward-look and side-scan sonar, possibly with a synthetic aperture. Cameras may be available, but if so, their field of view should not be assumed to allow for keeping other vehicles in sight. Realistic communications include acoustic modems with transmission rates of 5000 bps or less, possibly much less. Communications methods with higher transmission rates are unlikely to be available and may only be possible at extremely close range.

The prototype should assume that access to radar and satellite systems is extremely limited or non-existent. In particular, the prototype should not depend on regular access to global positioning system (GPS) data, and it should take into account the possibility that each vehicle is subject to position, navigation, and timing errors that increase in magnitude as each mission progresses.

The software prototype must include as an essential component a method of continuous validation that establishes and quantifies risk and trust for all autonomous decision-making, with an emphasis on repeatability. Deliverables must include the documentation and software necessary to implement this continuous validation method, as well as a report quantifying the efficacy of the method.

The ideal prototype will be mission agnostic, instead focusing on a generalized set of multi-vehicle behaviors and objectives.

The software prototype should minimize potential negative impacts on mission effectiveness, vehicle endurance, vehicle survivability, and operator workload. The prototype can include enabling hardware, provided that such hardware can be installed on existing autonomous undersea vehicles. The complexity of any vehicle modifications should be minimized. The prototype software and any accompanying hardware should also minimize their overall power consumption. Deliverable reports should include analysis identifying and quantifying any such impacts.

Phase I:
Develop a concept for an architecture for a prototype multi-vehicle mission module. Ensure that this architecture should provide an approach for decomposing missions into generalized multi-vehicle behaviors and objectives. Identify and design a method of continuous validation that establishes and quantifies risk and trust for autonomous decision-making. Provide required deliverables that include prototype module architecture designs; documentation for the method of continuous validation; and analysis of how those approaches attain the topic’s goals, including both academic research and validated modeling and simulation.

Phase II:
Develop a method of continuous validation and determine the extent to which that method can quantify risk for autonomous decision-making, including repeatability analysis. Validate the method itself against a series of reference vehicles running a set of standard missions.

Using the proposed method of continuous validation, develop the prototype software module. Analyze its performance on one or more reference vehicles running standard autonomy. Base the analysis on modeling and simulation, component-level testing, laboratory tank tests, and at least one in-water test outside of a laboratory environment.

Demonstrate reliability and operational effectiveness in subsea environments with low-bandwidth communications.

Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Assess the performance of the prototype method of continuous validation as it would be used by Fleet stakeholders for their autonomous vehicles. Modify the method as necessary in response to Fleet feedback and any discrepancies between expected and actual performance. Complete the prototype software module, any associated hardware, and the documentation necessary for integration into modular unmanned autonomy architectures already in use by the Navy.

References:
• Bovio, E., Cecchi, D. and Baralli, F. “Autonomous underwater vehicles for scientific and naval operations.” Annual Reviews in Control, 30(2), 2006, pp. 117-130. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S136757880600054X
• Fanelli, F. “Development and Testing of Navigation Algorithms for Autonomous Underwater Vehicles.” Springer, 2019. https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-15596-4
• Harris, C. A., Phillips, A. B., Dopico-Gonzalez, C. and Brito, M. P. “Risk and reliability modelling for multi-vehicle marine domains.” 2016 IEEE/OES Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUV). November 2016, pp. 286-293. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/7778685
• Razdan, R., Akbas, M. I., Sell, R., Bellone, M., Menase, M. and Malayjerdi, M. “Polyverif: An open-source environment for autonomous vehicle validation and verification research acceleration.” IEEE Access, 11, 2023, pp. 28343-28354. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/10075634
• Wang, F., Song, R., Zhou, R., Wang, X. and Chen, L. “Verification and Validation of Intelligent Vehicles: Objectives and Efforts From China.” IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Vehicles, 7 (2), 2022. Pp. 164-169. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/9826530

title: Self-Sustaining Wave Energy Capture for Persistent Autonomous Ocean-Going Systems
summary: Develop a human-portable wave energy capture device able to deploy autonomously and generate sufficient power to effectively recharge autonomous vehicles.
description:
Objective:
Develop a human-portable wave energy capture device able to deploy autonomously and generate sufficient power to effectively recharge autonomous vehicles.

Description:
Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles need regular recharging, and since they often operate far from human contact, their charging systems require a reliable, self-sustaining power source. The Office of Naval Research (ONR) believes the ideal power source will be a wave energy capture device (WECD). WECDs capture kinetic and potential energy generated by the movement of ocean waves on or near the surface of open water.

The desired WECD must be portable, specifically, designed as a set of components that can each be carried by one or two people who must be able to quickly assemble and disassemble those components. Components designed for one-person carry should weigh no more than 14 kg with largest dimension no greater than 1.9 m, while components designed for two-person carry should weigh no more than 45.4 kg with largest dimension no greater than 2.3 m. The WECD must be able to be relocated to areas of very different depths, including full ocean depth so the WECD’s design cannot require placement or anchoring on the sea floor. And since the WECD may need to deploy near the shore, its design must allow it to function in waters as shallow as 100 meters.

Ocean weather conditions can be challenging. The WECD should function reliably at Sea State 6 or less (very rough seas, with wave heights of 4 to 6 meters), and it should be able to survive conditions up to Sea State 8 (very high seas, with wave heights of 9 to 14 meters).

ONR assumes the WECD will be tethered to some device at or near the surface of the water. That tethered system may be an autonomous vehicle in loiter mode, and since loitering involves continuous vehicle movement, the WECD should operate reliably while in motion, and its design should leverage such motion to increase energy capture.

The WECD should produce a minimum of 20 kilowatt-hours (kWh) per day, but more is highly desirable. ONR believes 100+ kWh per day is achievable. Even in calm seas, the ideal WECD should produce sufficient electricity to charge a 2-kWh battery in 6 hours or less. Vehicle movement may be considered when ensuring this minimum level of power generation.

The desired WECD may be needed in areas where human assembly is impractical. Thus, the deliverables must include a prototype device capable of deploying the assembled WECD from the deck of a medium or large autonomous surface vessel. Like the WECD itself, the deployment device (DD) should function reliably in challenging weather conditions: Sea State 4 or less (moderate seas with wave heights of 1.25 to 2.5 meters).

Once deployed, very little of the WECD itself should be visible at the surface of the water. The WECD should minimize any increase in the visibility of the vehicle it is tethered to. This includes surface and airborne observation, both optically and by radar. Acoustic noise generated by the WECD should either be minimized or disguised to seem environmental or biological.

Cost for the WECD and associated DD should be minimized. ONR expects that under certain environmental conditions or mission requirements, WECDs may not be recoverable. At full-rate production, the ideal price will allow for multiple units per million dollars.

Under normal operating conditions, including Sea States of 6 or less, the expected operational duration of the deployed WECD should be at least one month, with three months or more expected if Sea State 4 or less is maintained.

Phase I:
Develop a concept for a WECD and DD capable of satisfying the listed requirements. Evaluate feasibility of the conceptual design by performing modeling and simulation, supplemented by component-level laboratory tests and water tank tests as appropriate. Provide required Phase I deliverables to include design plans and schematics for the WECD and DD, along with test and evaluation reports that are sufficiently detailed to enable ONR to assess the feasibility of the contractor’s proposed approach; and a Phase II plan.

Phase II:
Complete design and perform fabrication, verification, and testing of a prototype WECD and prototype DD based on the designs completed in Phase I. Perform testing that can include modeling and simulation (M&S); any such M&S must be validated and supplemented by in-water tests and must include at least one end-to-end sea test. Evaluate the performance of the WECD and DD during tests against the objectives expressed in the Description. Provide deliverables that include the prototype WECD and DD, along with an evaluation report that is sufficiently detailed to enable ONR to assess the performance of the contractor’s prototypes with respect to all objectives. Develop a plan for production of WECD and DD devices, making whatever improvements are appropriate based on the results of testing and evaluation in Phase II.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Validate the production plan with low-rate initial production (LRIP) of WECD and DD devices, and tests of those devices using a combination of M&S and in-water tests, including sea tests. Deliver at least one set of WECD and DD from LRIP to Navy operators for extended testing. (Note: All test data generated by the Navy will be shared with the contractor.) Evaluate the LRIP units for consistent performance and reliability based on the objectives expressed in the Description. Deliver LRIP WECD and DD units and evaluation reports that are sufficiently detailed to enable ONR to assess the units’ performance with respect to all objectives.

title: Compact Unmanned Aerial System for Marine Species Monitoring
summary: Develop an inexpensive, compact, and National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA)-compliant Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) – optimized for marine mammal monitoring.
description:
Objective:
Develop an inexpensive, compact, and National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA)-compliant Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) – optimized for marine mammal monitoring.

Description:
A major remaining hurdle with marine species management is to know if, and when, measurable short-term behavioral and/or physiological responses of marine species to sound exposure results in biologically significant or meaningful effects on individuals and/or their populations. Advances in UAS methods and technology present unprecedented opportunities to improve the capacity to collect this robust data with minimal disturbance to marine species. However, while UAS methods have led to significant advances in our understanding of marine species’ behavior, health, and body condition, thus far many obstacles remain including cost, flight duration, size, and image resolution.

This STTR topic seeks to develop a compact, inexpensive, and NDAA-compliant UAS and payloads designed to collect high-resolution photogrammetry imagery to improve marine mammal monitoring, health measurements, and behavioral sequencing. In particular, the prototype device should contain the following technical parameters: high resolution flat zoom lens camera integrated with a gimbal system; highly maneuverable and flexible payload system; lightweight batteries less than 100 Watt hours; an accurate Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) altimeter and range finder integrated with the camera and capable of measuring distances up to 50m or more; and a monitor that is operational in direct sunlight and with polarized sunglasses;. It should be designed for flight times as much as or greater than 40 minutes; be compact and portable in both size and weight such that the UAS and case can fit airline luggage restrictions; have the ability to be quickly calibrated, launched, and caught by hand during small boat-based operations and to tolerate temperature range of -20 degrees to +40 degrees Celsius; and have a minimum weather resistant rating of IP45 to allow for operations in wet conditions; be capable of dynamic home point positioning; and produces minimal noise.

While there are several existing NDAA-compliant drones available in the marketplace, the desired components and capabilities only exist in piecemeal and further, these UAS are prohibitively expensive for the field. The DON seeks to develop a prototype device to be designed and optimized for marine species monitoring, encompassing all the above technical parameters. Critically, this device must be affordable for the marine research community with the target market price between $10,000 - $15,000.

Phase I:
Develop concepts for and determine the feasibility of UAS technologies suitable for marine species-focused photogrammetry in a compact, efficient, and cost-effective design, including the identification of components to increase imagery resolution, increase flight time, and decrease size and weight of the prototype device. Develop key component technology milestones and conceptual designs for hardware. Prepare a Phase II plan.

Phase II:
Develop prototype hardware based on the Phase I effort. Establish hardware performance and develop a conceptual plan for integration into a compact system. Deliver the prototype ready for integration and testing by the Government at the end of Phase II. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Continue refinement and iterative field testing of the prototype. Provide documentation and support to the Navy and Government user community to ensure best practice use. Clearly identify and describe the expected transition of the product/process/service within the government under a Phase III effort.

Successful development of an improved UAS suitable for marine species research will open tremendous opportunities for small businesses to provide monitoring capabilities to a wide range of government agencies having equities in marine life issues. For example, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Marine Fisheries, National Ocean Service, Office of National Marine Sanctuaries, Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, U.S. Geological Survey, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, among others would benefit from this capability. Additionally, any commercial entity with a need or support mission to monitor and assess a small area from an aerial perspective with high-resolution imagery would benefit from this technology.

A key goal of this phase will be making the technology available to the broader research and Navy communities.

References:
• Álvarez-González, M., Suarez-Bregua, P., Pierce, G.J. and Saavedra, C. “Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in marine mammal research: A review of current applications and challenges.” Drones, 7(11), 667. https://doi.org/10.3390/drones7110667
• Bernier-Graveline, A. et al. “Drone-based photogrammetry provides estimates of the energetic cost of migration for humpback whales between Antarctica and Colombia.” Marine Mammal Science, 2025. https://doi.org/10.1111/mms.70048
• Christiansen, F. et al “Estimating body mass of free-living whales using aerial photogrammetry and 3D volumetrics.” Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 10(12), 2019, pp. 2034-2044. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13277
• Durban, J. W., Fearnbach, H., Barrett-Lennard, L. G., Perryman, W. L. and Leroi, D. J. “Photogrammetry of killer whales using a small hexacopter launched at sea.” Journal of Unmanned Vehicle Systems, 3(3), 2015, pp. 131-135. https://doi.org/10.1139/juvs-2015-0020

title: Multi-Modal Luminescent Paint Systems for Underwater Surface Diagnostics
summary: Develop an integrated, multi-modal luminescent paint system optimized for simultaneous, non-intrusive, large-scale, high-resolution global measurement of wall pressure, shear stress, and temperature fluctuations on complex, curved geometries in underwater environments.
description:
Objective:
Develop an integrated, multi-modal luminescent paint system optimized for simultaneous, non-intrusive, large-scale, high-resolution global measurement of wall pressure, shear stress, and temperature fluctuations on complex, curved geometries in underwater environments.

Description:
Quantifying coupled boundary layer interactions along hydrodynamic surfaces require non-intrusive, full-field imaging of surface pressure, temperature, and skin friction (shear stress). While optical diagnostics have revolutionized aerodynamic testing, adapting luminescent paints to hydrodynamic testing in water introduces fundamental physical and application constraints that current state-of-the-art systems cannot overcome:

• Pressure-Sensitive Paint (PSP): Conventional PSP relies on oxygen-quenching physics. When submerged, oxygen diffusion into the polymer binder is severely inhibited by the liquid boundary layer and low oxygen solubility, rendering standard PSPs insensitive or plagued by extremely slow response times. Furthermore, severe temperature cross-sensitivity corrupts the pressure signal.

• Temperature-Sensitive Paint (TSP): Accurate dynamic temperature measurements are crippled by the standard utilization of Taylor’s frozen-flow hypothesis, which inaccurately assumes turbulent structures remain unchanged as they advect. In water, non-equilibrium flow, high thermal mass and rapid localized diffusion cause this hypothesis to break down, failing to capture true high-frequency temperature fluctuations.

• Mechano-Luminescent Paint (MLP): MLPs offer a direct optical pathway to map shear stress via mechanical deformation. However, current MLP formulations are in their technological infancy, suffering from poor dynamic range, low luminous efficiency, and signal degradation from material fatigue and hydrostatic pressure cross-talk.

In addition to the above challenges, current formulations are difficult to apply uniformly over large areas. Existing techniques fail to maintain a consistent, repeatable coating thickness on complex, curved, or non-flat surfaces. This inconsistency skews calibration and compromises measurement reliability across large-field hydrodynamic models. Innovative material architectures, such as utilizing distinct, multi-color mechano-luminescent particles or multi-core/shell dye structures, may enable simultaneous, uncoupled optical separation of pressure, shear, and temperature in all flow environments, i.e. gas, liquid, and multiphase flows.

This STTR topic seeks an integrated material, application, and optical processing suite. The system must decouple cross-sensitivities and deliver simultaneous, high dynamic range, full-field quantitative maps of the wall pressure, shear, and temperature fluctuations.

Phase I:
Develop a concept for advanced formulations for water-compatible PSP, TSP, and MLP systems capable of measuring pressure fluctuations from 10 Pa to 100 kPa, shear stress from 0.1 to 100 Pa, and temperature variations from 0.05 to 20°C, as well as providing uniform spatial sampling capable of resolving unsteadiness up to 50 kHz without relying on Taylor’s hypothesis. Evaluate the conceptual system’s ability to decouple cross-sensitivities in simultaneous mapping of wall pressure, shear stress, and temperature through analytic modeling and laboratory testing. Identify potential application methodologies (e.g., specialized spray or deposition techniques) that ensure uniform, repeatable adhesion to curved, non-flat structures. Perform an initial cost estimate and identify technical risks to be addressed in Phase II.

Phase II:
Demonstrate a fully functional, multi-modal prototype paint system on a large-scale (greater than a square meter), curved hydrodynamic model in a test facility. Evaluate the dynamic range, resolution, and frequency response of the system. Validate analytic models of the cross-sensitivities developed in Phase I. Demonstrate a highly repeatable application process achieving less than 5% thickness variation across complex curves, ensuring consistent calibration. Evaluate paint degradation, peeling, or leaching under flow velocities up to 15 m/s over continuous 8-hour test windows. Conduct a detailed cost and manufacturing analysis. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Develop an improved formulation and manufacturing plans using the knowledge gained during Phases I and II in order to support transition of the technology for Navy use and use in hydrodynamics, aerospace, automotive, energy system, and electronics packaging applications.

References:
• Gregory, James W.; Sakaue, Hirotaka.; Liu, Tianshu and Sullivan, John P. “Fast Pressure-Sensitive Paint for Flow and Acoustic Diagnostics.” Annual Review Fluid Mechanics 2014, 46, pp. 303-330. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-fluid-010313-141304
• Running, C.L. and Juliano, T.J. “Global measurements of hypersonic shock-wave/boundary-layer interactions with pressure-sensitive paint.” Exp Fluids 62, 91, 2021. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00348-021-03194-8
• Miozzi, M. et al. “Skin-friction from temperature and velocity data around a wall-mounted cube.” Exp Fluids 65, 156, 2024. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00348-024-03881-2

title: Membranes for Separation, Purification, Compression, and Storage of Carbon Resources from Alkaline Water
summary: Develop a low-cost, robust, energy-efficient, and scalable membrane process to continuously separate, purify, compress, and store carbon dioxide from electrochemically processed alkaline water sources to support the local synthesis of fuels, nutrients, materials, and pharmaceuticals in austere, forward-deployed environments.
description:
Objective:
Develop a low-cost, robust, energy-efficient, and scalable membrane process to continuously separate, purify, compress, and store carbon dioxide from electrochemically processed alkaline water sources to support the local synthesis of fuels, nutrients, materials, and pharmaceuticals in austere, forward-deployed environments.

Description:
This STTR topic seeks to develop a low-cost, low-energy, low-temperature (not to exceed 50°C), high-throughput nonmetallic membrane process to purify and store carbon dioxide (CO2) (from acidic seawater solutions). Carbon resources harvested from seawater represent a critical renewable feedstock for the localized synthesis of tactical fuels, materials, nutrients, and pharmaceuticals. Developing the capability to generate these resources in-theater or at the tactical edge enhances multi-domain operational sustainment. Current technologies used to recover the dissolved CO2 produced from electrochemically processed seawater often result in dilution of the CO2 with air and water vapor that can lead to detrimental sintering and oxidation of catalysts used in thermochemical and biological synthetic approaches. In addition, there are volumetric and compression penalties associated with the dilution of the targeted gas. The proposed membrane process will reduce the complexity, size, and costs associated with supplying pure carbon dioxide resources from alkaline water sources.

The integrated membrane, purification, and compression process will provide equipment, process, design criteria, energy and material balance; and establish operational performance parameters.

Phase I:
Define a concept for a specific membrane process for the separation and purification of CO2 from acidified seawater solutions. Define, develop, and perform initial laboratory assessment of the proposed membrane process to validate the technical feasibility of the approach for the capture, purification, and storage of CO2 from seawater over a pH range of 2 to 5. Perform analysis of the CO2 to determine yield and purity. Perform analysis on the membrane to determine the membranes’ ability to maintain performance, structural and chemical integrity.

Phase II:
Develop a prototype process based on the work achieved in Phase I. Design the prototype as a continuous process to capture, purify, and store 90 to 100% of CO2 from a 25,000 gal/day acidified seawater source; and to purify the captured CO2 to 98% with the resulting purified CO2 stream free of oxygen (O2) and water (H2O), compressed to at least 300psi, and stored for utilization in various synthetic processes. Establish performance parameters and proof of concept for development of full-scale process. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Using data on the resulting integrated membrane, purification, and compression process, provide the design criteria for transitioning the technology to larger capacities. Develop and test a 250,000 gal/day process. Provide a cost-benefit analysis to show process outperforms current cryogenic distillation and pressure swing adoption processes.

Dual use applications include: (1) breweries and distilleries to recover and reuse CO2, (2) desalination plants for post treatment of CO2 capture and mineral scaling prevention, (3) offshore oil, gas, and maritime industries for commercial fuel synthesis, (4) commercial aquaculture, (5) fire suppression, and (6) dry ice for preservation.

References:
• Marquez, R. A., Nielander, A. C., Resasco, J., Jaramillo, T. F. and Mullins, C. B. “Electrochemical Ocean-Based Carbon Capture: Roadblocks to Scale-Up.” ACS Energy Letters, American Chemical Society, February 13, 2026, pp 1241-1259. https://carbondioxide-removal.eu/2026/02/07/marquez-et-al-2026-electrochemical-ocean-based-carbon-capture-roadblocks-to-scale-up/
• Digdaya, I. A.; Sullivan, I., Lin, M., Han, L., Cheng, W. H., Atwater, H. A. and Xiang, C. “A Direct Coupled Electrochemical System for Capture and Conversion of CO2 from Oceanwater.” Nat Commun 2020, 11 (1). https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-18232-y

title: Domestic Manufacturing of Large Area Raman Laser Materials
summary: Develop scalable domestic manufacturing technologies and processes for large Raman active optical crystals that will enable wavelength agile laser systems for Navy applications.
description:
Objective:
Develop scalable domestic manufacturing technologies and processes for large Raman active optical crystals that will enable wavelength agile laser systems for Navy applications.

Description:
The Navy employs laser systems on air- and sea-borne vessels that serve a wide range of applications including laser range finding, target designation, shipboard and airborne LiDAR, and directed energy platforms. Future naval systems require improvements in spectral agility, optical efficiency, and power, with reductions to size and weight while maintaining operation in harsh maritime environments.

Current laser architectures rely upon a limited set of mature gain and nonlinear optical materials including Nd- and Yb-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (YAG), potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP), lithium triborate (LBO), and barium borate (BBO). While these technologies provide reliable performance, wavelength conversion often requires multiple optical stages that increases system complexity, introduces alignment sensitivity, and can limit scalability to higher optical powers and larger apertures.

Raman active optical materials offer a pathway toward compact and wavelength agile laser architectures capable of generating multiple output wavelengths from a single pump source. Such materials may enable simplified optical systems with reduced alignment complexity, improved robustness to vibration and shock, enhanced spectral diversity, and compact eye-safe laser sources. Many Raman laser crystals have been demonstrated to be grown to large sizes at high quality, but broader adoption of Raman active optical materials in these systems hinges on improving domestic production. Many candidate Raman laser materials are produced in small quantities at limited sizes and lack established domestic manufacturing capability and therefore development of domestic manufacturing technologies compatible with large crystal sizes is of importance for future naval laser systems.

Candidate materials shall be compatible with bulk crystal growth processes capable of producing large aperture, high optical quality single crystals and offer a pathway toward crystal sizes of 50 mm and greater.

This STTR topic seeks to develop a prototype manufacturing technology and process which can produce one or more Raman active materials at large crystal sizes with the potential to scale to high throughput. The prototype should minimize reliance on expensive precious metal crucibles. The prototype shall produce Raman active crystals that are large (> 5mm x 5mm x 25mm), achieve laser damage thresholds exceeding 10 J/cm², support self-Raman operation through rare earth doping, and meet the following optical quality criteria:

Objective Threshold Notes

Refractive Index Homogeneity: Threshold = <10 ppm; Objective = <5 ppm

Transmitted Wavefront Distortion (at 50mm aperture): Threshold = Lamda/6; Objective = <Lambda/8

Surface Quality (Scratch-Dig): Threshold = 20-10; Objective = 10-5 (NOTE: The first number relates to the maximum allowable width of a scratch in micrometers, while the second number relates to the maximum allowable diameter of a dig or pit in hundredths of a millimeter.)

Dislocation Density: Threshold = <10 cm^(-2); Objective = < 1 cm^(-2)

Inclusion/Bulk Defect Density: Threshold = <5 inclusions greater than 1µm per cm^3; Objective = No detectable inclusions greater than 0.5µm per cm^3

Materials of interest include:

Undoped and doped (Nd, Yb, Er, Tm) potassium gadolinium tungstate (KGW) and Potassium yttrium tungstate (KYW) [Refs 1,2,3]

Undoped and doped (Nd, Yb, Er, Tm) Barium molybdate and Barium nitrate [Refs 4,5]

Other Raman active tungstate, molybdate, nitrate, vanadate or related compelling Raman crystal systems

Alternative material systems are encouraged provided performers demonstrate a credible pathway toward large aperture crystal production and significant Raman gain performance.

Phase I:
Develop a technical approach and concepts for manufacturing large and high-quality Raman active crystals. Develop and model a growth process and identify methods for optical characterization of grown crystals. Determine the technical feasibility of scaling the process to high throughput and provide a cost analysis. Produce a document containing the technical approach, concepts for manufacturing, growth model details and results, proposed optical characterization process, and approach to scale up the proposed manufacturing concept. Provide a Phase II development plan with performance goals and key technical milestones and that addresses technical risk reduction.

Phase II:
Based on the developed concepts in Phase I, develop and demonstrate the manufacturing prototype for growing large high-quality Raman active crystals. Fabricate one or more crystals and validate the prototype through characterization sufficient to establish technical feasibility and manufacturing viability. Characterize optical performance and laser damage thresholds. Use evaluation results to refine the prototype into an initial design that will meet the Naval Enterprise requirements. Prepare a Phase III development plan to transition the technology to Navy enterprise and commercial use.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Upon successful execution of Phase II and demonstration of a prototype manufacturing process that can produce large and high-quality Raman active crystals, support the ONR Navy ManTech program in transitioning the technology into program of record (PoR) manufacturing lines. Participate in the transition of manufacturing technologies and Raman active crystal materials into Navy laser systems supporting LIDAR, laser range finding, optical communications, and directed energy applications.

Commercial applications include industrial laser systems, environmental sensing, autonomous vehicle LiDAR, medical imaging, telecommunications, spectroscopy, and advanced manufacturing.

References:
• Kumaran, A. et al., Crystal growth and characterization of KY(WO4)2 and KGd(WO4)2 for laser applications, Journal of Crystal Growth, 292.2 (2006): 368-372.
• Pujol, C. et al., Growth and characterisation of monoclinic KGd1-xREx(WO4)2 single crystals, Optical Materials 13.1 (1999): 33-40.
• Gallucci, E., et al., Nonstoichiometric KY(WO4)2: crystal growth, chemical and physical characterization, Journal of Crystal Growth, 209 (2000) 895-905.
• Basiev, T., et al., Raman spectroscopy of crystals for stimulated Raman scattering, Optical materials 11.4 (1999): 307-314.
• Lin, X., et al., Large-Size Barium Nitrate Crystal Growth and Large-Energy, High-Efficiency Raman Frequency Conversion to Yellow–Orange Waveband, Crystals 16.3 (2026): 198.

title: Persistent, Geochemically-Driven Low-Temperature Power Systems for Subsea Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance
summary: Develop a modular, self-sustaining, non-toxic subsea energy-harvesting capability that exploits naturally occurring sediment-seawater geochemical gradients to provide persistent, logistics-free power for distributed Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) sensor nodes in Arctic marine environments, with reliable operation at -2°C, and providing at least 250mW average net harvested…
description:
Objective:
Develop a modular, self-sustaining, non-toxic subsea energy-harvesting capability that exploits naturally occurring sediment-seawater geochemical gradients to provide persistent, logistics-free power for distributed Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) sensor nodes in Arctic marine environments, with reliable operation at -2°C, and providing at least 250mW average net harvested power and storing sufficient energy in an onboard storage subsystem to operate up to a 5W (objective) sensor payload for 10 minutes every 4 hours over a projected 24+ month deployment.

Description:
The Department of the Navy’s expanding operational requirements in the Arctic domain demand persistent subsea situational awareness. Current seabed ISR nodes and Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV) docking stations rely on conventional lithium-chemistry batteries. These legacy power sources present severe logistical and operational limitations: they suffer from rapid capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess highly toxic/hazardous chemistries, and require frequent, resource-intensive physical replacement (battery swapping) in highly contested or ice-covered environments.

To achieve persistent, logistics-free ISR, the Navy has a critical need for an environmentally benign, deploy-and-forget power architecture. This STTR topic seeks the development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters to generate continuous electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between the anoxic marine sediment (mud) and the oxygenated overlying seawater. The proposed approach must demonstrate a credible path to 5W power and 24-month endurance in sub-zero Arctic conditions through a ruggedized seabed electrochemical power-harvesting architecture that maximizes long-term energy extraction while using only indigenous sediment microbial communities and naturally occurring geochemical gradients. Proposed solutions may use abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode design, power management, and optimum emplacement.

Biocatalytic Prioritization & Environmental Strictures:

While purely abiotic electrochemical approaches will be considered, approaches that leverage biologically-mediated processes (e.g., utilizing natural biocatalysis to enhance electron transfer at the anode) will be prioritized due to their potential for higher power density and self-renewing longevity.

However, to prevent any risk of ecological disruption to fragile Arctic ecosystems, solutions must strictly rely on harnessing the naturally occurring, indigenous populations already present in the local sediment. The introduction, deployment, or seeding of any exogenous, synthetic, lab-grown, or non-native biological agents (microbes/bacteria) is strictly prohibited.

By utilizing advanced electrode materials that naturally synergize with the local subsea environment, the system must reduce or avoid reliance on deployable primary batteries for the supported payload while ensuring operational viability in extreme cold and high-pressure conditions.

Phase I:
Formulate the theoretical electrochemical model for sub-zero geochemical harvesting. Identify and test advanced catalytic electrode materials that maximize electron transfer efficiency at -2°C, prioritizing architectures that optimize interaction with indigenous sediment microbial communities and/or indigenous electroactive microorganisms.

Conduct a benchtop prototype demonstrating the targeted voltage and current density in a simulated cold-water/sediment environment utilizing only native sediment samples, accompanied by a scalable power management design.

Phase II:
Scale the Phase I material architecture into a prototype ruggedized, modular power generation unit. Integrate the system with advanced, low-loss DC-DC boost converters to condition the output for standard ISR payloads. Conduct extensive tank testing in simulated Arctic conditions to validate the 24-month longevity and an objective of 5W output. Position the Phase II prototype to be tested against PMS 485-D2 surrogate sensor payloads to prove integration and power conditioning.

Deliver a TRL 5/6 deployable prototype system and comprehensive testing data proving capability integration with a surrogate acoustic or environmental sensor. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Transition the technology into a deployable form factor for Navy undersea infrastructure. Integrate the power module with operational subsea sensor networks, UUV charging nodes, or acoustic listening arrays. Deliver a qualified plug-and-play auxiliary power module that can be integrated into the next-generation Distributed Maritime Operations (DMO) surveillance architectures managed by PMS 485.

Transition the technology to commercial sectors for powering offshore oil and gas monitoring equipment, oceanographic research sensors, and early-warning tsunami detection networks.

References:
• Lowy, D. A., & Tender, L. M. (2008). Harvesting energy from the marine sediment–water interface: III. Kinetic activity of quinone-and antimony-based anode materials. Journal of Power Sources, 185(1), 70-75.
• Shang, Y., Huang, Y., Li, L., Wu, F., & Chen, R. (2025). Electrochemical energy storage toward extreme conditions: driving human exploration beyond current boundaries. Chemical Reviews, 125(12), 5674-5744.
• Tender, L. M., et al. “The First Demonstration of a Microbial Fuel Cell as a Viable Power Supply: Powering a Meteorological Buoy.” Journal of Power Sources / public university record, 2008.
• Reimers, C. E., et al. “Benthic Microbial Fuel Cell as Direct Power Source for an Acoustic Modem and Seawater Oxygen/Temperature Sensor System.” Environmental Science & Technology, 2011.
• Joiner, Kevin L., Eric Bozeman, Matthew L. Bond, Angelica Sarmiento, David B. Chadwick, Kevin Hardy, and Yolanda Meriah Arias-Thode. 2023. “Deep-Sea Benthic Microbial Fuel Cell Split-Release Landers”, Sustainable Energy and Environmental Technologies and Assessments, 58: 103352.
• Bond, Matthew, Y. M. Arias-Thode, Matias Andersson and Stefan Petrovic Wångerud. 2020. "The Undersea Surveillance and Communication Project Agreement (USC PA): Sea Trial 4 –Evaluation of Microbial Fuel Cells in the Baltic Sea," NIWCPAC-TR-3209; AD1144241.
• Joiner, Kevin, Gabriel L. Tukeman, Anna Y. Obraztsova, Y. Meriah Arias-Thode. 2020. Impact of sediment parameters in the prediction of benthic microbial fuel cell performance. RSC Advances 10: 26220-26228.

title: Heterogenous Swarm Control through Super Intelligence-embodied Architecture
summary: Develop Agentic Super Intelligence (SI) architecture and associated applications for control of low-cost Commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) uncrewed systems (Group 1 unmanned aerial vehicle [UAV] or small unmanned ground vehicle [UGV]) for use in adaptable heterogenous swarming applications.
description:
Objective:
Develop Agentic Super Intelligence (SI) architecture and associated applications for control of low-cost Commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) uncrewed systems (Group 1 unmanned aerial vehicle [UAV] or small unmanned ground vehicle [UGV]) for use in adaptable heterogenous swarming applications.

Description:
Current methods of heterogeneous swarming control often involve individual entities with incompatible messaging protocols, ridged data interpretation, and lack of broader situational awareness, generating a protocol/perception problem that results in fragmented decision-making. Model Context Protocol (MCP), Large Language Models (LLMs), and related Agentic SI architectures, can enable a Universal Serial Bus Type C (USB-C) solution to this fragmentation problem by allowing individual entities to communicate with human operators or other entities through natural language.

The Department of the Navy is seeking development of Agentic SI-enabled COTS small UAVs or small UGVs USB-C capabilities for demonstration of applicability in Naval and Marine Corps tasks. The goal is to deliver a small heterogenous swarm of low-cost uncrewed systems capable of receiving tasks through a natural language interface and performing complex tasks such as inspection of a facility for damage, evaluating road conditions, conducting security operations, and/or intercepting of other platforms. Performers should focus on software development to run on low cost and edge compute devices attached to highly expendable COTS platforms. Submissions will leverage preexisting DoW compliant hardware deployments using either compute resources organic to the UAV/UGV platform or flight-ready modules (e.g., Single Board Computer NVIDIA JETSON NDAA) with favorable Size, Weight, and Power (SWAP). Submissions should identify the unique nature of their Agentic-SI capability in accomplishing the objective.

Phase I:
Document and demonstrate an approach for Agentic SI control of small UAV or UGV. Required deliverables for Phase I include a demonstration and design approach for validation. GNSS may be used at this stage, but overall architecture must be GNSS optional. Hardware used in Phase I needs to be either NDAA complaint or have NDAA compliant analogs listed for Phase II. Individual unmanned systems must be tasked by human or other agent through natural language and respond similarly.

Demonstrate at least one Group 1 UAV or small UGV (such as an RC Car) performing 3 of the following 5 tasks. No priority is given to this list.

o Go to user defined location with a maximum flight distance of 2km

o Report scene observations from on-board sensors (e.g., individual vehicles including class and color, people in the area, structures including temporary)

o Report on user specified object in scene (e.g., confirm presence of user specified “Red Van”, or “Fishing Boat”

o Follow internal reference frame “left, right, up, down, turn left, move right 10 meters” commands and/or global reference

o Follow a leader vehicle or person

Phase II:
Using approach and results developed in Phase I, build and deliver 10-20 prototype UxSs and software that can demonstrate all of the following tasks.

Tasks

o Inspection of buildings, airfields, or roadways after weather events for debris or damage

o Go to location and report on activities in the area

o Interception of UxS

o Logistics resupply

o Security Alerts under GNSS Denied Conditions

Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

The swarm must be composed of at least 3 different hardware configurations and require minimal user configuration. This can be accomplished by adding different sensor packages to the same base platform or altering base platform to demonstrate different capabilities. A single user must be able to command and control the entire swarm from single device using bidirectional natural language. The swarm must decide how many and of which entities are needed to complete the task. By the end of Phase II, the entire swarm must be capable of operating without internet connectivity or GNSS. Reduced capabilities in GNSS-denied environments are acceptable.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Successful completion of Phase II results in products immediately useful to Heterogenous Swarming efforts for the Department of the Navy. Additional support would include field support, continued technical refinement, technical documentation, and integration into naval systems.

Additional commercial and government applications exist across several commercial sectors such as disaster relief, agriculture, and security applications in remote areas. SI enabled UAVs to aid post-disaster search-and-rescue teams by detecting hazards on roadways, locating survivors, delivery lifesaving supplies, and automatically coordinating with other SI agents to ensure area coverage. Agricultural applications include remote crop inspections and dynamic spraying based on real-time feedback. Lastly, SI enabled UAVs can be used as part of a security or building inspection posture for remote or hard to surveil areas by responding to remote sensors and confirming presence of absence of threats.

title: Mission-Specialized Large Language Models for Operational Training and Knowledge Integration
summary: Develop and demonstrate an explainable, adaptive super intelligence (SI) capability that enhances Navy workforce readiness, technical training, knowledge transfer, and personnel development through personalized instructional interaction, competency-based learning support, and integration of authoritative Navy workforce and training resources.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate an explainable, adaptive super intelligence (SI) capability that enhances Navy workforce readiness, technical training, knowledge transfer, and personnel development through personalized instructional interaction, competency-based learning support, and integration of authoritative Navy workforce and training resources.

Description:
The Department of the Navy faces increasing challenges associated with workforce modernization, technical skill development, personnel turnover, distributed operations, and the growing complexity of mission systems and operational environments. As experienced personnel retire or transition, critical institutional knowledge and operational expertise are frequently difficult to preserve, transfer, and scale across the workforce.

Simultaneously, Navy training and workforce development communities must support increasingly divergent learning requirements across accession, technical education, and qualification pipelines. Existing training approaches often rely on static instructional materials, fragmented knowledge systems, and limited mechanisms for adaptive or individualized instruction.

Commercial large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong broad-domain reasoning capabilities but are fundamentally limited in their ability to reliably incorporate organization-specific knowledge without hallucination. They are unable to incorporate organization-specific terminology, mission procedures, technical constraints, and authoritative instructional content unique to mission environments. Additionally, these systems frequently generate responses without traceable references, limiting user trust and reducing suitability for technical learning and operational instruction. This gap creates a strong need for a specialized LLM system precisely tuned to an organization's corpus and operational requirements.

The Navy seeks development of a hyper-parameterized, explainable LLM framework designed specifically to support mission-focused training and knowledge transfer. The system should enable personnel to learn new technical and operational topics through an interactive interface. Outputs should be grounded in authoritative manpower, personnel, training, and education (MPTE) documentation while also leveraging the broad contextual understanding available from foundation LLMs. The proposed capability shall support accelerated workforce proficiency development, preservation of institutional knowledge, and adaptive learning across operational, technical, and mission-support communities while providing transparent, auditable, and trustworthy instructional guidance tailored to user roles, experience levels, and training objectives.

Explainability is a critical requirement for organization-specific LLMs operating in mission environments. The proposed solution must provide transparent and auditable reasoning pathways that allow users to understand how conclusions, recommendations, or generated outputs were derived.

The proposed capability should function as an intelligent training and instructional assistant capable of:

• Teaching mission-specific topics using authoritative organizational documents and instructional materials
• Combining proprietary knowledge with broad-domain contextual reasoning from foundational LLMs
• Guiding users through complex technical, operational, engineering, and/or procedural concepts
• Adapting explanations and instructional depth based on user role, expertise, and/or training objectives
• Providing explainable outputs with traceable references to source documentation
• Reducing hallucination through structured retrieval and grounded response generation
• Supporting continuous updates as training materials, policies, and mission guidance evolve

Phase I:
Phase I will focus on assessing the feasibility of a concept for an explainable, mission-specialized training LLM built on sample Navy corpora. The effort will determine the technical feasibility of integrating organization-specific Navy MPTE corpora into a training-oriented conversational SI system. It will identify and characterize the types of Navy documents to be targeted, such as NETC curricula, qualification standards, MyNavy HR competency frameworks, and technical manuals, and define how each would be ingested and leveraged by the LLM. Building on this, the effort will define a concept for hyper-parameterized LLM fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architectures appropriate for Navy instructional environments. It will also develop and validate an initial approach for reducing hallucination through structured retrieval and grounded response generation. Required Phase I deliverables include a technical feasibility report and a Phase II development plan.

Phase II:
Develop a prototype operational training and knowledge-transfer platform suitable for deployment within Navy organizations. The effort will develop, demonstrate, and validate a scalable, mission-specialized LLM platform that incorporates full Navy MPTE corpus integration, including MyNavy HR, NETC qualification pipelines, and relevant technical documentation repositories. It will also develop, demonstrate, and validate adaptive instructional capabilities that respond to user role, experience level, and training objective, with competency-based learning path support aligned to the Defense Civilian Workforce Framework (DCWF) and Navy Knowledge, Skills, Abilities, and Tasks (KSATs). To support user trust and oversight, the effort will develop and validate explainability and auditability mechanisms that give users traceable reasoning pathways and source citations for all generated outputs. It will produce a prototype deployment package suitable for integration within Navy zero-trust data governance and cybersecurity frameworks, including documentation of data handling, model versioning, and update procedures. User evaluation will be conducted in representative mission environments, measuring time-to-proficiency, knowledge retention, and user trust. The effort will also demonstrate interoperability with existing Navy training management systems and learning record stores using xAPI and the IEEE 1484.20.3 Reusable Competency Definition standard. Final deliverables include a validated prototype platform, comprehensive technical documentation, and a transition plan for government evaluation, potential program-of-record insertion, and commercialization.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Support transition to NETC and associated subordinate training commands as an integrated SI instructional tool within Advana and/or Jupiter data management (or other Navy-specified system) and MyNavy HR ecosystem, supporting Navy-wide workforce readiness programs.

Potential expansion to other DoW components and the Intelligence Community is anticipated given the generalizability of the mission-specialized LLM architecture.

The commercial dual-use potential is significant. The underlying hyper-parameterized, explainable LLM framework is directly applicable to enterprise workforce training, knowledge management, and instructional SI markets across healthcare, finance, legal, and critical infrastructure sectors. Small businesses developing this technology will have a clear commercial pathway through SI-powered training platform products for regulated industries requiring auditable, organization-specific instructional SI.

title: Computational Frameworks for the Development and Qualification of Additive Manufacturing-Tailored Wire Feedstock for Naval Directed Energy Deposition
summary: Develop an integrated computational and experimental framework that engineers, qualifies, and specifies advanced metal wire feedstock specifically tailored for wire-fed Directed Energy Deposition (DED).
description:
Objective:
Develop an integrated computational and experimental framework that engineers, qualifies, and specifies advanced metal wire feedstock specifically tailored for wire-fed Directed Energy Deposition (DED). By leveraging Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME) and Super Intelligence / Machine Learning (SI/ML), this capability will enable high-confidence, point-of-need manufacturing of structural naval components by resolving the fundamental feedstock-process mismatch that currently limits DED mechanical performance.

Description:
As the Department of the Navy prepares for contested logistics environments, the ability to manufacture large, mission-critical replacement parts at the point of need has become a strategic imperative. Wire-fed DED is uniquely suited to this role: it operates safely with reactive metal alloys, achieves high deposition rates for large structural volumes, and is robust enough for shipboard and expeditionary deployment. Despite this operational advantage, a persistent and quantifiable performance gap prevents wire DED parts from meeting Navy structural qualification standards without extensive post-processing.

The root cause of this gap is a thermal physics and geometric mismatch. Additive manufacturing (AM) processes span approximately five orders of magnitude in solidification cooling rate, which is the master variable governing grain size, phase selection, and precipitate morphology.

Current wire feedstock is manufactured to welding wire specifications, engineered for arc welding thermal histories rather than the specific precision and cooling rates of robotic DED. The consequences are well-documented:

• Microstructural Deficits: Precipitation-strengthened aluminum alloys exhibit a 40-70% yield strength reduction in DED compared to laser powder bed fusion, driven by insufficient cooling rates to nucleate strengthening dispersoids. Titanium alloys (e.g., Ti-6Al-4V) develop continuous grain boundary alpha films that degrade ductility and fatigue life.
• Residual Stress Instability: Residual stresses retained from the wire drawing process cause wire tip instability (cast/helix) in the DED melt zone, producing porosity and build failures.
• Geometric and Surface Topography: Macroscopic inconsistencies in wire diameter dictate volumetric feed-rate errors, causing fluctuating energy-to-mass ratios in the melt pool. Simultaneously, surface roughness (poor smoothness) induces micro-stuttering in the robotic feed conduit and scatters laser impingement, severely destabilizing thermal absorption.

No existing ICME framework addresses these deficiencies upstream of the melt pool—every published AM modelling chain begins at deposition, leaving the wire manufacturing sub-chain entirely unmodelled.

The Navy seeks a comprehensive end-to-end computational framework that closes this gap through alloy-process co-optimization. Proposers should develop a model chain that links the entire wire feedstock lifecycle—from primary alloy synthesis and thermomechanical processing through final drawing and surface conditioning—directly to AM deposition dynamics and deposit properties. This model must account for the coupled effects of advanced state variables (e.g., dislocation density, oxide thickness).

The framework should incorporate Super Intelligence/Machine Learning (SI/ML) surrogate models that consume upstream feedstock history to predict how a specific wire lot will respond to DED thermal conditions and should employ SI-guided experimental design to identify the minimum number of physical tests required to achieve robust statistical qualification. The ultimate deliverable is a computational materials passport: a traceable digital record linking a wire lot's manufacturing history to its predicted and validated AM performance, supporting the Navy's Digital Engineering Strategy and enabling condition-based qualification for fleet sustainment.

Phase I:
Demonstrate the scientific and technical feasibility of the proposed ICME and SI/ML framework for one primary naval alloy system.

Develop initial multi-scale computational models linking upstream wire manufacturing variables to critical feedstock properties (including strict diametric tolerances, surface topography, and thermomechanical state) and AM deposit behavior, with the specific goal of predicting and mitigating a known and documented performance deficit in the selected alloy. (Note: Models shall be validated against existing data or targeted experiments.)

Deliver a comprehensive Phase II plan with a clear go/no-go criterion against a defined predictive accuracy target for the novel material/alloy being investigated.

Phase II:
Conduct a computationally guided experimental campaign to manufacture tailored feedstock lots that meet predicted specifications. Perform AM builds to demonstrate quantified property improvements against established baseline performance data for current commercial materials.

Leverage ICME and SI/ML-guided qualification paths to establish B-basis property allowables with a statistically significant reduction in physical testing.

Provide required Phase II deliverables to include: (1) A report on how the proposed novel alloy meets or exceeds current commercial offerings; (2) Details on how ICME and SI/ML techniques were leveraged to accelerate alloy development and scale-up; and (3) A prototype software tool embodying the integrated framework. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Deliver the final prototype alloy to U.S. Navy facilities ready for part-scale verification and validation along with the previously completed testing results to demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed alloy. Follow-on demonstrations to non-Navy participants will enable other DoW, DoE, government, and industry partners to ability to view the solution and continue transition to other facilities.

References:
• Allison, J.E. et al. “Integrated Computational Materials Engineering: a New Paradigm for the Global Materials Profession.”: JOM 58(11), pp. 25-27, 2006/2011). https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11837-011-0053-y
• Panchal, J.H. et al. “Key Computational Modeling Issues in ICME.” JOM 65(2), 2013, pp. 231-245. DOI: 10.1007/s11837-012-0512-3
