title: Conformal Printed Antennas for Missile and Weapon Composite Airframes
summary: Develop and demonstrate conformal printed antennas for Navy missile, weapon, or aircraft composite airframes, addressing the coupled electromagnetic, structural, and environmental design problem inherent to printing radiating elements on small-diameter, high-curvature carbon-fiber substrates with integrated environmental protection.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate conformal printed antennas for Navy missile, weapon, or aircraft composite airframes, addressing the coupled electromagnetic, structural, and environmental design problem inherent to printing radiating elements on small-diameter, high-curvature carbon-fiber substrates with integrated environmental protection. In particular, the Department is developing a number of low-cost counter-UAS effectors in the 40 mm, 70 mm, and 5” diameters. In order to keep costs down, one approach is to provide in-flight guidance updates until the seeker can detect the threat UAS. To reduce mass, we are seeking technology for printed or conformal antennas and circuitry.

Description:
Rockets, missiles, aircraft, and tactical weapons are extremely weight constrained. Antennas for Global Positioning Systems (GPS) (including anti-jam), command and control, telemetry, datalink, and seeker functions must coexist with structural, thermal, environmental constraints on curved airframes. Conventional fabrication produces these antennas as discrete elements mounted on brackets inside separate radomes, connected to receivers via coaxial cables and connectors. This architecture imposes parasitic mass, parasitic volume, signal loss through cables and connectors, and long-term reliability degradation as connectors corrode and radomes delaminate over shipboard storage life.

Conformal printed antennas integrated directly onto composite airframe surfaces offer substantial advantages: reduced mass, reduced volume, eliminated cable and connector losses, and structural integration with the airframe itself. The technical challenge: printing radiating elements onto curved carbon-fiber substrates couples electromagnetic design with structural design, environmental protection, and the complex electrical interaction between printed conductors and the underlying conducting carbon-fiber substrate.

Multi-material printed electronics, particularly aerosol-jet and inkjet direct-write processes, have matured to where conductors, dielectrics, and substrates can be co-deposited into conformal structures with controlled electromagnetic properties. The unaddressed capability is the integrated design of printed antennas on airframe substrates, with environmental protection co-designed for operational survival.

The antennas shall be designed using direct-write printed electronics methods (aerosol-jet, inkjet, or comparable approaches) capable of multi-material co-deposition on curved composite substrates. Coating or environmental protection schemes shall be integrated into the design from the outset, with explicit treatment of electromagnetic transparency, loss, and detuning effects.

Phase I:
Define a concept for the target antenna application, including the conventional baseline being displaced and quantitative performance, cost, and lead-time targets. In conjunction with the Navy participants. identify a representative composite substrate and configuration with justification of diameter and curvature (preference for the 70 mm to 130 mm diameter range).Identify a coating or environmental protection scheme appropriate to the target application, with justification against the operational environment. Conduct joint research on the coupled electromagnetic-structural-environmental design problem, including initial design methodology, characterization of electromagnetic transparency and detuning effects of candidate coatings, and characterization of printed conductor performance on carbon-fiber composite substrates. Deliver a final report that includes technology base documentation, coating selection rationale and characterization, and baseline comparison; and a Phase II plan.

Phase II:
Develop the conformal printed antenna capability prototype and mature to TRL 6 on a representative configuration, including environmental qualification per relevant MIL-STDs on the coated configuration. Demonstrate fabrication and performance at relevant curvature, including documented print process control, inspection, yield characterization, and coating application. In conjunction with identified Navy transition program, demonstrate platform level integration and test, including (where feasible) captive carry, static fire, sled test, or flight demonstration. Document the path to qualified production, including supplier identification, equipment requirements, and cost and lead-time projections at production rate. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Transition to the identified target Program of Record. Broader applications include Navy and Marine Corps strike weapons (PMA-242, PMA-201), air-to-air missiles (PMA-259), tactical rockets, small UAS (PMA-263), Marine ground-launched precision fires, and dismounted C4ISR antennas. Cross-service applications include Army PEO Missiles and Space, Air Force Armament Directorate, MDA, and Special Operations Command (SOCOM) antenna requirements on small-diameter platforms.

Commercial small UAS and advanced air mobility (conformal antennas on composite airframes); commercial space and small satellites (conformal antennas on composite stages and bus structures); automotive (conformal antennas for connected and autonomous vehicles); and consumer and industrial IoT. The qualification framework, including coating and protection, transfers to FAA-regulated aviation, commercial space, and other regulated markets where qualification of printed antennas on composites and other conductive substrates would provide weight and power advantages.

References:

• “IPC-2292, Design Standard for Printed Electronics on Flexible Substrates.” https://www.ipc.org/

title: Photonic-Crystal Surface Emitting Lasers (PCSELS) in the Near-Infrared (NIR)
summary: Develop and demonstrate scalable photonic-crystal surface-emitting laser (PCSEL) architectures that achieve higher output power while maintaining stable, single-mode, diffraction-limited beam quality using innovative photonic-crystal and optical metasurface designs in multi-aperture or integrated photonic configurations.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate scalable photonic-crystal surface-emitting laser (PCSEL) architectures that achieve higher output power while maintaining stable, single-mode, diffraction-limited beam quality using innovative photonic-crystal and optical metasurface designs in multi-aperture or integrated photonic configurations.

Description:
The Navy seeks innovations in PCSELs that combine novel in-plane photonic crystal designs with out-of-plane epitaxial and gain structures to overcome the limitations of current approaches and produce the next generation of semiconductor laser technologies. Current PCSEL architectures face power-scaling limitations as device aperture increases because the mode margin between the desired fundamental mode and competing higher-order modes decreases, making stable, single-mode, diffraction operations increasingly difficult at higher powers. Capabilities that enable single mode, high power density, combinable lasers in the one-micron regime are the focus for any near-term transition. Concepts that maximize laser device area above previous limits, either by increasing the number of photons generated per unit area or increasing conversion efficiency, are potential options. Other potential approaches include reducing optical, electrical, and other losses – either with single devices, or through multi-device combinations. For example, stacking multiple gain regions vertically and horizontally, a successful technique used in vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers ( VCSELs) arrays, may limit current PCSEL designs because of interactions between n++/p++ tunnel junctions in gain layers introducing unwanted absorption. Means to correct this issue through material modification might offer counteracting but beneficial additional total gain from a single device – especially when combined in the far field. Similarly, adding optical features as part of the photonic crystal to extend single-mode operation, especially those with higher conductivity material might reduce thermal distortions and lead to better performance even at the potential limits of vertical heat conduction. Further, adaptive metasurfacing of an existing PCSEL device (through micro- or nano-etching) might create new surface structures that modify laser output to enable more efficient photon conversion through the development of improved cavity properties.

The potential to demonstrate military utility by showing power scalability greater than single digit watts from an individual PSCEL, while maintaining single mode operation that result in combinable Solid State Lasers (SSLs) sources (through spectral beam combining or coherent beam combining) or other resonant gain media structures - where the result is a single mode - where emissions has already been demonstrated from fiber lasers, but can potentially be replaced by a single PCSEL integrated optical device - opens up the possibility of high energy laser (HEL) single stage output. The Navy desires higher power, higher efficiency laser and optics to increase engagement ranges, even in adverse marine atmospheric conditions.

The Navy seeks an approach with a scalable demonstration device in the evaluation of new combinable PCSEL devices that support Electro-magnetic (EM) Spectrum warfare dominance with an objective of gaining military advantages through increased laser power and efficiency - achieving freedom of action across missions in support of maritime, surface warfare.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

Phase I:
Develop, demonstrate, and deliver a small scale, efficient, coupled multi-aperture prototype PCSELs based high energy laser operating at 1.050-1.070 microns, suitable for testing and evaluation in a laboratory with output power measured in watts with a vertical and horizontal beam quality as close to the diffraction limit (M-squared=1.0, in horizontal and vertical dimensions) as possible. The device should include any required power and cooling to support a laser time of no less than 30 seconds. Provide multiple configurations and cross sections for initial laboratory testing.

Demonstrate the scalability in volume and combinability of individual PCSELs to increase power to achieve higher output power with higher beam quality based on the use of techniques such as nano-meter scale meta-surfacing modifications to die integrated electronic dies – showing improvements compared to standard manufacturing techniques.

Deliver one prototype to the Naval Research Laboratory to evaluate the performance of the system in terms of power specifications, wavelength, beam quality, and EO efficiency for a prototype laser system that can meet performance goals.

Phase II:
Develop, demonstrate, and deliver a batch scaled up (longer) prototypical high energy lasers, suitable for inclusion into a laser weapon system for testing and evaluation when mounted into an optical beam director with power combiner that is determined within the scope of Phase I. Document the design and demonstrate high power operation, including containment and ruggedization of the optical devices required on a shake table that emulates the motion and vibrational spectrum of Naval platform. Demonstrate higher efficiency and thermal stability of power gain amplifier fiber when individual components are integrated to achieve higher resulting beam quality and efficiency and compared to more traditional combined fiber laser gain media. Deliver the resulting prototype devices to the Naval Research Laboratory for evaluation of the performance of the subsystem components in terms of power specifications, wavelength, beam quality and EO efficiency – toward an anticipated HEL prototype system that would be used in field testing, reaching expected Navy performance goals. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Work in Phase II may become classified. Please see note in Description section.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Support the Navy with technology transition for Department of War use. Show the scalability of source power from micro or milliwatt levels to multi-kilowatt class operation and beyond in the near infrared regime.

Ultimately, laser source subsystems will be deployed on surface ships, ground vehicles, or air vehicles – with potentials for other Navy or U.S. Marine Corps platforms to advance the future electromagnetic spectrum operational warfighting capabilities. Both the power specifications and wavelength of operation and electrical to optical (EO) efficiency will be tested at either the Naval Research Laboratory test facilities or Naval Surface Warfare Center, Dahlgren Division.

There is a potential for dual use of this system for manufacturing such as cutting/welding, optical communication and use in space or airborne platform for sensing. The most important characteristic of this wavelength is it is less affected by atmospheric absorption than visible wavelengths.

title: TRIAGE-X: Autonomous Casualty Triage and Treatment in Chemically Contaminated Mass Casualty Events
summary: Develop and demonstrate capability with autonomous medical triage systems to recognize chemical toxidromes and physically deliver the corresponding antidote or life-saving intervention.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate capability with autonomous medical triage systems to recognize chemical toxidromes and physically deliver the corresponding antidote or life-saving intervention.

Description:
DARPA seeks innovative approaches to autonomous chemical, biological, radioactive, and nuclear (CBRN) triage that measurably improve casualty survival and increase the effective capacity of a medical response during CBRN disasters. Early situational awareness and timely treatment is a matter of life and death in battlefield and disaster medical triage. Responder vulnerability in hazardous environments caused by CBRN attacks adds significant difficulty to the medical response. When a mass casualty incident (MCI) occurs within a chemically contaminated area, the medical response is hindered by uncertainty while the threat is assessed and characterized. To ensure safety of the responders, they must don protective equipment before entry, delaying initial assessment, triage, and treatment with life-saving interventions (LSIs). Personal protective equipment (PPE) also imposes a physiological and functional penalty on responders resulting in slower movement, higher energy expenditure, heat stress, impaired respiration, and reduced manual dexterity; these penalties further impede responders’ ability to perform life-saving interventions. Effective stabilization occurs in the cold zone after casualties have been decontaminated [1,2], compounding the delay to evacuation and definitive care. The DARPA Triage Challenge (DTC) has demonstrated that autonomous air and ground systems, using standoff sensors, can locate casualties, characterize injury patterns, and support triage prioritization in realistic MCI conditions [3]. Using DTC triage support capabilities as a starting point, this solicitation aims to extend capabilities to operating in chemically hazardous environments where injury patterns have distinct signatures or toxidromes. Success here extends proven autonomous triage into the one of the most challenging settings where human entry is dangerous and delayed, and where early antidote delivery most directly determines casualty survival [4].Proposed systems should be able to locate and assess casualties for traumatic injuries and chemical toxidromes, generate triage recommendations, and deliver appropriate initial treatments to reverse, stabilize, or prevent the toxic effects of chemicals. Solutions should be designed for realistic operational use in difficult terrain under challenging environmental conditions. DARPA does not prescribe a specific platform, sensor suite, or level of autonomy. Offerors are encouraged to propose the human-machine teaming arrangement that best improves decision quality and casualty outcomes, and to define how their system fails safely when conditions exceed its competence. Approaches should be realistic in scope, repurposed within the period of performance, and grounded in how CBRN mass casualty response actually unfolds.At minimum, the effort shall deliver a demonstrated prototype that detects at least two representative chemical toxidromes and applies appropriate initial treatments for the assessed toxidrome following human-in-the-loop treatment approval.

Phase I:
Phase I work is expected to have been completed before award. Proposers must submit evidence that their existing prototype can:• Autonomously find and localize casualties and report their location to within 2m• Assess trauma patterns and assign a trauma triage category• Perform accurate standoff vital-signs assessment, including at minimum heart rate and respiratory rate • Operate at scale o At least 20 casualties in a single scenario o Perform assessment in <90 seconds for each casualtyo Survey a 30,000sqft area without battery change• Operate across diverse, realistic environments: indoor and outdoor, daytime and nighttime, ideally (but not required) in adverse weather conditions (rain, smoke)• Produce a human-interpretable output through a graphical interface that conveys casualty locations and priorities of care.• System must be portable. All components should be easily transported by a vehicle or drone.Capability demonstration:A written technical description or published report supported by data and video(s) demonstrating the prototype performing the capabilities above in the stated environments are required (provided via link).

Phase II:

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Military: Autonomous triage and toxidrome-directed treatment in chemically contaminated, battlefield environments, protects medics from entry and prolongs casualty survival until human care is possible. Civilian: Similarly, autonomous systems capable of assessing and delivering life sustaining treatments during disaster responses, industrial chemical accidents, hazmat operations, and chemical terror attacks in which fire/EMS response will be delayed provides additional safety for responders and a survival advantage for casualties during public-health emergencies [2]. The autonomous system will perform initial triage and treatment in the hot zone so that responders either avoid entry entirely or gain time to don protective equipment.

title: Autonomous Metacognitive Collection Orchestration for Multi-Domain Intelligence
summary: Develop and demonstrate an autonomous, metacognitive artificial-intelligence capability that orchestrates multi-modal intelligence collection across asynchronous sensing streams and produces traceable, causally-informed recommendations for multi-domain operations.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate an autonomous, metacognitive artificial-intelligence capability that orchestrates multi-modal intelligence collection across asynchronous sensing streams and produces traceable, causally-informed recommendations for multi-domain operations. The capability shall decide what evidence to collect, when, and why; weigh expected information gain against hard operational constraints including emissions, bandwidth, power, time-to-decision, and access posture; generate Pareto-optimal option-sets accompanied by “why / why-not” traces reproducible from internal system state; and locally refine its internal representation under denial, deception, or distribution shift without offline retraining. Operator interaction is confined to pre-mission intent specification and after-action audit of the decision record, enabling a human-machine formation in which the capability operates at machine speed inside a commander-specified envelope and the human sets intent, constraints, and rules of engagement at mission entry and reviews the auditable decision record at mission exit.

Description:
Modern intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) enterprises ingest multi-source indicator streams whose native tempos span four or more orders of magnitude. Overhead imagery (EO/IR, SAR, MSI, HSI) arrives at revisit cadences of minutes to hours; RF and SIGINT detections resolve in seconds to minutes; maritime AIS and acoustic returns update continuously at sub-second tempos; and open-source, supply-chain, and pattern-of-life indicators mature over hours to weeks. A single decision of operational consequence, such as whether a vessel of interest is a combatant or a civilian fisher, or whether an observed buildup presages a near-term operation or reflects routine activity, typically turns on whether causally related evidence drawn from several of these phenomenologies can be assembled, reasoned about, and surfaced fast enough and cheaply enough to matter.

Classical early- and late-fusion pipelines assume temporally aligned inputs and emit single snapshot outputs, useful when cadences match and brittle when they differ by orders of magnitude or when a depended-on sensor is denied. Reinforcement- and active-learning policies can select next observations but treat operational constraints as reward-shaped scalars the optimizer can trade away, and require retraining cycles measured in weeks when priority intelligence requirements or adversary tactics shift in hours. Neuro-symbolic and causal methods contribute structure and interpretability, yet in practice operate over hand-authored graphs and synchronous data, with post-hoc explanations rather than forward-looking traces. Agentic large-language-model orchestrators produce narrative rationalizations whose internal state cannot be audited, and whose plans cannot be inspected for constraint feasibility before execution. What is missing across all of these approaches is a structured, auditable, constraint-feasible substrate whose rationale for each recommendation is transparent, reproducible, and directly inspectable from internal state.

This topic seeks novel approaches to artificial metacognition: an orchestration substrate that reasons about its own reasoning while reasoning about the world. A metacognitive substrate maintains a structured model of evidence-to-outcome relationships across heterogeneous modalities and tempos; tracks its own uncertainty, prediction error, and representational coherence; computes expected information gain for candidate collection actions under hard operational constraints; returns option-sets rather than single collapsed policies; and, when denial, deception, or distribution shift is detected, locally refines its internal model rather than triggering a full retraining cycle. The resulting capability is the computational backbone of a human-machine formation: the autonomous system acts at machine speed inside a bounded operating envelope, while the human commander sets objectives, constraints, and rules of engagement before the mission and reviews the auditable decision record after.

Candidate substrate families for the metacognitive layer include hyperdimensional computing and vector-symbolic architectures; neuro-symbolic architectures that couple learned encoders with symbolic or probabilistic inference; and graph-based reasoning over typed knowledge graphs, causal graphs, and structured inference engines. Hybrids across these approaches are encouraged. This topic is deliberately substrate-agnostic within that class. Offerors are expected to justify their choice on quantitative grounds. Any viable substrate shall provide:

• Compositional, inspectable operators (algebraic, logical, graph-based, or probabilistic) that support real-time assembly and decomposition of multi-source evidence structures, rather than end-to-end learned embeddings whose compositional semantics cannot be examined.
• Bounded degradation under partial, corrupted, delayed, or adversarially manipulated input, quantified against a mainstream deep-learning baseline.
• Transparent, reproducible reasoning operations that yield auditable explanations directly from internal system state, rather than post-hoc narrative produced by a prompted language model.
• Efficient operation under sparse and few-shot regimes, with measurable performance at small label budgets on novel scenario classes.
• A credible path to tactical-edge deployment on Size-Weight-and-Power-constrained platforms.

Recent work across these areas has independently demonstrated subsets of these properties, including graph-structured anomaly reasoning, compositional multi-modal scene understanding, and interpretable edge AI with online adaptation.

Converging them into a single autonomous metacognitive orchestration substrate is the objective of this topic. Approaches that rely on monolithic end-to-end deep networks without compositional or causal structure, or on narrative-only explanations produced by prompted language models, fall outside the scope of this topic.

The program seeks novel approaches to key technical challenges, including:

• Representing and reasoning over time-lagged causal dependencies across multi-modal sensor streams whose native tempos span four or more orders of magnitude, under missing, late, corrupted, and adversarially manipulated inputs.
• Computing expected information gain over candidate collection actions while treating operational constraints (emissions, bandwidth, power, time-to-decision, access) as hard-binding semantic variables rather than reward-shaped scalars, and producing Pareto-optimal option-sets rather than single collapsed policies.
• Self-monitoring the system’s own confidence, prediction error, and representational coherence; detecting adversarial denial, deception, and distribution shift as learning signals; and triggering targeted local refinement of the internal model without offline retraining.
• Generating forward-looking “why / why-not” traces, reproducible from internal system state, that link each recommendation to its supporting evidence chain, the constraints it satisfies, the alternatives it dominated, and the expected futures it forecasts, supporting downstream review by a subject-matter expert (SME) or within a human-machine formation.
• Probabilistic root-cause analysis of observed outcomes, tracing back through the internal representation to identify contributing evidence across domains and timescales, with ranked alternative hypotheses and quantified confidence.

Phase I:
This SBIR topic is open to Direct-to-Phase-II (DP2) proposals only. Phase I proposals will not be accepted or reviewed. DP2 feasibility shall be substantiated through prior work completed outside of the SBIR program. Acceptable evidence includes peer-reviewed publications, pre-prints, patents, prototype demonstrations with video or data artifacts, technical reports, and test-and-measurement data. Proposers shall demonstrate scientific and technical merit and feasibility across the criteria below, each with quantitative side-by-side comparison against at least one mainstream baseline (classical fusion, reinforcement or active learning, agentic-LLM orchestration, or equivalent) on a shared task.

• Structured reasoning over asynchronous multi-source evidence. Evidence of a compositional or causally-structured representation, built using hyperdimensional and vector-symbolic architectures (HDC/VSA), neuro-symbolic, graph-based reasoning, or a hybrid, operating across at least two heterogeneous modalities whose native tempos differ by two or more orders of magnitude. The proposer shall characterize the substrate using metrics appropriate to the chosen family (for example, similarity-based retrieval and compositional-capacity metrics for HDC/VSA; inference accuracy and rule-coverage for neuro-symbolic; path-query accuracy and graph-completion metrics for graph-based) and quantify performance under at least 20 percent missing or delayed inputs.

• Cost-aware, forward-looking action selection. Evidence of an information-gain or value-of-information planning capability, implemented by any appropriate technique including adaptive submodular optimization, constrained partially-observable Markov decision processes, information-theoretic sensor selection, or equivalent, that incorporates at least one operational cost term (power, emissions, bandwidth, or latency) and produces multiple candidate actions or an option-set rather than a single collapsed policy, with quantitative information-per-cost gains over a uniform, random, or reactive baseline.

• Auditable decision outputs grounded in internal state. Example decision outputs accompanied by traces, reproducible from internal system state, that identify which evidence and which reasoning pathway drove each recommendation and, where applicable, which alternatives were dominated and why.

The DP2 feasibility documentation package shall include a consolidated technical report summarizing the criteria above with quantitative metrics; substantiating publications, reports, or artifacts; video or data artifacts demonstrating operation on at least one multi-domain task with asynchronous inputs; a risk register identifying the highest technical and programmatic risks with mitigations; and a Phase II transition plan.

Phase II:
The goal of Phase II is to mature the DP2-validated capability into an operationally representative prototype of an autonomous metacognitive orchestration engine for multi-domain intelligence collection, suitable for integration into a human-machine formation. The prototype shall be demonstrated against at least one mainstream baseline family (classical fusion, reinforcement or active learning, or agentic-LLM orchestration) on shared tasks. The capability shall advance from TRL 4 at award to TRL 6 by the end of Phase II. Phase II is a 24-month period with all required capabilities, targets, and capstone demonstrations completed within this period.

DP2 proposals should:

• describe a proposal to achieve the aforementioned goals;
• present a technical plan and approach, with notable risks and mitigations; and
• detail proposed metrics, baselines, and scenarios for final evaluation, aligned with the quantitative targets.

Staged modality scope. The Phase II effort is staged by modality count. In Months 1 through 12, the prototype shall operate across at least two heterogeneous modalities whose native tempos differ by two or more orders of magnitude, demonstrating the full required capability set on that two-modality configuration. In Months 12 through 24, the prototype shall scale to at least four heterogeneous modalities and shall be evaluated against active adversarial denial and deception, integration with one analytic or data-fabric environment identified during the period, hardening for tactical-edge deployment on Size-Weight-and-Power-constrained platforms in denied, degraded, intermittent, and limited-bandwidth (DDIL) settings, and human-machine-formation integration.

At the end of Phase II the integrated prototype shall demonstrate:

• Asynchronous multi-source ingest. Streaming ingest from at least four disparate modalities through modular encoder interfaces, with demonstrated tolerance to missing, late, corrupted, and spoofed streams.
• Compositional reasoning at multiple abstraction levels. A hierarchical structured representation, built in the proposer’s chosen substrate family, that supports primitive (sensor-level), composite (cross-sensor spatio-temporal), and semantic (contextual) abstractions, updated continuously from telemetry.
• Cost-aware, forward-looking collection planning. Computation of expected information gain over candidate collection actions, discounted by tunable cost terms including at minimum emissions or signature, power, latency, and bandwidth, with generation of Pareto-optimal option-sets rather than single collapsed policies.
• Auditable decision traces. Forward-looking “why / why-not” explanations for each recommendation, reproducible from internal system state, identifying supporting evidence, constraints satisfied, and dominated alternatives. Narrative-only explanations produced by prompted language models are not acceptable.
• Real-time re-orchestration without offline retraining. Replanning under sensor loss, intermittent denial, deception injection, or changes in specified objectives and weights, at plan-refresh latency below 3 minutes.
• Probabilistic root-cause analysis. Tracing observed outcomes back to contributing evidence across modalities and timescales, with ranked alternative hypotheses and quantified confidence.
• Metacognitive self-assessment and adaptation. Detection of internal reasoning drift, adversarial manipulation, or distribution shift, and targeted local refinement of the internal representation without offline retraining. Preserved or improved performance across at least five repeated exposures to the same class of adversarial perturbation, relative to a baseline that must retrain to recover, is the primary evidence of this capability.
• Human-machine-formation integration. Modular, open-schema APIs for option-sets, explanations, and constraints, suitable for integration with analytic and data-fabric environments used by a human-machine formation, together with a documented commander-intent interface for pre-mission specification and an after-action audit interface for post-mission review.

Baselines and the capstone scenario set will be finalized with the Program Manager at kickoff. At least one capstone scenario shall involve active adversarial denial or deception. Quantitative goals to be met or exceeded by the end of Phase II include:

• Time-to-decisive-cue at least 35 percent faster than a reactive fusion baseline at fixed sensing budget.
• Information-gain per unit energy at least 2 times over a reactive fusion baseline on an energy-instrumented testbed.
• Operational-constraint violation rate (including emissions-control posture) below 5 percent under adversarial stress.
• Plan-refresh latency below 3 minutes under induced sensor loss, deception injection, or mid-mission objective change.
• Subject-matter expert coherence rating of “why / why-not” traces at or above 85 percent against doctrine-aligned rubrics.

The following schedule of milestones and deliverables is provided to establish expectations for the Phase II effort. Proposers shall execute a Research and Development plan as described in their proposal, including the following:

• Month 1. Kickoff briefing (with annotated slides) to the DARPA Program Manager (PM), including any updates to the proposed plan and technical approach, risks and mitigations, schedule with planned capability milestones and deliverables, proposed metrics and baselines, specification of open-schema interfaces for option-sets, explanations, and constraints, and the planned human-machine-formation integration approach.
• Month 3. Architecture Design Review. Formal specification of the structured representation, value-of-information planner, and metacognitive self-assessment layer. Baseline benchmarks on one multi-domain scenario involving two modalities at asynchronous tempos and two operational cost terms. Quarterly technical progress report.
• Month 6. Two-modality prototype demonstration with asynchronous ingest and primitive-level structured reasoning; initial cost-aware planning with two cost terms and option-set generation; quantitative comparison against the reactive fusion baseline on time-to-cue and information-per-cost. Quarterly technical progress report.
• Month 9. Interim technical progress briefing (with annotated slides) to the DARPA PM. Demonstration of constraint-aware re-orchestration under induced sensor loss and mid-mission objective change; first SME evaluation of “why / why-not” traces against doctrine-aligned rubrics; updated risks, mitigations, and technical plan for the second half of Phase II.
• Month 12. Two-modality Critical Design Review. Integrated demonstration of the required capability set on the two-modality configuration with asynchronous ingest, meeting or approaching the 35 percent time-to-decisive-cue, 2x information-per-watt, and below-3-minute plan-refresh targets. Documented transition plan from two-modality to four-modality scope. Quarterly technical progress report.
• Month 15. Four-modality ingest and primitive-through-semantic reasoning demonstration. Quantitative results on representational capacity, noise tolerance, and inference latency on four modalities. First integration with an analytic or data-fabric environment identified during the first half of Phase II.
• Month 18. Metacognitive adaptation demonstration. Scripted denial-and-deception injection. Quantitative demonstration of performance preservation or improvement across at least five repeated adversarial exposures without external retraining, compared against a baseline that must retrain to recover. Quarterly technical progress report.

Option Milestones

• Month 21. Human-machine-formation integration and tactical-edge hardening. Full quantitative-target evaluation on at least two capstone scenarios, including at least one with active adversarial denial or deception. Commander-intent and after-action-audit interfaces exercised with SMEs. Quarterly technical progress report.
• Month 24. Final technical progress briefing (with annotated slides) to the DARPA PM. Capstone demonstration across four modalities on at least three scenarios drawn from the kickoff-agreed set. Final Phase II Report documenting architecture, algorithms, evaluation methodology, quantitative results against all Phase II quantitative goals, API specifications, user and administrator manuals, adversarial-robustness characterization, commercialization plan, and a Phase III transition plan with named non-SBIR funding source(s).

Capstone scenarios. The prototype shall be demonstrated on at least three scenarios drawn from the categories below, agreed with the Program Manager at kickoff. At least one shall involve active adversarial denial or deception.

Scenario 1. Multi-modal collection under emissions control. Orchestrate collection across EO/IR, SAR, RF, and AIS (or equivalent) modalities under a restrictive emissions-control posture with variable spectrum availability. Demonstrate improved information-gain-per-cost against the proposer’s chosen baseline, emissions posture enforced as a hard constraint, bounded degradation under spectrum denial, and recovery when access is restored. Include a scripted injection of a contact-of-interest whose correct classification requires cross-referencing at least three modalities.

Scenario 2. Cross-INT corroboration within a human-machine formation. Support development of a decision product that requires corroboration across at least three independent modalities against a commander-specified hold-fire confidence threshold. Demonstrate that the engine autonomously sequences supporting collection (for example, tasks a revisit to disambiguate an ambiguous cue), returns option-sets at varying confidence, latency, and signature trade-offs, surfaces a reproducible decision trace for downstream review within the human-machine formation, and declines to cross the threshold when corroboration is insufficient, articulating why.

Scenario 3. Denial-and-deception resilience with metacognitive adaptation. Against scripted adversarial injection of coordinated deceptive indicators (spoofed tracks, falsified pattern-of-life, counterfeit logistics signatures, misleading RF emissions), detect semantic incoherence through metacognitive self-assessment and autonomously refine the internal representation to compensate. Demonstrate that performance is preserved or improved across at least five repeated adversarial exposures, measured against a baseline that must retrain to recover.

The awardee shall participate in at least one simulation exercise or demonstration event during the 24-month period of performance, coordinated with the Program Manager.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III work will be oriented toward transition and commercialization. Funding is obtained from the private sector, a non-SBIR Government source, or both, to develop the prototype into a viable product or non-R&D service for sale in military or private-sector markets. Military applications include autonomous orchestration of persistent multi-domain ISR collection; multi-INT corroboration and decision support for Joint and Combined Joint All-Domain Command and Control (JADC2 / CJADC2) mission threads; cross-domain indications and warning at theater scale; and human-machine-formation decision tooling for multi-domain formations operating under emissions, bandwidth, and access constraints. The capability’s constraint-aware, causally-informed, and auditable reasoning directly supports Department of Defense Responsible AI principles and downstream Operational Test and Evaluation, Mission Assurance, and Authority-to-Operate review processes for AI capabilities that influence collection, tasking, and other consequential decisions. Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific (NIWC Pacific) is a representative candidate Government transition venue. Additional transition opportunities will be identified during execution.

Commercial applications are broad and immediate. The underlying capability (constraint-aware, auditable orchestration of heterogeneous asynchronous multi-source evidence, with operator-retunable objectives and without retraining cycles) is directly applicable to commercial satellite-constellation tasking and cross-mission sensor-resource management; maritime-domain-awareness products for port authorities, coast guards, and commercial insurers; critical-infrastructure monitoring across electricity, water, transportation, and pipeline sectors; supply-chain security and provenance verification; public-health biosurveillance; sensor-resource management for commercial autonomous fleets; and enterprise security-operations-center augmentation in which heterogeneous multi-modal indicators must be correlated under cost, latency, and regulatory constraints.

References:
• U.S. Department of Defense. “Summary of the Joint All-Domain Command and Control Strategy.” Department of Defense, 2022.
• Gabrielle Kaili-May Liu, Areeb Gani, Jacqueline Lu, Jordan Thomas, Mark Steyvers, Arman Cohan. “Metacognition in LLMs: Foundations, Progress, and Opportunities.” ArXiv preprint arXiv:2607.11881v1, 2026.
• Hua Wei, Paulo Shakarian, Christian Lebiere, Bruce Draper, Nikhil Krishnaswamy, Sergei Nirenburg. “Metacognitive AI: Framework and the Case for a Neurosymbolic Approach.” arXiv:2406.12147v1, 2024.
• Aditya Taparia, Noel Ngu, Mario Leiva, Joshua Shay Kricheli, John Corcoran, Nathaniel D. Bastian, Gerardo Simari, Paulo Shakarian, and Ransalu Senanayake. “VLC Fusion: Vision-Language Conditioned Sensor Fusion for Robust Object Detection.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.12715, 2025.
• Shahriar Rifat, AQM Sazzad Sayyed, Nathaniel D. Bastian, and Francesco Restuccia. “Metacognitive Artificial Intelligence in Vision Foundation Models: Research Challenges.” IEEE Intelligent Systems, 2026.

title: Human Universal Remote
summary: The objective of the Human Universal Remote DP2 SBIR topic is to further develop surface electromyography (sEMG) sensors, piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs), or other non-invasive sensor modalities as a user interface for warfighter multi-system operations1-6.
description:
Objective:
The objective of the Human Universal Remote DP2 SBIR topic is to further develop surface electromyography (sEMG) sensors, piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs), or other non-invasive sensor modalities as a user interface for warfighter multi-system operations1-6. The cited references serve as representative baselines of the state-of-the-art human machine interfaces and do not limit the scope of acceptable technical approaches.

The vision is for a single warfighter to execute simultaneous, multi-domain tasks without compromising their primary physical posture or situational awareness. For example, controlling a drone while handling a rifle, or sending/receiving audible, out of line-of-sight communications via radio without speaking. The envisioned system may combine micro-scale ultrasonic cellular stimulation, ultrasound and EMG sensor fusion, and deep learning driven gesture recognition. The system must translate and discern between sub-millimeter muscle contractions and intentional, full-range movements to trigger external system commands. In a series of readiness tests, performers will develop the sensor suite and processing framework to serve as a hands-free, eyes-free human-machine interface for multi-system warfighter operations.

Description:
Surface electromyography (sEMG) is a proven technique for detecting biomedical voltage measurements from the skin generated by the electrical current of muscle fibers during skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation. These signals, which reflect neuromuscular activity, typically range in amplitude from 0 to 10 millivolts and operate at frequencies between 20 and 450 Hz. While historically used to restore hand function for transradial amputees via non-invasive fiber membrane potential measurement, this topic proposes leveraging state-of-the-art sEMG in concert with other non-invasive muscle sensing modalities to significantly enhance the operational capability of the warfighter. For example, ultrasound is a high-resolution non-invasive sensing modality capable of probing deep muscle tissues and providing complementary information to electromyographic signals. This topic is divided into two distinct, parallel Technical Areas (TAs) that must be addressed concurrently. Proposers must deliver an integrated solution spanning both domains:

Technical Area 1 (TA1): Microphone

Signal capture will focus on the non-invasive detection and extraction of EMG signals and/or electrical, acoustic deep muscle sensing signals from the user. The approach should include the utilization of signals for arm control as both a command and as biological sensors to understand where muscle activity is occurring and to function as an active indicator of warfighter stress. Hardware systems developed under this Technical Area must reliably detect, isolate, and extract these microvolt-to-millivolt level biopotential signals directly from the warfighter’s skin without invasive techniques. Proposers should address the following TA1 criteria:

TA1 Criteria

Description

Array design

Single or multimodal sensor arrays that conform to the forearm or targeted muscle groups

Form factor

Integrates with standard-issue warfighter apparel without causing skin irritation or impeding range of motion over extended wear

Ruggedization

Maintain a high signal-to-noise ratio under stress:

• Sweat
• Dynamic movement & collision resistance
• Electromagnetic interference

Dual-use sensing

Capture intent-driven neuromuscular firing patterns to facilitate hands-free control of external systems while serving as passive biological monitoring of muscle fatigue, physical overexertion, and cognitive stress

Calibration

The system must be designed for recalibration once during initial outfitting of the sensor array onto the warfighter. Calibration techniques should require minimal to no additional cognitive load and take as much time as to be doable during mission briefing.

Technical Area 2 (TA2): Speaker

This Technical Area focuses on translating decoded physiological intent into standardized, platform-agnostic output modalities. The system must reliably differentiate between passive muscle strain and active, intentional micro- and macro-gestures to generate high-confidence external commands. The approach should include command output that translates the processed signals into an actionable trigger via standard communications channels designed for easy integration into Team Awareness Kit (TAK). To prevent over-engineering to a singular use case or platform, the generated signaling protocol should be standardizable for use across multiple external systems. At a minimum, the platform should be built with at least one communications channel using radiofrequency (RF). Example platforms include enabling users to task robotic systems, low-level ISR drones, comms drones, trigger communications, and generate visual indicators directly on a TAK display. Proposers should address the following TA2 criteria:

TA2 CriteriaDescription
Compute Implement low latency machine learning or pattern-recognition algorithms capable of running on power-constrained processors
Modular OutputGenerate control packets transmittable via RF waveforms such as Bluetooth
Multi-Platform

Validate the versatility of decoded gesture triggers (pick 2):

• Android TAK (ATAK) Control
• Communication Device Control
• Communication Transmission
• Unmanned System Tasking (Air, Ground, Water, etc.)

Phase I:
Since this is a DP2 topic ONLY, a successful proposal must already contain evidence of a working prototype. The success criteria for a working prototype are the following:

• Working non-invasive sEMG sensor array that employs a computationally efficient machine-learning based control algorithm driven by input from a high-density array of electrodes.
• Functioning hardware that interfaces with a machine learning algorithm capable of real-time gesture classification.
• A developed training and calibration software interface that prompts users through gesture protocols, records performance metrics, measures gesture classification accuracy, and misclassification error rates.

The above information should be presented in such a manner that it is evident that the proposer’s prototype technology can be tailored to meet the criteria in Phase II.

Phase II:
A successful proposal will address the overarching technical areas with performer-defined metrics over the course of 18 months or less. The program is structured with readiness tests at Month 12 and Month 18. Proposers will be expected to define at least one deliverable per month to meet incremental technical milestones to sufficiently advance the technology to meet the Controlled Environment Readiness and Environmental Resilience tests. Proposals should outline a work plan to technically advance the design to meet the demonstration scenarios within the provided timeline.

Controlled Environment Readiness Test – Jam Session

This readiness test will serve as the gatekeeper metric to prove the system can successfully transition from controlled development environments into unpredictable operational settings. The system must be tested on a diverse cohort of previously untrained and unexposed human subjects. The software calibration must adapt to varied anatomical structures, body mass indexes, and physiological signal variations without developer intervention. Testing will occur during a series of continuous baseline of physical activities. These activities will include high-exertion tasks designed to introduce physical noise to test rejection of background muscle activity. While performing the baseline physical activities, subjects will be prompted to execute specific micro- and macro-command gestures. The system must dynamically isolate and decode these intentional commands from the background physiological "noise" of the active baseline tasks.

Session CriteriaDescription
Gesture accuracy92% true-positive command recognition across the user pool
False alarm2% accidental command triggers during continuous baseline physical activities
CalibrationCalibration and training in under 30 minutes

Environmental Resilience – Arena Concert

The Month 18 evaluation will transition the system from controlled laboratory settings into an austere field environment at a representative military training installation (e.g., Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton), subjecting the user to the following parameters while executing gestures for one command output that translates the processed signals into an actionable trigger via RF and/or ATAK integrations:

• Ingress Protection (IP) rating IP68
• In tandem with standard military uniform/dress
• Chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) protective gear
• High-exertion physical activity/collision testing
• Simulated weapon manipulation

Gesture Output can include any of the following, for example:

• Audible communication without speaking and out of line-of-sight

o Ground and Water Testing

• Autonomous system tasking of any variety
• TAK manipulation
• Radio control
• Demonstration of ability to remove radio from weapons space

Concert CriteriaDescription
Gesture accuracy92% true-positive command recognition across the user pool
False alarm2% accidental command triggers during physical activities
CalibrationCalibration and training in under 30 minutes

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III will be oriented toward military transition and further commercialization.

• Military: Autonomous system tasking, enabling raid teams to communicate without speaking, and providing visuals and status through fatal funnel.
• Commercial: Accessibility technology, quantitative biomechanical baselines to monitor neuromuscular health for rehabilitation, open-source code for personal drone piloting and gaming applications.

title: UAS-based Precision Aim for Device Render Safe in CBRN Environments
summary: Develop novel precision-aiming payload capability that can be employed by UAS and operated remotely. Hand-emplaced precision aiming is a common technique used by all militaries and civilian defense forces.
description:
Objective:
Develop novel precision-aiming payload capability that can be employed by UAS and operated remotely. Hand-emplaced precision aiming is a common technique used by all militaries and civilian defense forces. Warfighters require the ability to remotely emplace and precisely aim, adjust, and employ disruptor shells against explosive ordnance threats often associated with Chemical or Biological warheads, supporting standoff and remote render-safe operations. The proposed approach should include one or more payloads that can be integrated with one or more Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) platforms and be capable of operating in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, or Nuclear (CBRN) environment.

Description:
DTRA is in need of technical innovations associated with warfighting units performing very long range WMD device render-safe missions from a safe distance, outside of potentially CBRN contaminated environments. Explosive Ordinance Disposal (EOD) definitions and terms are commonly used by many nations and exist on the public internet including steps involving EOD detection, identification, field evaluation, render safe, recovery and disposal. Successfully performing stand-off EOD missions with personal positioned away from the contaminated environment requires a payload capable of remotely and accurately aiming via employment of currently fielded EOD disruptors against the explosive ordnance threat with a high degree of precision.

Payload capabilities of the proposed solution should ideally be sized to be compatible with currently fielded Department of War UAS systems. The desired end state is a system weight that is designed for small-unit operations UAS.

DTRA conducts counter WMD science and technology research and testing efforts for Joint Services EOD missions. Ground robotic platforms currently provide the only fielded remote-employment method for EOD disruptors, but these lack terrain-independent access and approach-angle flexibility that an aerial platform would provide. Small unit operations UAS platforms with sufficient flight endurance and payload capacity to carry current EOD-relevant payloads into contested or austere environments. This topic seeks novel approaches to providing precision remote-aiming payloads delivered and emplaced by remote UAS with subsequent operational render safe execution orchestrated from remotely. The capability should be able to be remotely recovered and re-charged to enable system re-use at another location after the render safe mission is completed

Phase I:
Design a system architecture and conduct an Analysis of Alternatives (AoA) to identify and evaluate candidate remote precision-aiming disruptor payloads against Joint Service EOD operational requirements. Assess mechanical, electrical, and software adaptability and versatility of leading candidates from each technology category, and define the specific engineering interfaces (mechanical mounting, power, control/data links, payload release and re-attachment mechanisms) required to integrate the at least one proposed system. Include in the proposed architecture a proposed method to communicate and control from a remote location, outside and upwind of a potential CBRN contaminated area. If feasible, a visual simulation of the proposed architecture executing an example mission would be helpful.

Phase II:
Construct the engineering integration and prototype effort identified in Phase 1. Construct and bench-test the set of key physical and electronic interfaces using the proposed UAS platform and the selected precision-aiming disruptor payload, including pickup/drop-off release mechanisms, remote aiming control integration, and command-and-control software integration. Demonstrate subsystem functionality in a Government identified controlled test environment.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Revise prototype design based on operational feedback and any testing results during Phase 2. Produce two complete sets of proposed system prototype capability including methods to enable remote command and control. Conduct two integrated field employment and demonstrations of the combined system, in representative austere and in an urban operational environment, the government will provide access to government test ranges and assist in test planning. Demonstrate end-to-end mission execution: aerial transit, precision payload emplacement, remote disruptor aiming and adjustment, and (as an objective capability) payload retrieval/repositioning.

title: Remote UAS-based X-Ray for Device Assessment in CBRNE Environments
summary: Develop a novel stand-off X-ray capability by integrating appropriate x-ray transmitter and x-ray receiver capabilities into multiple cooperating UAS systems to enable remote threat device imaging capabilities from a safe distance away from potential Chemical, Biological, Radiological, or Nuclear (CBRN) environments.
description:
Objective:
Develop a novel stand-off X-ray capability by integrating appropriate x-ray transmitter and x-ray receiver capabilities into multiple cooperating UAS systems to enable remote threat device imaging capabilities from a safe distance away from potential Chemical, Biological, Radiological, or Nuclear (CBRN) environments.

Description:
DTRA is in need of technical innovations associated with Warfighters performing long range WMD device assessment and characterization from a safe distance outside of potentially CBRN contaminated environments. Explosive Ordinance Disposal (EOD) definitions and terms are commonly used by many nations and exist on the public internet including steps involving EOD detection, assessment, identification, field evaluation, render safe, recovery and disposal. Current device assessment is manual, requiring personnel to approach closely and manually move x-ray transmitters and x-ray receivers around an unknown device to perform the required assessment mission. Current stand-off capabilities are typically ground robots manually driven a short distance which may be safe for some unexploded ordinance (UXO), but are not safe for suspected WMD warheads. Recent UAS innovations associated with coaxial form factor systems that can perch or land as part of their mission flight profile appear to offer a novel approach to conducting bi-static x-ray image collection.

STATE OF TECHNOLOGY.

• Current Portable digital radiography systems that depend on hand- or robot-emplacement of a source and flat-panel detector near the device are limited in a CBRN environment. There is no current technology solution that can generate diagnostically useful transmission images (sufficient penetration of ordnance casings plus resolution of fine fuse features such as wires, switches, or delay elements) without any ground contact or personnel entry into the contaminated zone.
• Mobile x-ray transmitters and various options for exposing images, and stitching multiple images together to create a 3-D assessment of an unknown device exist, but they are generally hand-carried and emplaced. Complex mathematics and algorithms for capturing and rendering X-ray results from multiple simultaneously moving transmitters and receivers each with potential uncertainties in position and angle are limited.
• Tactical UAS systems are generally small, carry lighter payloads, do not have open architectures for payloads, and payload options are generally difficult and limited to the bottom side to integrate without adversely affecting flight profiles.
• Robotic x-rays exist but are typically fixed, large and devices are brought to them and put on a turntable. This topic is for x-rays done in the field, at 5km distances, without moving the threat device.
• No UAS-based x-ray capability currently exists.

Phase I:
Design a novel stand-off X-ray capability concept that would integrate portable x-ray transmitter and receiver capabilities into multiple cooperating UAS systems. Create an in silico model of system performance with mathematical assessment of anticipated image quality as a function of time, motion, and navigation uncertainties. A functional transmission X-ray source (high-voltage generation, cooling, radiation shielding) plus a suitable detector must be integrated while preserving flight stability for sharp imaging, supporting open real-time data architectures.

Phase II:
Build one working prototype of proposed system to demonstrate capability to collect data for post-processing at a later date. Prototype design should look to fill persistent and newly heightened technical gaps to include: lightweight, high-flux (preferably pulsed) X-ray sources and detectors suitable for prolonged airborne carriage; robust real-time algorithms for motion-compensated multi-view reconstruction from independently flying platforms; methods to extract fuse-function information from low-signal, limited-angle, or single-pass data; sealed or disposable system architectures that eliminate the need for recovery of contaminated hardware; and practical techniques that achieve usable diagnostic quality at greater effective standoffs while still resolving internal mechanisms without any ground presence.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Extend Phase 2 capabilities to scale performance of missions at multiple sites, allowing for multiple swarming transmitters and/or receivers spread over time and space. Demonstrate ability to generate integrated X-Ray image results rapidly, on location in near-real-time during or soon after completion of swarming activities.

title: Dynamic Sensor-Tasking and Routing System for Subsurface Hazard Detection
summary: Develop an explainable, adaptive machine learning architecture using Super Intelligence (SI) that dynamically schedules, sequences, and gates geophysical sensor modalities based on real-time environmental physics, learned sensor operational envelopes, and predictive target response models.
description:
Objective:
Develop an explainable, adaptive machine learning architecture using Super Intelligence (SI) that dynamically schedules, sequences, and gates geophysical sensor modalities based on real-time environmental physics, learned sensor operational envelopes, and predictive target response models. The system will enable autonomous platforms to perform in-stride characterization and clearance of subsurface hazards, including potential WMD devices or components, in high-tempo, contested tactical environments.

Description:
Current field-deployable capabilities for WMD device and component defeat, route reconnaissance, and sensitive site exploitation have made significant strides in rapid surface-level mapping and visual threat triage using unmanned aerial and ground platforms. However, these operational systems encounter a critical bottleneck when confronting subsurface hazards. Visual, optical, and topographic sensors are fundamentally blind to threats that are partially buried, completely subsurface, or obscured beneath soil, blast debris, or disturbed earth. When subsurface geophysical instruments are integrated onto these unmanned platforms to address this blind spot, current field architecture suffers from a severe "collect everything" bottleneck. Lacking localized intelligence, platforms typically execute static, pre-programmed survey scripts which force sensors to operate continuously and indiscriminately across an entire area. This floods constrained tactical communication networks with massive volumes of raw sensor data, overwhelms field computing devices, drastically slows operational tempo, and results in sensor operational blindness when local soil physics degrade or invalidate specific sensor modalities. When conducting standoff reconnaissance of suspected hazard areas—which may contain buried chemical or biological munitions, radiological dispersal device (RDD) components, bulk precursor storage vessels, or associated explosive triggers and conventional ordnance—these bottlenecks force operators into dangerous, prolonged exposure on target. Furthermore, relying on rigid, static classical logic to manage these complex sensor suites in real time introduces a critical limitation, as traditional rule-based programs cannot adapt to highly dynamic, uncharacterized environments where the boundary conditions are not known beforehand.

A proactive system is required to answer:

"Given this specific environment and mission profile, which sensor should be deployed first, what detection threshold triggers the next modality, and which sensors may be inhibited due to the environment or other physical boundary conditions?"

This topic seeks an adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine capable of scheduling sensor deployment and routing platform payloads in real time using probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods. The primary need is an intelligent edge capability that continuously monitors changing site conditions and dynamically queues, activates, or inhibits physical sensor payloads on an autonomous platform. Rather than streaming raw data or running all sensors simultaneously, the system must govern sensor execution through learned decision policies (utilizing techniques such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) that optimize performance based on sensor-inferred environmental physics (such as electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity), immediate mission constraints (such as required advance speed, standoff distance requirements, and target priority), and real-time sensor performance signatures. When an initial screening modality detects an anomaly, the engine must evaluate the environmental context to dynamically determine if a secondary, higher-fidelity sensor is required to verify and classify the threat, or if the platform should continue its route. By automating this sensor-queuing and routing logic at the edge through explainable and efficient AI, the system will overcome the subsurface bottlenecks of current field suites, eliminate tactical network saturation, minimize time on target, and ensure reliable detection and defeat of subsurface WMD devices and associated hazards across diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.

State of Technology: Currently deployed military and commercial technologies have reached a high level of maturity in distinct, stove-piped domains, but they do not integrate these capabilities into a single, closed-loop, in-stride subsurface decision engine. The current technical landscape is characterized by the following:

• Standoff Aerial and Surface Visual Mapping Systems: Existing fielded systems utilize unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and ground platforms to perform rapid photogrammetric, optical (EO/IR), and LiDAR mapping of surface terrains. These systems feature mature edge-computing architectures that run real-time automated target recognition (ATR) to classify surface munitions, craters, and obstacles on tactical hand-held tablets in under 30 minutes. However, these systems lack subsurface sensing capability, limiting their ability to detect and characterize hazards that are partially buried, covered by debris, or below the ground surface.
• Geophysical Post-Processing Classification Suites: For subsurface detection, advanced electromagnetic induction (EMI) and ground-penetrating radar (GPR) systems are highly mature and accredited for DoW munitions response. These systems utilize sophisticated physics-based inversion models to extract target polarizability tensors and classify anomalies against standard munitions libraries. However, these software suites are strictly designed for post-processing desktop environments. They are not integrated into real-time, in-stride robotic platforms, and they cannot make autonomous decisions in the field regarding active sensor scheduling.
• Uncoordinated "Collect-Everything" Sensor Payloads: Current multi-sensor ground platforms operate in a fixed, concurrent acquisition mode where all integrated sensors (such as magnetometers, GPR, and EMI) run continuously regardless of whether the local terrain and environment is physically compatible with the sensor. For example, when a platform transitions into wet, highly conductive clay, a ground-penetrating radar (GPR) antenna suffers from severe signal attenuation, rendering the collected data ineffective for its intended detection purpose. Current systems lack the real-time feedback loops to recognize these environmental changes and limitations then automatically adjust, disable, or redirect sensor payloads. This lack of dynamic management creates a major operational inefficiency, resulting in the collection of highly degraded data that requires excessive post-processing, while unnecessarily consuming onboard battery power, communication bandwidth, and valuable mission time.
• Static Autonomous Path Planning: Existing autonomous ground and aerial navigation algorithms plan paths based on surface traversability, geometric obstacle avoidance, and pre-mapped terrain features. They do not ingest real-time subsurface hazard maps or dynamically adjust their routing, payload dwell times, or sensor modalities based on changing subsurface soil electromagnetic properties or detected anomalies.
• Adaptive AI/ML for Sequential Decision-Making and Path Planning: In adjacent fields such as autonomous warehouse robotics, dynamic network routing, and space domain awareness, machine learning is highly mature for solving complex, real-time sensor scheduling and path-planning challenges. State-of-the-art approaches utilize Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and Contextual Multi-Armed Bandits to train autonomous agents that make optimal sequential decisions under extreme uncertainty. These AI models observe dynamic environmental contexts (e.g., localized obstacle density or changing wireless signal-to-noise ratios), weigh the trade-offs between exploring unknown areas and exploiting known paths, and automatically adjust sensor power cycles or update the platform’s route on-the-fly. However, these advanced decision-making frameworks have not yet been integrated with or trained on subsurface geophysical physics, leaving a critical gap where current autonomous AI agents remain incapable of managing multi-modal subsurface sensor suites.

Phase I:
Demonstrate the technical and operational feasibility of an adaptive, machine-learning-Super Intelligence (SI) driven decision engine for dynamic sensor-tasking and routing. Efforts will focus on identifying the theoretical machine learning models, policy optimization frameworks, and reward structures (e.g., reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or other decision-making algorithms) governing a representative sensor suite, which may include multiple sensor phenomenology’s to identify representative subsurface and surface hazards, including potential WMD devices or components.

The investigator will develop an Super Intelligence (SI)-based software emulator or conceptual model to evaluate the feasibility of the learned sensor-gating policies and decision rules under varying environmental and mission constraints. Phase I will conclude with a demonstration showing that the adaptive, machine-learning-driven system can successfully execute sensor-gating, anomaly escalation, or vehicle routing to prove a reduction in survey time and data overhead compared to static multi-sensor acquisition.

Phase II:
Transition the theoretical machine learning models, policy optimization frameworks, and adaptive sensor-gating logic developed in Phase I into a functional software prototype of the decision engine. The investigator will design and program an edge-deployable software package optimized to execute real-time model inference on embedded processors without requiring cloud reachback or high-performance computing resources during operations.

The prototype design and engineering effort will focus on converting Phase I's learned decision models and policy algorithms into robust, real-time software capable of ingesting in-stride environmental feeds and continuously calculating the optimal sensor-tasking sequence at the tactical edge. The investigator will conduct demonstrations using real physical sensor data to verify that the machine-learning-driven decision engine successfully executes the correct sensor-sequencing commands (activating, disabling, or swapping sensor modalities based on physical environmental transitions) and adapts simulated platform routing based on learned, unclassified target-detection thresholds.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III will scale the testing and validation of the machine-learning-driven software prototype developed in Phase II through larger-scale field demonstrations and expanded evaluations across highly diverse, uncharacterized environments. This phase will focus on scaling the system's capabilities by validating the generalization of the trained decision policies against significantly larger, multi-site real-world environmental datasets and conducting testing across larger geographical search areas to ensure the model adapts to novel terrain without requiring real-time retraining. Testing and evaluations should focus on demonstrating the software's execution on representative unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) and unmanned aerial system (UAS) platforms configured with the sensor payloads identified in the previous phases.

The expanded demonstrations will evaluate the SI decision engine's ability to repeatably execute sensor-gating commands and adapt platform routing when encountering a wider array of subsurface hazards and simulated WMD-relevant components under diverse, live-field terrain and soil conditions. This expanded validation will provide the necessary performance data to support future technology transition pathways into DTRA C-WMD technology suites, Joint Service EOD robotic systems, and automated route-reconnaissance and breaching suites to support future engineering requirements. For commercial dual-use, the scaled software will transition to geophysics and environmental remediation contractors conducting UXO clean-up at Formerly Used Defense Sites (FUDS), as well as subsurface utility engineering (SUE) platforms to enable more efficient, rapid subsurface mapping in complex civil environments.
