title: Low Cost / Rapidly Producible Booster Insulation Methods
summary: This topic will develop affordable, scalable, high production rate insulation technologies for solid rocket motors.
description:
Objective:
This topic will develop affordable, scalable, high production rate insulation technologies for solid rocket motors.

Description:
Solid propellant rockets use insulation to protect motor cases from the high temperature combustion gases and, in the case of composite cases, prevent egress of gases. Heritage methods for insulating motor cases utilize filled polymers with low thermal conductivities which absorb heat as they decompose. The insulation layer is typically applied through time consuming processes on custom mandrels which require significant manual labor. The Government seeks novel insulation material/processing technologies which reduce insulation processing time and/or cost compared to legacy processes for a variety of motor case geometries and sizes. The primary motor case materials of interest for this solicitation are polymer matrix composites, though applicability to metallic cases is also desirable. Proposals developing reusable or low-cost consumable mandrels which can be easily and quickly removed after insulation lay-up and winding are also of interest. The proposed insulation solution must consider stress limitations in the propellant with variations in temperature during storage and operation. The proposed insulation technology should also meet or exceed the insulating ability of the current state of the art with equal or lower inert mass with an increased production rate and/or lower per unit price.

Phase I:
Phase I-like proposals will not be evaluated and will be rejected as nonresponsive. For this topic, the Government expects the small business would have accomplished the following in a Phase I-like effort via some other means, e.g., independent research and development (IRAD) or other source, a concept for a workable prototype or design to address, at a minimum, the basic capabilities of the stated objective above. Work submitted within the feasibility documentation must have been substantially performed by the proposer and/or the principal investigator (PI).

Phase II:
Produce subscale insulated cases with novel, scalable insulation technology, and characterize the erosion rate compared to the current state of the art in sub-scale motor tests with relevant motor propellants. Show that the proposed insulation should meet a 20-year storage life as well as storage conditions as low as -40 °C. The proposed insulation technology must demonstrate adequate adhesion to the propellant to survive storage and operating conditions. title: Configurable Operator Decision Models for Constructive Test and Evaluation Simulations
summary: Develop and demonstrate a government-configurable software capability that improves the representation, tuning, execution, and validation of human operator decision effects in constructive test and evaluation simulations.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate a government-configurable software capability that improves the representation, tuning, execution, and validation of human operator decision effects in constructive test and evaluation simulations. The capability shall enable Government analysts to instantiate credible operator behavior models across selectable conditions such as experience level, workload, decision latency, engagement posture, rules of engagement, mission priority, and information availability; execute repeatable scenario ensembles; capture decision traces and outcome metrics; and integrate with Government-owned or Government-approved constructive simulation environments used for missile defense test planning, mission engineering, wargaming, and analysis.

The desired outcome is an analyst-facing prototype that makes operator-dependent effects measurable, repeatable, explainable, and suitable for verification, validation, and accreditation (VV&A) consideration without requiring extensive scenario-specific software development.

Description:
Government problem: Missile defense test and evaluation rely on constructive simulations to examine large numbers of scenarios, explore operational concepts, evaluate system-of-systems interactions, and reduce risk before live flight events. These simulations can represent physical platforms, sensors, weapons, communications, terrain, and threat laydowns, but operator decision effects are often represented by fixed scripts, simplified timing rules, or manually coded behaviors. This can cause analysis results to overstate or understate operational performance because human choices influence detection, classification, engagement, prioritization, communication, and response timing across the kill chain.

Capability gap: The Government lacks a reusable and validated way to generate, configure, execute, and assess operator decision representations across many scenario variations and proficiency levels. Current approaches can require extensive custom programming for each model, scenario, or operator role; may not provide traceable rationale for actions taken during simulation; and may be difficult to compare across test events, analysis teams, or simulation environments. The gap affects the Government’s ability to understand sensitivity to operator behavior, evaluate alternate tactics, and support VV&A with documented evidence of intended use, assumptions, limitations, data pedigree, and risk.

Why innovative solutions are likely available: The Government believes innovative small businesses can apply advances from artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled simulation, human behavior representation, synthetic data generation, reinforcement learning, design of experiments, digital engineering, development, security, and operations, and modular simulation integration to address this problem. Related industry capabilities already demonstrate AI-assisted constructive simulation, synthetic data generation, intelligent agents, and integration of commercial simulation toolchains with Government simulation environments. This topic seeks to mature those types of innovations into a Government-purpose capability suitable for missile defense test and evaluation workflows.

Government interest: The Government is not seeking a vendor white paper, a visualization-only training game, or a single hard-coded operator model. The Government is seeking a Direct-to-Phase-II prototype capability that can be adapted to multiple missile defense analysis contexts; that can use Government-provided scenarios, models, data, and subject matter expert (SME) input; that can be evaluated against explicit measures of performance and effectiveness; and that can produce artifacts needed for future transition, reuse, and accreditation.

Desired characteristics:

• Open, modular interfaces for integration with constructive simulations and analysis workflows.
• Configurable operator roles and behavior profiles that can be reviewed and adjusted by authorized Government analysts or SMEs.
• Support for scenario ensembles, design of experiments, and repeatable Monte Carlo-style analysis.
• Decision traceability, data provenance, uncertainty characterization, and explainable outputs suitable for analyst review.

Responsible AI, cyber, data-management, and VV&A considerations incorporated from the beginning of Phase II.

Phase I:
Phase I-like proposals will not be evaluated and will be rejected as nonresponsive. For this topic, the Government expects the small business would have accomplished the following in a Phase I-like effort via some other means, e.g., independent research and development (IRAD) or other source, a concept for a workable prototype or design to address, at a minimum, the basic capabilities of the stated objective above. The documentation provided must substantiate the proposer’s development of a preliminary understanding of the technology to be applied in their Phase II proposal in meeting topic objectives.

(i.e., the small business must have performed a proof of concept like “Phase I” component and/or other validation in a relevant environment, and/or at a much higher Technology Readiness Level (TRL) level (5 or higher) and describe the potential commercialization applications. The documentation provided must validate that the proposer has completed development of technology in previous work or research completed.)

IRAD work: Documentation should include the most relevant information including, but not limited to: technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and/or performance goals/results. Work submitted within the feasibility documentation must have been substantially performed by the proposer and/or the principal investigator (PI).

Phase II:
The Phase II effort shall mature, integrate, demonstrate, and document a prototype capability suitable for Government evaluation within missile defense constructive modeling, simulation, test, and evaluation workflows. The Government seeks an innovative capability that improves the representation of operator decision effects in constructive simulations, enables repeatable analysis across scenario variations, and provides evidence needed to assess credibility, limitations, and transition potential.

Offerors shall propose their own technical approach, architecture, tools, algorithms, data strategy, and integration methods. The proposed solution shall address the following Key Technical Objectives:

Key Technical Objective 1: Establish a Government-relevant use case and evaluation baseline.

The contractor shall coordinate with Government stakeholders to define at least one representative missile defense constructive simulation use case. The baseline shall include the intended use, operator roles or decision functions to be represented, data assumptions, measures of performance, measures of effectiveness, credibility considerations, and transition constraints. The use case shall be scoped to support meaningful prototype demonstration within the Phase II period.

Key Technical Objective 2: Develop a modular prototype capability for representing operator decision effects.

The contractor shall develop a prototype capability that can receive relevant simulation state information, represent operator-relevant decisions or actions, return those decisions or actions to a simulation or analysis workflow, and record the information needed for Government review. The prototype shall include well-defined interfaces, configuration controls, and logging sufficient to support repeatable analysis, technical assessment, and future integration into Government modeling and simulation environments.

Key Technical Objective 3: Provide configurable and analyzable operator behavior representations.

The contractor shall demonstrate a method for representing operator decision behavior across Government-defined conditions, such as experience level, risk posture, workload, degraded information, rules of engagement, mission priorities, or other operationally relevant factors. The capability shall allow Government users, analysts, or subject matter experts to adjust key assumptions without requiring major software redevelopment for each new scenario. The approach may use AI/ML, statistical learning, reinforcement learning, rules-based methods, hybrid methods, SME-informed models, or other innovative techniques proposed by the offeror.

Key Technical Objective 4: Enable repeatable scenario analysis, validation, and explainability.

The contractor shall provide a workflow to execute and assess repeated simulation runs across Government-defined scenario variables and operator-behavior assumptions. The prototype shall generate outputs that allow the Government to compare decision behavior, mission outcomes, and sensitivity to operator assumptions. The contractor shall provide analyst-readable decision traces, uncertainty and limitation statements, validation evidence, and documentation that supports responsible AI use, VV&A considerations, and reduction of unreviewed automation bias.

Key Technical Objective 5: Demonstrate transition-ready prototype performance and documentation.

The contractor shall conduct a mid-period technical demonstration and a final demonstration in a representative constructive simulation or analysis workflow. The final demonstration shall show configurable operator-behavior representation, repeatable scenario execution, decision/output logging, outcome analysis, and evidence generation suitable for Government evaluation. The contractor shall deliver the prototype software or executable evaluation package, architecture/interface documentation, user guidance, test plan, test report, validation evidence, cybersecurity/deployment notes, data rights assertions, and a Phase III transition plan identifying Missile Defense Agency (MDA) and non-MDA transition opportunities.

Threshold expectation: The contractor shall demonstrate a prototype capability at a relevant-environment maturity level appropriate for Direct-to-Phase-II evaluation, with sufficient integration, documentation, and test evidence for Government users to assess technical performance, credibility, limitations, cybersecurity posture, and transition risk.

Objective expectation: The contractor shall demonstrate a modular, reusable capability that can be adapted to additional constructive simulation environments, operator decision functions, missile defense mission areas, and other Government or commercial modeling and simulation applications with limited new software development.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Scale up the capability from the Phase II prototype into a mature, fieldable capability for Government modeling, simulation, test, evaluation, mission engineering, wargaming, training, and analysis workflows. Work with MDA, other Department of War organizations, Intelligence Community users, and commercial partners to integrate the technology into system-level testbeds, constructive simulation environments, and analyst workflows.

title: Multi-Fidelity Transfer Learning for Defense Applications
summary: Use new and evolving Artificial Intelligence (AI) training techniques, algorithms, and protocols to rapidly reduce the resources required to integrate AI into the Missile Defense System (MDS).
description:
Objective:
Use new and evolving Artificial Intelligence (AI) training techniques, algorithms, and protocols to rapidly reduce the resources required to integrate AI into the Missile Defense System (MDS).

Description:
Rapid Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration into the MDS is required for the United States to properly defend itself against its adversaries. The development of robust Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML) agents for complex missile defense and aerospace applications is often constrained by the computational cost, limited availability, and security restrictions of high-fidelity simulation environments. Transfer learning provides a critical pathway to overcoming these barriers. By initially training agents on low-fidelity models or unclassified representations—where data is abundant and computational demands are reduced—core behaviors, strategies, and decision-making frameworks could be efficiently developed and refined. These pretrained models could then be adapted and optimized in high-fidelity and/or environments at higher classification levels, allowing the agent to leverage its foundational knowledge while rapidly acquiring the nuanced performance required for operational deployment. This staged approach significantly reduces training time, minimizes resource expenditure, and mitigates the risk of overfitting to scarce high-fidelity/classified data. Moreover, it enables iterative development cycles where low-fidelity environments serve as agile testbeds for innovation, and high-fidelity environments refine and validate for mission-readiness. Leveraging transfer learning in this manner not only accelerates capability delivery but also ensures that AI/ML systems achieve the precision, resilience, and adaptability necessary for real-world mission success.

Phase I:
Phase I-like proposals will not be evaluated and will be rejected as nonresponsive. For this topic, the Government expects the small business would have accomplished the following in a Phase I-like effort via some other means, e.g., independent research and development (IRAD) or other source, a concept for a workable prototype or design to address, at a minimum, the basic capabilities of the stated objective above. Proposal must show, as appropriate, a demonstrated technical feasibility or nascent capability. The documentation provided must substantiate the proposer’s development of a preliminary understanding of the technology to be applied in their Phase II proposal in meeting topic objectives.

Documentation should comprise all relevant information including, but not limited to, technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results. Feasibility = maturity and what have you already done/validated.

Proposers interested in participating in Direct to Phase II must include in their responses to this topic Phase I feasibility documentation that substantiates the scientific and technical merit and Phase I feasibility described in Phase I above has been met.

(i.e., the small business must have performed a proof of concept like “Phase I” component and/or other validation in a relevant environment, and/or at a much higher Technology Readiness Level (TRL) level (5 or higher) and describe the potential commercialization applications. The documentation provided must validate that the proposer has completed development of technology in previous work or research completed.)

IRAD work: Documentation should include the most relevant information including, but not limited to: technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and/or performance goals/results. Work submitted within the feasibility documentation must have been substantially performed by the proposer and/or the principal investigator (PI).

Phase II:
Create a full prototype capability implementing the tools and demonstrating the processes required to enable AI transfer learning for MDS applications. Design and conduct a case study using the prototype implementation with representative data and models.

Key Technical Objectives:

-Establish a low fidelity training environment based on limited data for AI agent learning applicable to MDS use cases.

-Develop, apply, and implement transfer learning methodologies to drive transfer learning.

-Develop and integrate high fidelity representations of MDS simulation environment across multiple levels of classification.

-Demonstrate resource savings of transfer learning methods versus traditional training methods.

-Design and implement a human-machine interface to seamlessly orchestrate the AI training workflows.

-Deliver prototype AI training workflows for mission relevant use cases that integrate with existing MDS agent training systems.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Scale up the capability from the prototype utilizing the new

processes and software technologies developed in Phase II into a mature, fieldable capability. Work with additional DoD or commercial organizations to integrate the technology into a system level testbed for analyst use.

References:
• Suder, Piotr M., Jason Xu, and David B. Dunson. "Bayesian Transfer Learning." Statistics 2024.2312 (2023).
• Reeve, H., Cannings, T., & Samworth, R. (2021). Adaptive transfer learning. Computing Research Repository, 2021(2106).
• Cody, T., & Beling, P. (2021). A Systems Theory of Transfer Learning. Computing Research Repository, 2021(2107).

title: Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems Rapid Maturation
summary: Mature commercial and dual-use technologies that detect, track, identify, or defeat small low-flying drones (Group 1 and Group 2 unmanned aerial systems) in hostile or contested areas.
description:
Objective:
Mature commercial and dual-use technologies that detect, track, identify, or defeat small low-flying drones (Group 1 and Group 2 unmanned aerial systems) in hostile or contested areas.

Description:
Inexpensive, highly maneuverable, commercially available unmanned aerial systems (UAS) threaten tactical forces, critical infrastructure, and installations. Current defenses are limited by cost, by the operator attention they require, and by their vulnerability to countermeasures. A capability gap against Group 1 and Group 2 UAS remains.

This topic seeks mature or maturing technology at any point in the counter-UAS kill chain. The three areas below are where capability is most needed. They are examples. A proposal may address one area, more than one, or a gap not listed here.

Detection and Tracking. Detect and hold track on highly agile targets in cluttered low-altitude airspace. The proposer selects the sensing modality. Approaches that hold track when the target is not emitting are preferred. Solutions that require permanent site infrastructure or mains power, including fixed perimeter sensor installations, are out of scope for this area. The system must move with the force.

Identification and Decision Support. Classify and identify unauthorized platforms and support an engagement decision. Processing must run on tactical computing hardware carried or emplaced with the force. Proposals should describe a pathway to interoperate with existing command and control. Conformance to a named standard is not required at this stage and will not be scored.

Mitigation and Defeat. Kinetic, non-kinetic, or cyber approaches that defeat hostile UAS in remote tactical theaters and in densely populated areas. Proposals must address collateral effects.

Operating preferences. The operating environment is denied, contested, and unattended. The four conditions below are preferences, not eligibility requirements.

Every proposal must state where it stands against each one.

(a) The system does not require the target to emit radio frequency (RF) energy. Passive RF may be part of a solution; the preference is that track holds when the target is silent.

(b) The system does not radiate. The Government favors kinetic and cyber defeat over approaches that require the friendly system to emit. Jamming, active illumination, and transmission into a target's control or navigation link are in scope. A proposal that uses any of them must say so and describe the operational effect.

(c) The system does not require cloud services or reachback. Training and analytics may occur off-platform. The processing that produces the operational output should run on the platform, and the system should continue to function with all external network interfaces disabled.

(d) The system does not require a dedicated operator, meaning no person whose only task is attending it. Human judgment over the use of force is expected and is not addressed by this preference.

Out of scope: work requiring classified access or a facility clearance at the time of award, and approaches that depend on cooperative identification, including Remote ID broadcast.

Phase I:
This topic solicits Direct-to-Phase-II (DP2) proposals only. Direct to Phase II proposers shall submit documentation showing that Phase I-equivalent feasibility has already been achieved outside the SBIR/STTR program. Adequate documentation is a written record of at least one test of the proposed approach stating the conditions under which the test was conducted, the dates, the target, threat, or surrogate used, the measured result, and how it was measured.Test data, technical reports, and third-party evaluation metrics are acceptable. A system design alone is not sufficient. A self-declared technology readiness level unsupported by a documented test is not sufficient.

As required by the DoW solicitation, the feasibility documented may not rest solely upon, or logically extend from, prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work; the proposing firm and/or the principal investigator must have substantially performed the work relied upon; and the firm must demonstrate ownership or licensure of the associated intellectual property prior to proposal submission.

Phase II:
Phase II is a major research and development effort. Performers refine the Phase I concept into an operational prototype that demonstrates real-world functionality. The primary deliverable is a functional system, software package, or physical prototype ready for test and evaluation in a militarily relevant or simulated field environment. The technology shall reach TRL 6 by the end of Phase II.

The period of performance is twelve months rather than the twenty-four the announcement allows. The intent is to move a demonstrated capability to a transition decision within one year. Proposals should be scoped to that schedule.

The Government may host a showcase about six months after award. Attendance is by invitation and is based on end user interest in the capability. It is not required of every performer. Performers shall provide operational evidence supporting a follow-on funding decision whether or not they are invited.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Commercial applications are those in which the equipment deploys with a team rather than being installed at a site: temporary airspace security for outdoor events, venues, and construction or energy sites; convoy, executive, and site-survey protection; wildfire, disaster, and critical infrastructure response; and mobile detection kits for law enforcement and allied partners. Detection, tracking, and identification technologies have a direct commercial market in these roles. Authority to mitigate or defeat unmanned aircraft in the United States is limited by statute to covered federal entities. A defeat-focused proposal is not expected to show a near-term domestic commercial market for that function.

Military applications include integration into point-defense systems for tactical units, forward operating bases, and naval vessel protection platforms, which may be funded via non-SBIR/STTR acquisition budgets.

References:
• Congressional Research Service. Department of Defense Counter Unmanned Aircraft Systems: Background and Issues for Congress. Report R48477. https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48477
• Statement of General Michael E. Kurilla, Commander, U.S. Central Command, before the Senate Armed Services Committee on the posture of U.S. Central Command, 10 June 2025.
• U.S. Department of Defense Counter-Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Strategy (2021). https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jan/07/2002561080/-1/-1/1/DEPARTMENT-OF-DEFENSE-COUNTER-SMALL-UNMANNED-AIRCRAFT-SYSTEMS-STRATEGY.PDF

title: Real-World Applications for Prototype ISAC Demonstrations (RAPID) Small Business
summary: Design, develop and demonstrate an innovative 5G/6Gdual-use Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) prototype that provides sensing capabilities without degrading communication performance.
description:
Objective:
Design, develop and demonstrate an innovative 5G/6Gdual-use Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) prototype that provides sensing capabilities without degrading communication performance.

Description:
The Department of War (DoW) seeks to accelerate U.S. leadership in Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC), a 5G-Advanced feasibility-study area and a key technology for 3GPP 6G specifications. This project addresses the challenge of adding sensing capabilities to communication networks without degrading the primary communication link across diverse missions and environments, from established bases to remote and contested areas. The goal is to develop innovative, dual-use ISAC prototypes that leverage existing cellular infrastructure including 5G, emerging Open RAN interfaces, and AI-native networking. These solutions should offer a smaller, more cost-effective footprint than separate radar and communication systems. The effort will focus on three pathways: ISAC on fixed infrastructure, ISAC on mobile platforms, and joint AI optimization of radio resources. Success of this project will reduce barriers to market entry, enable new ISAC and AI applications, and strengthen U.S. industrial competitiveness in a field receiving substantial investment from adversaries.

The following documents are incorporated as part of this topic.

• Appendix A - ISAC KPI Framework for RAPID
• RAPID Statement of Objectives (SOO)

Phase I:
This topic solicits Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) proposals only; Phase I proposals will not be accepted. Offerors must document that Phase I feasibility has already been established through prior work. Acceptable feasibility evidence includes results from prior research and development performed by the small business; prototype, breadboard, model, simulation, test, demonstration, or experimental results; analytical studies, calculations, trade studies, or modeling and simulation results; data demonstrating performance against relevant technical parameters; prior relevant contract, commercial, internal research, or customer-funded work performed by the small business; and/or peer-reviewed publications, technical reports, patents, or other supporting documentation directly relevant to the SBC’s approach. Existing research publications, analytical studies, simulation results, and prototype demonstrations have already established the technical feasibility of dual-use Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) systems leveraging commercial cellular infrastructure, including 5G and emerging 5G-Advanced capabilities. Industry-led standardization efforts, including ongoing ISAC work within 3GPP Release 19 and related 5G-Advanced studies, further validate the viability of the underlying concepts and technologies. As a result, the fundamental scientific and technical feasibility questions that would normally be addressed during a Phase I effort should have already been sufficiently demonstrated. The remaining challenges are focused on system integration, prototype development, performance optimization, and operational evaluation in representative environments.

Phase II:
Design, implement, and demonstrate a prototype that has potential for both military and commercial use. The prototype, whether technology, product, or service—must meet the topic objectives (Attachment 1 and Appendix A) and account for both commercial and military deployment requirements.

Prototypes shall be demonstrated in the context of military and civilian scenarios such as non-RF emitting objects, Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) detection, vehicle detection, or biometrics. The prototype should support Open-RAN interfaces (e.g., 7.2x functional split, E2 Service Model and so on) and the prototype shall be integrated or interoperable with the Open Centralized Unit/Distributed Unit (OCUDU) software baseline, as published by the Linux Foundation where applicable. The design architecture shall utilize "Secure by Design" principles and align with the Department of War's (DoW) Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) framework.

Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) Refer to Appendix A - ISAC KPI Framework for RAPID for complete details.

Offerors, at a minimum, shall propose the below set of deliverables:

1. Program Kickoff- Format to be provided

2. Monthly Status Report- Format to be provided

3. Quarterly Technical Review- Format to be provided

4. Demonstration and Demonstration Report

5. Key Performance Indicators

6. Final implementation of the Phase 2 demonstrations

Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) Refer to Appendix A - ISAC KPI Framework for RAPID for complete details.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Smart transportation and connected infrastructure: The firm may commercialize ISAC-enabled 5G-Advanced and future 6G network products for transportation agencies, roadway operators, ports, rail systems, airports, logistics centers, and smart-city providers. These capabilities could support collision warnings, intersection safety, autonomous-vehicle infrastructure, traffic-flow optimization, perimeter monitoring, and all-weather situational awareness.

Industrial, warehouse, and critical-infrastructure monitoring:

Private 5G networks deployed in manufacturing plants, warehouses, energy facilities, mining operations, and distribution centers could use ISAC to combine reliable wireless connectivity with passive sensing. This approach could reduce the cost, complexity, and maintenance burden associated with deploying separate radar, camera, and communications systems.

Public safety, disaster response, and search-and-rescue:

ISAC-enabled portable or fixed 5G infrastructure could support first responders operating during natural disasters, infrastructure failures, and mass-casualty events. Communications nodes could simultaneously restore broadband connectivity and assist with locating vehicles, personnel, or survivors in degraded-visibility environments. Commercial transition opportunities may include emergency communications providers, public-safety agencies, temporary-network vendors, and telecommunications equipment manufacturers.

Installation protection and counter-unmanned aircraft system support:

The firm may transition ISAC technology to fixed military installations, expeditionary bases, depots, airfields, ports, and other critical sites. Existing or deployed cellular and tactical-network infrastructure could be used as a distributed sensing layer to detect, localize, and track non-RF-emitting objects, including small, unmanned aircraft systems, ground vehicles, and personnel.

Tactical edge sensing for distributed and contested operations:

Mobile ISAC solutions may support mounted and dismounted formations, unmanned systems, tactical communications relays, and mobile command posts operating where Global Positioning System access, dedicated radar coverage, or reliable backhaul is degraded or unavailable. A mobile platform could maintain command-and-control or data-backhaul connectivity while using the same radio hardware and waveforms to identify obstacles, map local terrain, detect moving objects, and support route awareness. This would reduce the need to carry, power, protect, and sustain separate sensing systems.

• 3GPP TS 22.137, 5G; Integrated Sensing and Communication.
• 3GPP TR 22.837, Feasibility Study on Integrated Sensing and Communication.
• 3GPP TR 38.901, Study on Channel Model for Frequencies from 0.5 to 100 GHz.
• 3GPP TS 33.501, Security Architecture and Procedures for 5G System.
• NIST, 6G Communications Roadmap.
• Ropitault et al. (NIST), Characterization of Monostatic Base Stations Sensing Resolution Using 5G Reference Signals.

title: Resilient Tactical Edge Networks
summary: The objective of this Phase II effort is to design, validate, and demonstrate a fully open-source, private 5G network platform for Resilient Tactical Edge Networks—integrating OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC components—to provide highly reliable, cost-effective, and scalable wide-area connectivity for autonomous field equipment, precision crop intelligence, and livestock monitoring.
description:
Objective:
The objective of this Phase II effort is to design, validate, and demonstrate a fully open-source, private 5G network platform for Resilient Tactical Edge Networks—integrating OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC components—to provide highly reliable, cost-effective, and scalable wide-area connectivity for autonomous field equipment, precision crop intelligence, and livestock monitoring. This platform will be validated at a representative rural site against specific key performance metrics, establishing a secure, interoperable, and procurement-ready reference architecture that supports both commercial precision agriculture and dual-use DoW mission-support applications.

Description:
The realistic near-to-mid-term serviceable addressable market for private 5G in U.S. agriculture is the subset with real mobility, coverage, reliability, or data-volume pain: row-crop operations running GPS-guided and autonomous equipment, specialty-crop growers using machine vision and agricultural robotics, dairies and feedlots with dense livestock-monitoring deployments, irrigated operations with distributed pump and center-pivot control, and large ranches requiring wide-area coverage for animal and asset tracking. The scale of the opportunity is well documented. USDA Economic Research Service data show about 1.88 million farms in 2024 (roughly 39% of all U.S. land). Only 79% of farms reported internet access of any kind, leaving roughly one in five farms without even basic connectivity. There is also documented evidence that productivity of farms with connectivity is significantly higher than the ones without any connectivity. Furthermore, FCC data show that 39% of rural Americans lack access to minimum fixed broadband speeds, compared with 4% of urban Americans, and coverage on cropland and rangeland specifically is worse still. Public carrier networks will not close this gap on their own; carrier tower economics favor population density, and most agricultural land has almost none.

This segment buys on measurable operational outcomes (machine uptime, yield per acre, input cost per acre, water use, herd health, labor hours saved), not on global platform standardization, and its stated barriers to adoption are consistent and compounding: ROI ambiguity, high capex against tight and cyclical farm margins, no in-house RF/cellular or IT staff, harsh outdoor operating environments, a fragmented device ecosystem spanning tractors, drones, sensors, and wearables, and coverage requirements measured in thousands of acres rather than thousands of square feet. A proprietary private 5G platform from a tier-one vendor addresses almost none of these barriers directly; it is priced and supported for industrial campuses and multi-site enterprise accounts, not a single farm with a handful of mission-critical connectivity problems to solve.

An all-open-source stack removes the structural cost and lock-in that makes proprietary platforms a poor fit for this segment. Because OCUDU's O-CU/O-DU communicate with the rest of the network over open, standardized interfaces (especially the O-RAN 7.2x split to the O-RU), the network can be assembled from whichever RU vendor best fits a given operation's coverage geometry and budget, including high-power CBRS Category B radios and high-gain sector antennas mounted on existing farm infrastructure (grain legs, silos, center-pivot towers, farmstead masts) to maximize covered acres per radio. Together, OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC form one integrated, fully open-source 5G stack that a regional systems integrator, agricultural equipment dealer, rural wireless ISP, or electric/telephone cooperative can deploy, support, and price as a right-sized, as-a-service offer for a single operation, instead of selling a broad, vendor-locked platform. That directly answers this market's stated preference for outcome-first, economically flexible offers, and it supports a coexistence posture (private 5G for mobility, coverage, and uplink-intensive problems; existing farmstead Wi-Fi and LPWAN sensors where they already work) rather than a rip-and-replace sale.

The trade-off of an all-open-source stack is that the burden of proving interoperability, stability, and security shifts from a single vendor's warranty to the integrator and the open-source community itself. Agricultural buyers, who by their own account lack in-house cellular and cybersecurity expertise, have little tolerance for integration failures discovered mid-season, when planting, spraying, irrigation, and harvest windows cannot be rescheduled. This is exactly the gap the on-going OCUDU Testing & Validation Plan, and its Radio Access Network (RAN) Testing and Evaluation Center (RTEC)-centered extensions, are designed to close: independently witnessed, multi-vendor testing of device diversity, RU diversity, long-range outdoor RF performance, Core/RIC/SMO integration, and security. The proposal should leverage the current, on-going testing and evaluation activities in RTECs and associated results on this front.

Although this topic is anchored in a specific vertical to ensure a concrete deployment environment, real users, and a defensible commercialization path, proposers should recognize and are required to present the technical work in terms of the generic network performance classes it advances. Improvements made to the OCUDU O-CU/O-DU under this effort (scheduler behavior, mobility management, uplink capacity, stability under sustained load, security features) are expected to generalize across verticals and to benefit the broader community of RAN developers building on OCUDU. The Technical Volume shall include a mapping of each selected use case, and its associated Section 3.0 KPMs, to the performance class or classes it exercises, and shall identify which anticipated OCUDU code or feature enhancements correspond to each class.

For this topic, the dominant performance classes are massive scale and wide-area coverage: maximizing covered acres per radio using high-power CBRS Category B configurations, supporting large, sparse populations of low-rate sensor devices alongside high-uplink mobile equipment, and maintaining session continuity across long-range outdoor propagation conditions, with an evolution path to NTN integration.

Research and development for this effort should address, at minimum, the following questions:

• All-Open-Source Economics: What is the fully loaded cost (integration, support, spectrum, hardware, mounting infrastructure, and backhaul) of an OCUDU + SD-Core + SD-RAN + OSC deployment at farm scale relative to carrier coverage extensions and proprietary private-network platforms, and how should that be packaged as a CBRS-based, as-a-service offer within the price point agricultural buyers require ($75,000-$200,000 for a reference deployment covering approximately 2,000 acres)?

• Last-Acre Coverage Economics: What combination of high-power CBRS Category B radios, high-gain sector antennas, existing vertical assets (grain legs, silos, pivot towers), and backhaul options (fiber where available, fixed wireless, or satellite/NTN) maximizes reliably covered acres per dollar, and how does the open RU ecosystem enabled by the O-RAN 7.2x split change that optimization relative to a single bundled radio line?

• Use-Case-First Automation: Which of the use cases defined below deliver the fastest, most measurable ROI on the open-source stack, and what RTEC-executed interoperability tests (Device, RU, Core, RIC/SMO, and Infrastructure dimensions) are needed to validate each one end-to-end under realistic seasonal, weather, and terrain conditions?

• Trust in Open Source: How does RTEC-executed testing of the full open-source stack (not just OCUDU) reduce the integration risk and skills-shortage barrier that agricultural buyers most often cite, and what evidence package best converts community-maintained, no-license-fee software into a procurement-ready proof point for a buyer with no in-house cellular expertise?

Solutions leveraging super intelligence (SI) and machine learning (ML) for variable-rate input optimization, crop and livestock analytics, predictive equipment maintenance, network optimization, or automated fault resolution are encouraged but not required. DoW will consider any novel concept that increases the reliability, economics, and trustworthiness of an all-open-source private 5G/FutureG platform for the resilient tactical edge networks. Dual-use opportunities are expected across commercial agricultural operations, DoW installation land- and range-management, perimeter and agricultural-buffer operations on DoW installations, expeditionary logistics over large unimproved areas, and food-supply-chain resilience as a national-security concern.

Proposers should address at least two of the following four use cases in their Phase II Statement of Work, and must identify which use case(s) their reference architecture and pilot deployment are designed to validate. Each use case below is defined in terms of the operational scenario it supports, the connectivity requirement it places on the platform, and the corresponding KPM table in Section 3.0. Because agricultural traffic spans extremes (from low-throughput, high-device-count telemetry such as soil sensors, livestock wearables, and irrigation command-and-control, to high-throughput, latency-sensitive streams such as UAS (unmanned Aircraft System) imagery backhaul, machine vision, and equipment teleoperation video) proposers are strongly encouraged to employ 5G network slicing to serve these disparate service classes simultaneously on the same physical network. Proposals that demonstrate slice-based traffic isolation and per-slice quality-of-service enforcement, with at least one low-throughput and one high-throughput use case operating concurrently on separate slices of a single deployment, will be viewed favorably. Device-Class Diversity and 5G RedCap. Each use-case set spans device classes from full-capability UEs (equipment modems, cameras, broadcast and production units) to reduced-capability IoT endpoints (sensors, wearables, tags, and trackers). Proposers shall address how the platform serves reduced-capability device classes, including 3GPP Release 17 Reduced Capability (RedCap) and Release 18 eRedCap UEs, and shall identify any OCUDU scheduler or feature enhancements required to support RedCap operation; such enhancements are strongly encouraged as upstream contributions under the common OCUDU benchmarking and enhancement work package. Where RedCap-certified devices are not commercially available for a given endpoint type at demonstration time, proposers may demonstrate with available device classes (or emulated RedCap UE profiles) and shall document the RedCap migration path.Use Case 1: Autonomous & Semi-Autonomous Field Equipment Connectivity

GPS-guided and autonomous tractors, sprayers, harvesters, and field robots move continuously across fields, along farm roads between fields, and in and out of farmstead staging areas, requiring an uninterrupted control-plane, telemetry, and remote-supervision connection as they roam. Fully autonomous equipment cannot legally or safely operate without a live, low-latency link for remote monitoring and emergency stops, and farms without high-speed coverage cannot use it at all. So, this use case requires the platform to sustain low-latency, high-reliability connectivity and seamless handover as equipment moves between cells across the full field footprint, including possible road transit between non-contiguous parcels.

Use Case 2: Aerial & Fixed Crop Intelligence Backhaul

Drones/UAS performing scouting, mapping, and spot-spraying missions, machine-vision cameras on harvesters and sorting lines, and dense fields of soil-moisture, weather, and plant-health sensors generate continuous, uplink-heavy data streams that must reach an on-farm edge analytics system or agronomy platform with low delay to support same-pass and same-day decisions on irrigation, fertility, and pest control. This use case requires the platform to sustain high uplink throughput with low jitter for multiple simultaneous UAS and camera streams while concurrently aggregating telemetry from thousands of low-rate sensors per cell.

Use Case 3: Livestock Monitoring & Ranch Operations

Cattle, dairy, and other livestock operations increasingly rely on connected ear tags, collars, rumen boluses, and virtual-fencing systems that must reliably reach a monitoring platform to detect health events (calving, lameness, illness), enforce virtual fence boundaries, and locate animals across grazing land that public carrier networks do not cover. This use case requires the platform to sustain consistent, wide-area, low-rate coverage for high device counts across pasture and confinement areas, with low-latency alerting for time-critical animal-health and containment events.

Use Case 4: Connected Farmstead, Irrigation & Grain Operations

The equipment that keeps a farm running is scattered across the farmstead and the fields around it: center-pivot irrigation systems, pump stations, grain dryers and grain-handling equipment, security cameras, and safety devices such as lone-worker monitors and confined-space alarms for grain bins. The cost of a lost connection is high: a stalled pivot or failed pump during peak heat can cost yield within days, an unmonitored grain dryer is a fire risk, and a missed confined-space alarm at a grain bin can cost a life. Yet most of this equipment sits beyond the reach of farmstead Wi-Fi, leaving operators dependent on unlicensed, best-effort wireless links that were never designed for critical operations. This use case requires the platform to close that gap by extending secure, private coverage from the farmstead to all surrounding equipment on the same OCUDU-based network, delivering (1) reliable, low-data-rate command-and-control for irrigation and grain equipment, and (2) continuous uplink capacity for security video and worker-safety alerts.

Phase I:
This topic is accepting Direct to Phase II proposals ONLY. Therefore, a formal Phase I award will not be issued.

To qualify for a Phase II award, proposers must submit Feasibility Documentation (as part of their proposal package) demonstrating that they have already completed "Phase I-type" research and development. The purpose of this documentation is to prove that the underlying technology is mature, scientifically sound, and ready to transition immediately into the Phase II prototyping and testing environment.

The Government will accept a wide variety of documentation styles. Proposers do not need to have a perfect, finished product, but they must show that their core ideas have been successfully tested. One or more of the following items should be included to prove technology readiness:

• Test Data & Metrics: Real-world measurements, performance charts, or network test data from previous lab environments or early field trials.
• Technical Reports & White Papers: Written summaries explaining your previous research, system designs, or software integration efforts.
• Prototype Designs & Simulation Models: Diagrams, architectural blueprints, or computer simulation results showing how your proposed software and hardware components interact.
• Previous Project Outcomes: Success criteria, milestone reports, or commercialization results from prior private, academic, or non-SBIR federally funded work.

Phase II:
The desired end product of this Phase II effort is a working prototype Minimum Viable Product (MVP) of a fully open-source private 5G network deployed and validated in a relevant agricultural environment. Proposers must design, integrate, and test a reference architecture consisting of OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC that successfully addresses at least two of the agricultural Use Cases defined in the Description section. The final product must demonstrate measurable interoperability, scalability, and security under realistic rural outdoor propagation conditions.

Key Performance Metrics (KPMs) & Testing:

Proposers shall propose specific, justified KPM targets in their Technical Volume, calibrated to their selected use cases, demonstration environment, and spectrum plan. Required KPMs include session success rate, handover success rate, latency, jitter, coverage completeness, and service availability (e.g., sustaining a >99.5% session success rate for autonomous equipment handing over between 3 cells at 15 mph).

• Latency Measurement: Latency KPMs denote round-trip application-layer latency measured between the User Equipment (UE) application interface and the local edge application endpoint. Handover time denotes user-plane interruption time at the RAN.
• Target Values: Threshold values represent the intended standard of Phase II demonstration success; Objective values are stretch goals. Final KPM targets will be finalized at kickoff and confirmed at the Critical Design Review (CDR).

Prototype Demonstration Environment:

Demonstrations must be performed at a rural site secured by the proposer. Acceptable sites, in order of preference, are: (1) an operating farm or ranch; (2) an agricultural research/extension facility; or (3) a representative outdoor rural environment of comparable scale. If a non-agricultural site is used, the proposer must document the differences and account for effects like crop-canopy attenuation via link-budget margins. The mobility and coverage KPMs must be validated using physical instrumented vehicles moving across fields/roads at operational speeds, using real radio signals.

OCUDU and Open-Source Integration:

Proposers must integrate the stack with no proprietary core, RIC, or SMO components. The MVP demonstration must utilize physical Radio Units (RUs) and UEs (e.g., equipment modems, UAS, sensors, or wearables). Performers must address backhaul diversity (fiber, fixed wireless, satellite/NTN) and scalability across multiple RU vendors, including high-power CBRS Category B options.

Security Requirements:

Security must be a first-class design requirement. The architecture must cover 3GPP security (TS 33.501), O-RAN open interface protection (WG11), zero-trust principles (NIST SP 800-207), and CVE monitoring. The MVP demonstration must include at least one security capability shown live (e.g., rejection of an unauthorized device or encrypted fronthaul).

Schedule and Milestones (18-Month Period of Performance):

• Month 1: Kickoff and Technical Interchange Meeting (TIM)
• Monthly: Status Reports (MSRs) presented to the sponsor and the OCUDU T&E Working Group
• Month 10: Critical Design Review (CDR)
• Month 14: Final design review, demonstration, and assessment
• Month 16: Prototype MVP demonstration
• Month 18: Final Phase II Report

Phase II Deliverables:

• Kickoff and TIM presentation materials.
• Monthly Status Reports (MSRs).
• Critical Design Document (detailing the full reference architecture and coverage/backhaul design).
• Documented Key Performance Metrics (KPM) targets and testing methodology.
• MVP Demonstration Package (slides, documentation of site fidelity, and KPM results).
• Reference Configuration Package (executables, integration documentation, and RTEC test results).
• Live prototype integration into an RTEC-affiliated test network or farm-representative site.
• Final Design Document.
• Final Technical Report.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The Resilient Tactical Edge Networks platform, built on an open-source private 5G network, offers significant dual-use capabilities for both commercial and Department of War (DoW) applications. Commercial Use: The primary commercial application is to provide reliable, high-speed connectivity to farms and ranches, which are currently underserved by traditional networks. This enables the use of precision agriculture technologies such as autonomous equipment, aerial crop monitoring, and dense sensor deployments for livestock and irrigation management. The goal is to increase farm productivity, improve operational efficiency, and provide a clear return on investment for commercial agricultural operations.

Department of War (DoW) Use: The same technology can be leveraged for various defense and national security purposes. Expected applications include managing land and ranges on DoW installations, monitoring perimeters and agricultural buffer zones, supporting expeditionary logistics over large and unimproved areas, and bolstering food supply-chain resilience, which is a key national security concern.

In essence, the technology developed for enhancing commercial farm operations can be directly adapted to meet the DoW's needs for robust, private communication networks in diverse and challenging environments.

References:
• https://www.juniper.net/us/en/solutions/solution-briefs/2025/gain-the-advantage-with-5g-tactical-edge.html

title: Robust and resilient optical modulators for extreme environment applications
summary: The objective of this project is to develop and demonstrate Epsilon-Near-Zero (ENZ)-based optical modulating devices that can be resilient/robust to extreme environments such as high temperatures and strong UV irradiation.
description:
Objective:
The objective of this project is to develop and demonstrate Epsilon-Near-Zero (ENZ)-based optical modulating devices that can be resilient/robust to extreme environments such as high temperatures and strong UV irradiation.

Description:
This topic solicits new ENZ based optical modulators that can be manufactured by new approaches to improve the techniques explored in the past. If a new material (or approach) is proposed, it would be useful if the proposers discussed why this new material (or approach) is promising. Offerors must address the high temperature stability and durability of ENZ materials in air under either high temperature (up to 800C) and demonstrate ENZ-based modulation device structures, such as metal-insulator-metal or waveguide structure, at MWIR regime. Furthermore, the proposers must address optical light modulation by utilizing electrical or optical tuning, and demonstrate ultrafast switching capability with high-speed, power efficient, and compact optical modulator designs. The successful team will design and demonstrate proof-of-concept devices under high temperatures.

Phase I:
Phase I seeks complete characterization data of new ENZ material that can be used in extreme environments such as high temperatures and high UV laser irradiation with an ultrafast optical modulation in the MWIR window (3-5 um). Offerors must address the high temperature stability and durability of ENZ materials in air under either high temperature (up to 800C) or intense laser irradiation up to 10 MWcm-2 and demonstrate ENZ-based modulation device structures, such as metal-insulator-metal or waveguide structure, at MWIR regime. If this Phase I is successful, plan to manufacture ENZ-based optical modulators operatable in the near-IR to mid-IR windows in this extreme environment. Documentation may comprise technical reports, peer-reviewed publications, measured data, and design artifacts sufficient to substantiate the scientific, technical, and commercial merit required to enter Phase II.

Phase II:
Awardee(s) will develop, fabricate, and demonstrate a robust and resilient optical modulator based on ENZ material for improved image processing, refining system requirements in coordination with the topic’s principal investigator. The effort will include: electro-optic phase and amplitude modulation in single device in ENZ material-based waveguide structure at MWIR; optical field confinement effect occurring in near ENZ wavelength that can be tuned by electrically or optically. Key metrics include throughput, low optical losses, low operating voltages, bandwidth, and robustness to high temperatures and laser irradiations.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Energy-efficient, ultrafast, and compact devices of this type have broad defense and commercial applications. Military uses include compact thermal-imaging systems, RF-independent communication, payload, and deployable platforms where SWaP-C reduction is critical. Commercial applications include high temperature energy harvesting systems, ultrafast switching modulators, and all-optical switching devices. Devices meeting the desired criteria would provide a considerable improvement over existing solutions and find widespread application in these areas.

References:
• M. Shabaninezhad, H. Mehrvar, E. Bernier, L. Ramunno, and P. Berini, "Plasmonic electro-optic modulators based on epsilon-near-zero materials: comparing the classical drift-diffusion and Schrödinger-Poisson coupling models," Opt. Express 33, 4474-4490 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1364/OE.544216
• A. Jahid et al, “A contemporary survey on free space optical communication: Potentials, technical challenges, recent advances and research direction, Journal of Network and Computer Applications 200, (2022) 103311. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnca.2021.103311.
• H. Jiang et al, “Broad-Band Ultrafast All-Optical Switching Based on Enhanced Nonlinear Absorption in Corrugated Indium Tin Oxide Films,” ACS Nano 16, 12878 (2022). https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.2c05139

title: Wafer-scale low-loss hyperbolic optical material
summary: The overall goal of the R&D effort is to develop wafer-scale, fabrication-ready thin films of a low-loss naturally hyperbolic optical material that operates across the visible to telecommunication wavelength range. Films should be of high optical and crystalline quality, with controlled thickness and orientation, on substrates at least one inch in cross-sectional diameter.
description:
Objective:
The overall goal of the R&D effort is to develop wafer-scale, fabrication-ready thin films of a low-loss naturally hyperbolic optical material that operates across the visible to telecommunication wavelength range. Films should be of high optical and crystalline quality, with controlled thickness and orientation, on substrates at least one inch in cross-sectional diameter.

Description:
Conventional optical systems are limited by diffraction, which sets the smallest features they can pattern, image, or confine to roughly the wavelength of the light used. A class of strongly anisotropic, or "hyperbolic," optical materials can confine and route light far below this limit, enabling a family of compact, low size-weight-and-power photonic components of direct interest to OUSW (R&E). Hyperbolic behavior has historically been realized in artificial metamaterials, which are optically lossy, and difficult to fabricate and scale. Certain naturally occurring crystals exhibit the same behavior with far lower loss, but the available examples operate only in the infrared and have been produced only as small, research-grade crystals by batch methods incompatible with standard microfabrication. There is presently no commercial source of wafer-scale, low-loss hyperbolic material that operates at visible and telecommunication wavelengths in a form compatible with standard semiconductor fabrication, and it is important for the Air Force to establish a domestic supply source for such a material.

Phase I:
Establish the feasibility of producing the hyperbolic material as wafer-scale, device-grade thin films with the required optical quality and crystalline orientation across the target wavelength range. Characterize and/or predict the optical performance of the films and benchmark it against existing artificial metamaterial approaches. Identify a viable approach for lithographically patterning and integrating the material.

As a Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) effort, the work must be performed in partnership with a research institution; a partner with established expertise in optical measurement of hyperbolic materials is encouraged. Deliverables include a feasibility assessment with supporting analysis and/or preliminary data, quantitative performance projections, and a detailed Phase II plan. Documentation may comprise technical reports, peer-reviewed publications, measured data, and design artifacts sufficient to substantiate the scientific, technical, and commercial merit required to enter Phase II.

Phase II:
Deliver wafer-scale films/wafers (at least one inch in cross-section, with a demonstrated path to larger wafers) of the low-loss hyperbolic material, with controlled thickness, orientation, and uniformity, reproducibly and with reasonable yield. Demonstrate lithographic patterning and integration of the material. Provide quantitative performance data benchmarked against incumbent approaches, together with a manufacturing-readiness and transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The awardee will pursue commercialization of the technologies developed in Phase II, transitioning expanded capability to government and civilian users to microelectronics fabrication and inspection, compact optics and photonics, and/or quantum light sources. Direct access to end-users and government customers will be provided, with opportunities for Phase III awards for additional research and development or direct procurement of the products and services developed in coordination with the program. Phase III efforts are intended to transition technologies developed with further scaling of performance metrics for dual use applications into operational use and/or commercial markets, leveraging non-SBIR/STTR funding. Phase III work may include productization, integration, certification, and large-scale deployment of the capability developed in Phases I and II. By effectively executing Phase III effort and transitioning the technology into operational and commercial use, the project aims to maximize the impact and value of the STTR-funded R&D efforts, ultimately contributing to national security, economic growth, and technological innovation. A design for performance approach for defense system in partnership with a defense contractor and a design for cost for commercial applications will be planned.

References:
• A. Poddubny, I. Iorsh, P. Belov, Y. Kivshar, "Hyperbolic metamaterials," Nature Photonics 7, 948–957 (2013).
• C. Liu, T. Liu, Z. Zhang, Z. Sun, G. Zhang, E. Wang, K. Liu, "Understanding epitaxial growth of two-dimensional materials and their homostructures," Nature Nanotechnology 19, 907–918 (2024).
